News.title: Bayeux Tapestry tickets: where is famous historic artwork being shown – and how to see it
News.content:
ONE OF the world’s most famous historical treasures has hit the road, offering history fans a chance to see a 1,000-year-old masterpiece up close.

The legendary Bayeux Tapestry is making headlines as the crown jewel of a major new exhibition at the British Museum in London.



Visitors can see the continuous embroidery laid flat in a specially designed glass display case for the very first time.

At its usual home in France, the medieval artefact is traditionally displayed mounted vertically along the walls.



Marking the artwork’s first return to British soil in nearly 10 centuries, the exhibition runs from September 10, 2026 until July 11, 2027.

The tapestry made its historic cross-Channel journey after its permanent home, the Musee de la Tapisserie in Bayeux, Normandy, closed for a multi-year renovation set to wrap up in late 2027.

What is the Bayeux Tapestry?

Despite its famous name, the Bayeux Tapestry isn’t technically a tapestry – it’s a hand-embroidered linen cloth stitched with vibrant wool threads.

At 68 metres long, it spans nearly the length of three basketball courts while standing just under two feet tall, and acts as something of a medieval graphic novel.

Across 58 panels, it tells the story of the 1066 Norman Conquest of England, tracking the fierce rivalry between Harold Godwinson, the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, and William, Duke of Normandy.

The story reaches a bloody climax at the Battle of Hastings, depicting charging warhorses, armoured knights, clashing shields, and King Harold’s downfall.



Along the top and bottom edges, decorative borders feature detailed depictions of farming life, fables, and mythical beasts.

Who made the Bayeux Tapestry?

While the narrative celebrates a French conquest, the physical masterpiece was almost certainly crafted in England.

Historians agree the embroidery was commissioned around 1070 – 1077 by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, the ambitious half-brother of William the Conqueror.

Odo hired highly skilled Anglo-Saxon embroiderers – likely working in Canterbury – who were renowned across Europe for their fine needlework.

Once completed, Bishop Odo took the masterpiece across the English Channel to Normandy to display in his newly built Bayeux Cathedral.



The tapestry remained in Normandy for centuries, first recorded in a cathedral inventory in 1476.

Over the ages, it miraculously survived multiple near-disasters, including the French Revolution, when local citizens saved it from being torn apart to cover military wagons.

Napoleon later took it to Paris to rally public support for a planned invasion of Britain, and it was hidden away from Nazi forces during World War II.

France has carefully preserved the national treasure ever since, housing it in Bayeux until this historic loan brought it back to British shores.

How much are Bayeux Tapestry tickets?

While general entrance to the British Museum is free, the Bayeux Tapestry loan is a paid, timed-entry exhibition.



Peak adult tickets start at £33, though several discounted tiers and free entry options are available depending on when you visit.

All ticket prices can optionally include a small voluntary donation toward museum preservation (raising a peak adult ticket to £36.50).

Under-16s are granted free entry because the 1066 Norman Conquest forms a key part of the national school curriculum – though they still require a pre-booked ticket.

How to get Bayeux Tapestry tickets

Demand for tickets has been high, with initial opening dates selling out in just 24 hours.

Tickets are only being sold online through the official British Museum ticket portal, so you’ll need to head there if you want to snag a spot.



Additional allocations are being released in staggered waves, with the next batch of tickets for January through March visits dropping in October.

That will be followed by a final release in January for April through July slots.



Book weekday slots early in the morning or take advantage of extended evening hours on Fridays for the best chance at beating the crowds.

Is there a copy in Reading?

If you’re not able to secure tickets to the British Museum’s display, there is a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry at Reading Museum.



Created in the 1880s by 35 skilled women from the Leek Embroidery Society, the hand-stitched copy was made so Britain could have a version of its own.

Displayed in its entirety inside the museum’s dedicated Bayeux Gallery, the Reading replica captures the medieval story stitch-for-stitch, but with a few famous Victorian tweaks.

Perhaps most famously, the embroiderers added small pairs of shorts to cover up the original’s naked figures.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Located roughly 30 minutes by train from London Paddington, Reading Museum offers general admission to see the replica.

Crucially, though it’s not the real deal, you don’t need to book tickets or pay an entry fee to view Reading Museum’s replica – the museum suggests a £5 donation.

News.title: UK asylum appeals backlog skyrockets to record over 90,000 – 17 TIMES higher than six years ago
News.content:
THE UK asylum appeals backlog has skyrocketed to a record high of more than 90,000 – and is now over 17 times higher than it was six years ago.

Andy Burnham‘s government has been blasted amid the spiralling crisis, with claims ballooning by more than half in the space of a year.



The number has now topped 90,000 for the first time, according to figures released by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ).

There were 90,341 cases in the system by the end of June, dwarfing the 59,925 figure recorded at the same time last year.



And it is incredibly 17 times larger than the 5,209 claims in June 2020.

The huge increase in cases waiting to be heard by immigration judges comes after Labour’s push to quicken initial decisions on asylum claims.

Data released last month by the Home Office showed the number of people waiting for an initial decision is at its lowest level since 2019.

The total has more than halved in the space of a year, falling from 90,812 in June 2025 to 40,168 in June 2026.

But the move – designed to clear cases from the Home Office – has instead pushed the backlog onto the courts.

It has led to a growing number of claimants going to tribunals and appealing against the initial decision in a bid to have it overturned.



The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) say the Home Office has focused on short-term fixes and does not have a clear strategy.

It has also called for a “complete overhaul” of the system for monitoring those facing removal.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy accused Labour of making courts a “holding pen” for immigration.

He told MailOnline: “Sadly, Labour will never tackle the lawfare holding this country back.

“The Conservatives would scrap the immigration tribunal and restore control over our border to elected ministers.



“We also need to look more widely at how courts act as a block on the functioning of government.”

The latest MoJ figures also show more than a third of asylum appeals were successful between April and June this year.

And the average waiting time to clear an asylum appeal was 72 weeks, up from 67 weeks in January-March.

An asylum appeal case can refer to one person or to a group of people – typically a main applicant and their family members.

The Home Office has been approached for comment.



Earlier this year, we revealed how four in five asylum decisions were made with insufficient evidence.

An internal quality check of 47 random calls by Home Office staff, from August and September 2025, revealed 37 were “likely to be incorrect”.

Independent border inspection chief John Tuckett said: “Although this was only one limited exercise… these results suggested that the quality of asylum decision-making was not in a good state.”

And inspectors warned managers had prioritised “quantity over quality”.

A huge 83 per cent of staff told an internal survey they were pressured to make decisions quickly to reduce waiting times.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Home Office said: “This is from a small sample of 47 cases.

“Our assessment of nearly 4,000 cases shows 94 per cent of decisions are considered ‘correct’ against agreed criteria.”

News.title: World’s biggest dog festival is taking over iconic English lido this weekend with 16,000 pups
News.content:
THE world’s biggest dog swim event is set to kick off in the UK in just two days’ time – and will bring four weekends of four-legged fun.

This year marks the event’s 10-year anniversary.



The paw-fect event for furry friends is set to come to Saltdean Lido this Saturday, with the start of the biggest dog swimming event in the world – Dogtember.

Set across four weekends starting from September 12 and 13 until October 3 and 4, pets will be able to run, splash, and swim to their hearts’ delight at the iconic Art Deco location.



Drawing in more than 16,000 dogs last year, the Lido’s heated 40m pool will host four 90-minute sessions and one quiet session each day.

All sessions are open to any breed of dog, however there are a number of Small Dogs and Large Dogs sessions running throughout the day if your pet prefers to be among similar-sized companions.



Owners will be able to swim alongside their pups, or can choose to simply let their pooch do all the work with the purchase of a spectator ticket.

Able to accommodate 500 bathers at one time, the event will also feature a number of stalls filled with goodies to treat your canine companion.

This year also marks its 10-year anniversary, with last year’s festival proving to be a sell-out event.

Created in partnership with pet insurance Petgevity, the annual occasion helps promote swimming as an effective, non-weight bearing exercise for dogs.



It also seeks to raise funds for the restoration and upkeep of the historic 88-year-old lido, located just minutes away from Brighton.

Tickets can be purchased online via the Saltdean Lido website, which are priced at £14.85 for a Dog Swim and Human Swim ticket, and £6.40 for a Spectator pass.

News.title: Popular baby gadget sold in John Lewis and Boots is urgently recalled over fears it will burst into flames
News.content:
A POPULAR baby gadget sold in John Lewis and Boots has been urgently recalled over a serious fire risk.

Anyone who has bought the product has been urged to stop using it immediately and to unplug it from chargers.



Popular retailers have issued an urgent recall for batches of the Love to Dream Sleep Machines due to its lithium-ion battery presenting a severe overheating hazard.

When the machine was charged using third-party devices, it was found to overheat to the extent of creating a fire hazard, creating a risk of severe burns and property damage.



As a result, machines sold between January 2, 2025 and September 3, 2026, and displaying the codes 7T12TN, 7W15TN and 8P01TN, have been recalled from end users by the manufacturers.

The affected batches have also been pulled in a number of major retailers, including Boots, Harrods, John Lewis and Partners, Currys and Mamas & Papas.



Love to Dream’s Sleep Machine is described as a portable white noise sound machine with a night light, catered to parents hoping to help their babies develop healthy sleeping habits.

Retailing for £45 in Boots, the machine is part of the brand’s larger range of sleep products for babies, toddlers and children, including babygrows, swaddles and pyjamas.

Love to Dream has urged buyers to stop using the machine immediately, unplug it from any charger and store it away from anything flammable.

Then, customers should see if the ‘date code’, displayed on the side of the unit or on the box, matches the affected batches.



If your machine is impacted, use a permanent marker to write ‘RECALLED’ and today’s date on the side – then, take a photo of the whole unit and the date code.

Once these steps are followed and the images are sent to Love to Dream, the brand will either give you a full refund, a free replacement Sleep Machine, or a store credit.

After this, customers have been advised to dispose of the machine in line with local requirements for electricals containing batteries, and to not put it in a bin at home.



Love to Dream has reminded buyers that any products that do not include the specific date code are not impacted by this recall, and are safe to use.

News.title: Will the Europe heatwave bring hot weather to the UK? Latest Met Office forecast for September 2026
News.content:
BRITS hoping the scorching temperatures seen across parts of Europe will make their way to the UK may be left disappointed.

Spain has already seen the mercury soar above 45C this month, while southern France has experienced temperatures topping 40C.



But the latest Met Office forecast points to much more typical early-autumn weather in Britain.

It comes after an exceptionally hot and dry July, which contributed to drought conditions in almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales.



August was also warmer than average across the UK, and drier than usual in much of the country.

A fifth heatwave baked parts of England and Wales in the middle of the month – the hottest day of the year so far was recorded on August 13, with the temperature reaching 38.1C in Kew Gardens.

However, a period of more unsettled weather, heavy downpours and thunderstorms arrived later in the month.

Will the Europe heatwave bring hot weather to the UK?

The latest Met Office forecast shows no sign that the high heat seen in southern Europe will spread to Britain.

Cloud and rain is predicted to spread east today.

The rain could turn heavy at times, particularly in northern areas, while the southeast is likely to remain dry until the evening.



Conditions will remain changeable from Friday through Sunday, with further showers or longer spells of rain broken up by sunnier intervals.

It is expected to feel a little warmer by Saturday, but nothing in the current forecast suggests temperatures approaching those recently recorded on the continent.

How hot is the Europe heatwave?

Spain recorded some remarkable temperatures at the beginning of September.

Official weather agency AEMET recorded a maximum of 45.7C at El Granado in Huelva on September 3, with 45.1C reached at Sevilla Tablada.

France has also experienced an unusually late spell of intense heat.



Meteo-France said temperatures in the south had reached levels rarely seen in September, including 40.3C at Lavaur on September 6, and 40.2C at St-Geniez-d’Olt.

However, the heat is now easing in France, with temperatures dropping sharply today and many areas returning to around normal for the time of year.

What is the Met Office long-range forecast for September?

Changeable weather is expected to continue through the middle of the month.

Between September 13 and 22, the Met Office forecasts occasional rain or showers arriving from the North Atlantic, particularly across northern and western areas.

Strong winds will also be possible at times, although there should be some decent dry and more settled spells, especially in the south.



Later in September, high pressure could become more dominant around the UK and bring more widespread settled conditions for a time.

Temperatures across the period are expected to be close to average overall, but there is “scope for some rather warm days at times”.

From September 23 to October 7, temperatures are forecast to be “a little above average overall”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

High pressure could initially maintain more settled conditions before its influence may weaken later in the month and heading into October, increasing the chance of rain, showers and stronger winds.

So another taste of summer is possible – but the latest Met Office forecast does not currently signal another UK heatwave.

News.title: Tommy Robinson’s convicted pal Danny Tommo burst into my home and tried to kidnap me at knifepoint – he’s an idiot
News.content:
'SWUNG FOR ME' Tommy Robinson’s convicted pal Danny Tommo burst into my home and tried to kidnap me at knifepoint – he’s an idiot

TOMMY Robinson’s convicted friend Danny Tommo burst into a man’s home and tried to kidnap him at knifepoint alongside two accomplices.

Graham Page, 38, said he would join activists protesting at Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend because of his history with the demonstrations’ organiser.



Daniel Thomas, the man behind the protests, once tried to kidnap Graham at knifepoint in a case of mistaken identity.

A court heard how Thomas burst into Graham’s home in Hayling Island, Hampshire, with two accomplices – shouting “you’re coming with us.”



The trio are then said to have punched and kicked Graham and tried to drag him out into the street but Graham managed to cling onto a door frame.

During sentencing in 2016, the judge described the incident as an “extraordinarily frightening incident” and berated Thomas and the other two men for their “stupidity.”



Portsmouth Crown Court was told that the trio had wrongly accused Graham of stealing £10,000 worth of drugs from them before the attack.

But the incident was reportedly a case of mistaken identity, Graham said, with Thomas and his accomplices believing Graham was a man of the same name from Bognor Regis, The Times reports.



Graham told the publication: “They pushed my door open with machetes, but they couldn’t get me out of the bungalow.”

He added that Thomas had “swung for me” and that the harrowing incident left him in shock.

Following the attempted kidnapping the activist organiser pleaded guilty and was sentenced to two years behind bars.

Once he was released from prison Thomas adopted the name he goes by today and connected with Tommy Robinson, the founder of the English Defence League.

Following his release, Thomas said “everyone deserves a second chance” and told how he attended church weekly to “pray for forgiveness.”



Graham said he was asked to attend the protests organised by Thomas over the weekend but didn’t go because of his history with the organiser.

The dad said: “I don’t like him: I think he’s an idiot because of the previous things [he has done]. He trails in Tommy Robinson’s shadow.

“I see stuff on Facebook [and] what he is doing is good. I just don’t like him. Everyone tries to invite me to these protest groups, but it’s just not my kind of thing.”



Thomas helped rally hundreds of balaclava-clad supporters to descend on the south coast across two huge anti-migrant protests over the weekend.

He claims to have turned his life around after finding Christianity and took credit for a “stop the boats” protest that brought Dover to a standstill on Saturday.

Thomas was filmed in Dover alongside hundreds from Patriot Platform – a group he launched in June.

He describes it as a “growing Christian patriotic army” and has claimed more than 40,000 people have signed up.

On social media, he shared footage of protesters marching through Kent on Saturday, adding “this is only the beginning”.



Another video showed the words “blood is on your hands” spray-painted on the ground near the UK’s busiest ferry port.

The privately educated dad-of-four, from Hampshire, previously worked as a tank driver with the King’s Royal Hussars, according to reports.

But it is understood he was discharged on medical grounds before seeing active service.

Prior to giving up work to dedicate “everything to the cause”, Thomas also reportedly worked as a bricklayer and ran his own web design firm.

Before launching Patriot Platform, he helped organised a UKIP rally and Brexit Betrayal march.



After launching Patriot Platform, Thomas managed to find himself receiving a large sum of cash from an American conservative think tank.

However he was accused of misappropriating some of the money for his own use.

Yesterday, he appeared outside the Daily Mail’s offices in London after claiming they had revealed his mum’s address online.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Outside the newspaper office he was heard shouting: “I am going to give you 48 hours to buy my mum a new house or to get the money to get her a new house.

Thomas is now due to appear at Folkestone magistrates court in October accused of using threatening behaviour and trespassing on Dover Western Docks in April.

News.title: RNLI volunteers warned not to wear their uniform after ‘abuse’ from anti-migrant protesters
News.content:
RNLI volunteers have been warned not to wear charity-branded clothing following “unacceptable abuse” from anti-migrant protesters.

Demonstrators sparked fury after branding lifeboat staff “traitors” for rescuing a boat carrying asylum seekers on Sunday night.



Around 200 people, some wearing face coverings, descended on Eastney ferry port in Portsmouth after 140 migrants were brought to shore.

Cops guarded coaches parked near the marina as protesters blocked the flow of traffic and stopped RNLI teams from accessing the port.



And as the brave lifeboat crews returned to shore, they were branded “traitors” and met with abuse from the balaclava-clad crowd.

One shouted: “Look at these guys absolute traitors to this country. Look at the state of you.”



Protests have also been held at sites belonging to the charity, including an anti-migrant gathering outside the RNLI College in Poole, Dorset.

The RNLI has now issued security advice for its hardworking staff in the wake of protests in Portsmouth and Dover.



In a statement today, the charity said it had taken action to ensure the “safety and wellbeing” of staff following the “unacceptable abuse”.

It said: “As well as enhancing security at RNLI locations, we issued guidance to our people earlier this week on how to keep themselves safe.

“This guidance included how to manage potentially challenging interactions with members of the public, and where appropriate, choosing not to wear RNLI-branded clothing.

“Our people have been reminded that their safety comes first.

“They are encouraged to report relevant incidents internally and, where appropriate, to the police.”



One RNLI volunteer, named only as Neil, was pictured on social media and labelled a traitor.

He told the BBC: “We were tasked to Langstone Harbour to carry out illumination of the beach for safety of the protesters.

“We were there, as I said, purely for the safety of the protesters that were in the water.

“It’d be nice for those people who called me a traitor to know that I’m not a traitor.”

The protesters have also been accused of launching rocks and bricks at cops who were “caught off guard” during the clashes on Sunday.



Chaos was sparked following the arrival of a migrant boat from Normandy – thought to be the longest-ever Channel crossing by people smugglers.

It was intercepted in the Solent between the Isle of Wight and Portsmouth earlier on Sunday.

Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had “serious questions to answer” over the decision to bring migrants to shore in the area.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Police said a number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

The force added: “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.”



Reform leader Nigel Farage said the country was on the precipice of “serious civil disturbance” and called on the protests to remain peaceful.

Posting to social media, he said: “Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution.”

His remarks prompted Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, to urge the Reform leader to be “careful” with his words.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Livestreaming the mayhem, the far-right figure had called on his supporters to “get down to Eastney”.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp also condemned the violence in Portsmouth.

News.title: Teacher who had sex with teen boy also admitted sex offences against two schoolgirls – including one in back of car
News.content:
PAEDO PAST Teacher who had sex with teen boy also admitted sex offences against two schoolgirls – including one in back of car

A PAEDO teacher who had sex with a teen boy also admitted sex offences against two schoolgirls, it was revealed today.

Bronwen James, 30, was today convicted of bedding the 16-year-old boy after they began messaging on Snapchat.



At the time she was teaching PE at Bitterne Park School in Southampton, Hampshire.

James has now been found guilty of three counts of sexual activity but cleared on a fourth charge.



It can now be revealed that before the trial, she pleaded guilty to nine charges relating to two girls aged 13 and 14.

James admitted four counts of sexual activity and one of engaging in sexual communication with a child relating to the younger girl.



The teacher picked the girl up in her car when she turned 14 and had sex with her at the home she shared with her boyfriend, it was said.

She further pleaded guilty to two counts of sexual activity, one of engaging in sexual communication with a child and a final count of making an indecent photograph of a child.

This related to another 14-year-old who James had sex with in the back of her car.

It was further revealed James received a written warning from a £54,000-a-year private school prior to the incidents.



The teacher had shared her mobile number while working at the exclusive Seaford College, West Sussex.

Despite being reprimanded, James went on to form sexual relationships at two of her workplaces – Bitterne Park School in Southampton, Hants, and Hardenhuish School in Chippenham, Wilts.

The prosecution wanted to tell the jury in the trial about her “propensity” but reporting restrictions were put in place.

Winchester Crown Court heard the teacher “flirted” with the boy before accepting his request to add her on Snapchat.



After exchanging messages, she drove him to Weston Shore, Southampton, where they parked and kissed in her car.

The pair then went back to James’ house where they had sex, which happened on three or four occasions.

Edward Culver, prosecuting, said: “The tennis was on at Wimbledon. They began watching TV before kissing and touching each other.

“She took her clothes off and then he took his clothes off.”



Mr Culver said that the pair performed sex acts on each other before they had unprotected sex.

Besotted James told the boy she “loved him” and wanted to move away with him in daily messages to each other.

She also begged him to call her “Miss” as part of a sordid “fantasy”, the court heard.



The school was made aware of the relationship when a student showed a teacher some messages between James and the boy.

Mr Culver said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship, he was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover, him being the eighth man she had slept with.

“Her photo was visible on the phone screen.”

After the offences were exposed, James was later spoken to by police while under caution.

She prepared a statement claiming she had received communication from an unknown number, which turned out to be him, and suggested he was “being put up” to make these allegations by another student.



In her evidence, James told a jury she felt she was immature, easily influenced and very lenient with pupils.

But she denied flirting with the teen and having sex with him – claiming the boy made up the allegations to look “cool” in front of his mates.

James also said she began teaching aged just 21 and described herself as “immature” and conceded she did not think she was a good teacher.

She said: “I just don’t think I was ready for it. As my career progressed, I realised maybe I was seeking validation from the wrong people.

“I think I was a very lenient teacher, I was not strict, there were behaviour policies I would not necessarily follow, such as using mobile phones in lessons.



“But I did not want to upset them, I did not want to anger them. I wanted them to like me.”

James, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, will be sentenced at a later date.

Bethany Adams, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse. This was not a lapse in judgement; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care.

“The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”

News.title: England's mayors to get power to impose tourist tax
News.content:
Mayors in England will be given the power to impose a new fee on visitors' overnight stays, in a move the government says will mean more money can be invested into local areas.

Under the plans, local leaders will be able to bring in an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation rather than a flat fee.

Hospitality leaders have warned it will put jobs at risk and hit families in the pocket.

But the government said it would protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.

Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner said: "This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it's needed most.

"It'll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best."

Some mayors have backed the move, while others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.

Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites.

However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.

The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy.

News.title: Two arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service
News.content:
Two people have been arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service, the Metropolitan Police has said.

A 60-year-old man and 42-year-old woman were arrested at properties in London on Wednesday as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act (NSA) offences.

The suspects, who were both held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, have been released on bail under strict conditions until late October, the Met said.

Police said the arrests were not "connected to any of the incidents or attacks" linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London earlier this year.

The arrests took place following two searches carried out at properties in north and north-west London in June, the Met added.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said she knows "news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public" but stressed she does "not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public".

She added: "We've seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.

"As we've shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action."

She added the UK's terror threat level was severe and called for people to be vigilant.

News.title: Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over
News.content:
"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!"

This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment.

There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective".

Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans.

"BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough.

"Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack.

Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen.

What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree.

Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance.

News.title: Catherine joins William at suicide prevention campaign
News.content:
The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health.

It's being supported by sport stars including Harry Kane, Dame Kelly Holmes and Alan Shearer.

Royal sources said that Catherine wanted to attend to highlight the difference that can be made when people feel able to talk openly about how they are feeling and when someone is there to listen.

The project aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

This event will be Prince William's biggest public appearance in the UK since the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex from the US.

Earlier this week, William attended the funeral of Norway's King Harald in Oslo and accompanied his son Prince George to his first day as a boarder at Eton College.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it's the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK.

And sport is seen as an effective way of communicating that help is available.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William will say.

The royal couple will see a bench at the ground dedicated in memory of Gary Speed, a footballer who once played at the club, and who died by suicide in 2011.

The bench, unveiled last year, is intended to give people a space to speak openly about their anxieties as part of efforts to tackle mental health challenges and loneliness.

Alan Shearer, former England football star and TV pundit, was a friend of Gary Speed and is backing the call for people to try to support people they have worries about.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

A film has been made, featuring England football captain Harry Kane and boxer Carl Frampton, talking about the importance of stepping in and offering help if people see someone who seems to be facing mental health problems.

Prince William helps to narrate the video, which wants to tackle the stigma around mental health and suicide, with 7,000 lives being lost to suicide each year in the UK.

The initiative has a practical toolkit, on a free website, for people who are worried or embarrassed about what to say to someone if they have concerns about their well-being.

It offers a sports-themed way of approaching the topic, called GOALS, representing G: get ready; O: open the conversation; A: ask the question; L: listen and respond and S: support and signpost.

News.title: Drone display recreates the Twin Towers over New York City
News.content: According to organisers, 2,977 drones recreated the Twin Towers at full scale with each light representing a victim of the 9/11 attacks. The artwork, titled "2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor", is a commemorative public art installation in collaboration with artists, producers, and members of the 9/11 community, including victims' families, survivors, and first responders.

News.title: RNLI reviews security after volunteers targeted online
News.content:
The RNLI is reviewing its security procedures to ensure the safety of its members after protests in Dover and Portsmouth which saw its members targeted.

As part of this, volunteers have been told to consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity.

It comes after the charity helped carry around 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight, to Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, where roads were blocked by protesters.

Following this, some crew members had their photos and names shared on social media, in posts accusing them of treason. RNLI chief executive Peter Sparkes called the abuse "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

As a charity, the RNLI relies on donations from the public to fund its work.

Many lifeboat stations have shops attached to them, not just to raise money, but also to raise the profile of the organisation.

Volunteers have been told they are "empowered to make decisions to keep yourself, your team or crew safe" and "go home or close for the day if you need to".

For it to tell its volunteers they should feel empowered to shut shops or even lifeboat stations if they do not feel safe shows how seriously it is taking potential issues.

Sussex Police are looking to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

The Home Office said that platforms should enforce their own terms of service over this matter, and "take swift action against discriminatory content".

In a statement to the BBC, a Home Office spokesperson said: "Directing abuse at people who risk their lives in the service of others is appalling."

They added: "Where content is shared to intimidate, harass or incite violence against someone, that can cross into criminality," adding the Home Office would work "with platforms and law enforcement to ensure appropriate action is taken".

Speaking to BBC Breakfast about the new safety guidance for RNLI volunteers, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "My concern is about people calling them traitors and accusing them of treason, that is quite wrong.

"It is the government's job to stop the boats. They should not be attacking volunteers."

In a message sent to volunteers, Sparkes said its participation in the rescue on Sunday had been requested by HM Coastguard.

"This was the first time we have been involved in a Channel crossing incident of this magnitude this far west," he said.

Initially crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth stations were involved, later being joined by crews from four more stations after "large numbers of protesters were in and near the water in Portsmouth".

During the incident, the RNLI said it also helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant protesters in the sea off Portsmouth.

BBC Verify spoke to Neil, one of the volunteers who was called a "traitor" and whose image was shared online.

"We were there, purely for the safety of the protesters in the water," he said.

"It would be nice for those people who called me a traitor to know that I'm not a traitor."

News.title: Gruffalo illustrator says rise of AI images 'worrying'
News.content:
The illustrator for the Gruffalo books has said images created by artificial intelligence (AI) are "worrying".

Axel Scheffler said AI pictures are "a breach of copyright" and lose their charm when compared to the hand-drawn originals.

He was speaking to the BBC alongside author Dame Julia Donaldson for the launch of their new book Gruffalo Granny, with Dame Julia reading an extract.

News.title: Badenoch denies housing benefit cuts plan would make people homeless
News.content:
Badenoch said the government should cut housing benefit to fund defence spending now, adding she would exempt pensioners and existing tenants from the plans.

Speaking on the Today programme, she said: "What we're doing is making sure that people are protected, but capping the amount that people get on benefits because we need to look after our national security.

"Without national security, there aren't going to be any benefits. We're all going to be in danger, far more people will be homeless, and the government's first duty is defence of the realm."

Her proposed changes would be part of a package that would cut Â£23bn from welfare to partly fund an increase in defence spending.

But Karen Buck, chairwoman of Generation Rent and a former Labour MP, said Badenoch's proposals would lead to "homelessness, temporary accommodation costs crippling local councils, renters in severe financial hardship".

Housing benefit can be paid to people who are unemployed or on a low income to help cover the cost of rent.

The amount someone can claim is linked to the Local Housing Allowance rate, which varies for different council areas.

The number of people eligible to claim housing benefit has increased by more than one million since 2020, driven by the soaring cost of private rents.

The total cost of housing benefit is forecast to hit Â£39bn this year, according to the Department for Work and Pensions, due to the increasing number of claimants.

The Conservatives have set out how they plan to cut Â£4bn in total from the housing benefit bill, which they said would include a saving of at least Â£2.2bn from freezing social sector rents, by removing annual inflation-linked increases.

Another Â£1.8bn would be saved by lowering Local Housing Allowance rates, which are based on private rental costs in the area, for new tenancies.

For existing tenancies, rates would be frozen until they gradually fall in line.

In an interview with BBC Breakfast, Badenoch was asked who would be affected by her plans to cut housing benefit.

She said: "We have people who live in areas that are quite expensive and if people need local housing allowance they will need to move somewhere cheaper.

"I think you should aspire to live wherever you want to live, but you shouldn't aspire for the government, i.e. other taxpayers, to pay for you to live wherever you want to live...

"We're not removing people from homes - this doesn't cover pensioners, it doesn't affect existing tenants - but I do think you need to be fair."

Responding to Badenoch at PMQs, Burnham had said the policy would worsen homelessness and end up costing the government more.

He said: "I don't think, myself, that taking Â£4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation."

News.title: Migraines and acne among five more conditions pharmacists can treat
News.content:
People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first.

Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections.

Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list.

NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently.

After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen.

"For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said.

Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time".

The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are:

low frequency migraines in adults

hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children

ear infections in adults

mild to moderate acne in young people and adults

mild skin infections and scabies

That's in addition to these seven:

sore throat

sinusitis

earache

insect bites

impetigo

shingles

uncomplicated UTIs

Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says.

There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England.

Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations.

News.title: Funeral for second officer killed in A66 crash to be held
News.content:
The funeral for the second police officer killed in a wrong-way crash while on duty will take place later on Thursday.

PC Tom Clough, 38, died on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 22 August alongside his colleague PC Matthew Blades when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed police car. The five young men in the Passat also died.

PC Blades' funeral took place in Hartlepool on Wednesday with hundreds of police officers from around the country and members of the community lining the street.

Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said PC Clough's partner had said public support "brought them so much strength".

Officers had been pursuing the Passat seconds before it collided with PC Blades and PC Clough's car on the dual carriageway.

The pair had been looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

News.title: August joint-hottest month on record as climate change and El Niño drive heat
News.content:
August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded, tying with July 2023, according to the EU's climate service.

The record was driven by a combination of climate change and the rising influence of El NiÃ±o, pushing heat into the atmosphere across the Pacific.

Temperatures for the month were 1.65C above pre-industrial levels - surpassing the critical 1.5C threshold agreed by countries to avoid the worst consequences of climate change.

While a single month above 1.5C does not mean it has been permanently crossed, it shows a trend towards breaching that limit.

The month also capped western Europe's warmest summer, with high temperatures pushing the season past the deadly heat of 2003.

News.title: Teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools
News.content:
A teacher has been found guilty of sexually abusing a 16-year-old boy after previously admitting offences against two teenage girls.

Former PE teacher Bronwen James, 30, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, admitted nine sexual offences against two teenage girls - one a pupil at Bitterne Park School in Southampton and the other at Hardenhuish School in Chippenham.

She was convicted earlier at Winchester Crown Court of three counts of sexual activity with a 16-year-old boy who also attended Bitterne Park School.

During the trial the prosecution said James "craved" attention and "abused the trust put in her" as a teacher.

The jury found James guilty of the three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust by a majority of 11 to one and acquitted her of a fourth charge.

Due to legal restrictions covering the trial, media had been unable to report James' guilty pleas against two girls - which she made in January - and the jury were not told about them until after they had passed their verdict.

James showed no emotion as the verdict was read out and stood looking at the floor as the jury left the courtroom.

She was told by the judge she must surrender her passport and would be monitored with an electronic tag until Monday, when she will be taken to prison ahead of her sentencing.

During the five-day trial, prosecutors said James had entered into a "flirty" relationship with the pupil and they had communicated via Snapchat before they had sex at her house "three or four" times.

The jury also heard that James told the boy she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.

Giving evidence in court, the teenager said: "I thought she cared about me."

"I thought this was great, any teenage boy's dream, but [now] I think it was wrong. At the time I wasn't thinking that."

James denied all charges, alleging that the boy had made them up to "look cool".

News.title: Attack victim's mum to seek justice for 'rest of my life'
News.content:
The mum of a 19-year-old who was among three people stabbed to death during the Nottingham attacks says she will continue to campaign for justice for the rest of her life, after the public inquiry into the killings ended this week.

Barnaby Webber, of Taunton, Somerset, was fatally stabbed along with Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane.

Barnaby's mum, Emma Webber, said: "The rest of my life is going to be dealing with this." The inquiry heard this week her son's death was "potentially preventable".

During the inquiry that ended on Wednesday, counsel to the inquiry Rachel Langdale KC gave credit to the families for bringing to light "one failure after another".

Emma Webber told BBC Somerset: "We've had some shocking new evidence disclosed as late as last Friday that requires further questioning.

"It's harrowing stuff. Barney did have a chance of survival had he had quicker emergency response intervention, and had there been better coordination from the police control room."

The inquiry was told a "more rapid administration of blood products" could have increased his chances of getting to hospital with enough of a heartbeat to undergo surgery.

However, multiple other rapid and particular steps would have had to have taken place for him to have survived, the inquiry was told.

News.title: Group entered hotel of cricketers mistaken for migrants
News.content:
A group of people reached the hotel floor where members of the Pakistan under-19 cricket team were staying after protesters wrongly believed they were migrants, the Pakistan Cricket Board has said.

About 30 to 40 people congregated at the Marriot Hotel in Cosham, Portsmouth, on Tuesday evening after false rumours circulated that a coach carrying migrants had arrived.

Sumair Syed, chief operating officer of the Pakistan Cricket Board, said the team reported people "knocking on their doors" during the incident, but the players "behaved responsibly and didn't escalate the situation".

Hampshire Police said officers found no offences had been committed, and the crowd dispersed by about 21:00 BST.

The team went on to play a scheduled match the following day, Syed said.

He described the incident as "unfortunate" but said he was in contact with the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB), which had "assured us that every possible measure should be taken for the security of the escort".

"This is the responsibility of the whole sport to ensure the safety, security and well-being of the visiting team," he said. "They are on it and we are hopeful that nothing of such sort will happen in the future."

News.title: Two friends who died on mountain ridge tried calling 999, inquest hears
News.content:
Two friends who died on a mountain ridge during extreme winter conditions tried calling 999 but the alert was not escalated "as it should have been", according to a police expert at an inquest.

The bodies of Eddie Hill, 20, and Jayden Long, 19, both from Dereham, Norfolk, were found by a mountain rescue team in Eryri, also known as Snowdonia, on 19 February.

They died on Crib y Ddysgl, a ridge that peaks at 1,065m (3,494ft), less than a mile north of Yr Wyddfa's summit and linking it to the notoriously narrow ridge of Crib Goch.

The mountain rescue team said it did not have enough information about the location or nature of the 999 call to act immediately.

Philip Benbow, lead co-ordinator of Llanberis Mountain Rescue team, told Gwynedd Coroner's Court in Caernarfon he had been alerted by North Wales Police on the evening of 18 February to an abandoned 999 call made three hours earlier from a man who was thought to be on Crib y Ddysgl.

The call was later identified as coming from Long's mobile phone.

News.title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
News.content:
The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.

The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises.

The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC.

"What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said.

"That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening."

The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians.

The recommendations include:

Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over time

Giving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involved

The power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standards

An AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision

"The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said.

He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models.

"Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said.

"As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift."

And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge.

"I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said.

The Spice Girls are releasing never-before-heard demos as part of a new box set of their music.

The Singles Collection will feature two limited-edition 14-disc sets, available on 7-inch coloured vinyl and CD from 6 November.

Timed to mark the 30th anniversary of their debut album Spice, it is the first complete gathering of the pop group's singles, alongside B-sides and unreleased recordings.

Among the included chart-toppers are Wannabe, Spice Up Your Life and Goodbye, all packaged inside a handbag-style box trimmed in white holographic gloss and matt black foil.

It will also include five new messages from each of the Spice Girls as well as previously unreleased recordings from the Spice Girls archive.

open image in gallery ( PA )

This includes Do You Think About Me, one of the group’s earliest demos.

The CD edition will feature an exclusive disc featuring four previously unreleased demos.

Meanwhile, the 7” edition will feature every single on colour vinyl for the first time, paired with its original lead B-side on 14 individually-coloured records with 14 original sleeves.

Both sets will also include five collectible art cards and a 30th anniversary acrylic charm.

The band had teased a major announcement on social media and the news came as a disappointment to fans who were hoping the group would reunite for a tour.

A cryptic video was shared on the pop group’s Instagram page which featured a newspaper ad from The Stage, the same trade paper that advertised for an all-female group in 1994 that became the Spice Girls.

The paper was placed on the stairs featured in their Wannabe music video in 1996.

open image in gallery Rumours have continued to swirl over a Spice Girls reunion. ( PA )

Underneath the announcement on the Spice Girls’ Instagram page, a fan commented: “For the collectors this is amazing! But I feel the iconic The Stage advert teaser would’ve been so much more suited to a reunion announcement, just saying.”

While another user said they could hear “the millennial sign of devastation from across the world.”

The Spice Girls – made up of Victoria Beckham, Melanie Brown, Emma Bunton, Melanie Chisholm and Geri Halliwell-Horner – shot to global fame after the release of their debut single Wannabe in 1996, which celebrated its 30th anniversary this year.

The award-winning group also produced hits such as Stop, 2 Become 1, Who Do You Think You Are? and Viva Forever, amassing nine UK number one singles and two chart-topping albums.

Halliwell-Horner left the band in 1998, citing “differences between us”, and in December 2000 the rest of the group went their separate ways, announcing an indefinite hiatus.

They reunited in 2012 for the closing ceremony of the London Summer Olympics and in 2019 for their Spice World tour, but have since been the subject of speculation about a return to the stage.

Beryl Cook, one of Britain’s most-loved artists, is being honoured with an ambitious installation to celebrate what would have been her 100th birthday.

Cook, who died aged 81 in 2008, is known for her instantly recognisable, colourful paintings of joyous and often humorous moments in everyday life.

Her most enduring images depicted glamorous women in nightclubs, eating in cafés or enjoying raucous hen parties – and now, members of the public will be able to immerse themselves in Cook’s works, thanks to a mile-long open-air installation at Bicester Village.

Spanning the length and breadth of the shopping village, the display – which opens on Thursday (10 September) – will feature life-size cutouts of some of Cook’s most recognisable characters, and large-scale murals from her paintings.

Shoppers will also be able to pose for a photo with a full-scale recreation of Breakfast at Elvira’s, Cook’s famous 1996 painting of a busy morning at a seaside café.

open image in gallery Cook became one of the UK’s most celebrated artists during her decades-long career ( Sotheby's )

Even the bushes and trees at Bicester Village will host works, with recreations of Cook’s rotund pigeons, cats and dogs nestled among the branches.

The characters will lead visitors to a House of Voltaire pop-up, where shoppers can purchase items from an exclusive capsule collection celebrating Cook, with prices ranging from just £7 to £70,000.

The project has been organised in close collaboration with Cook’s family. Her granddaughter Sophie Cook said: “My grandmother loved nothing more than watching people enjoy themselves, laugh and dress up.

“Seeing her characters come to life along the vibrant streets of the Village is the perfect, playful tribute to her life and work.”

open image in gallery Many of the artist’s works featured shoppers ( Courtesy of ourberylcook.com © John Cook )

James Lambert OBE, deputy chairman of the Bicester Collection, told The Independent that Cook’s “penchant for documenting everyday British life through such a joyful lens makes her work a natural fit for Bicester Village, a destination centred around the enjoyment of shopping, dining and time spent together”.

“She is a true national treasure and the cultural significance of her pieces deserves to be celebrated,” he continued. “Bicester Village is delighted to collaborate with House of Voltaire to honour Cook’s enduring legacy in what would have been her 100th birthday year.”

Lambert added that he hopes the installation “will create plenty of moments to make [guests] smile”.

“Designed to be seen, shared and enjoyed, this cultural experience crafted in collaboration with House of Voltaire celebrates Cook’s exuberant painting style and her lifelong fascination with people, social encounters and the simple pleasures of daily life,” he said.

“Guests are invited to spend the day in the playful world of one of Britain’s best-loved artists as they shop, eat and stroll amongst a larger-than-life cast of characters finding joy in everyday pursuits.”

open image in gallery An enamel pin of two famous Cook characters will be available for purchase ( Courtesy of ourberylcook.com and Studio Voltaire )

The project also marks the launch of a major three-year partnership between Bicester Village and Studio Voltaire, which will see the former provide funding to the studio’s Learning Programme.

The programme sees the not-for-profit Studio Voltaire work with local schools, colleges and community groups, championing those with limited access to creative opportunities by providing free, artist-led workshops, drop-in activities, and skills-development sessions.

President Donald Trump made one of his boldest promises yet on stage Wednesday night at the Republican midterm convention in Texas.

He vowed to send $5,000 to every adult American citizen if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections.

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” the 80-year-old president told a crowd of supporters gathered in Dallas. “We'll call it the Trump dividend. Congratulations! Now all we have to do, now all we have to do is win.”

The pledge fits a pattern for Trump. Since returning to the White House last year, he has repeatedly floated proposals to send cash directly to tens of millions of Americans, whether framed as stimulus checks or dividends.

But 19 months into his second term, no such large-scale payments have been issued.

open image in gallery On Wednesday, President Donald Trump vowed to send every American adult a $5,000 'Trump Dividend' if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterms. It's not the first time he's made such a promise ( AP )

DOGE dividends

Early in 2025, when Elon Musk was slashing the federal workforce via DOGE, an investor floated the idea to him of sending Americans $5,000 checks — taken from the savings that DOGE would accrue.

“American taxpayers deserve a ‘DOGE Dividend’: 20% the money that DOGE saves should be sent back to hard-working Americans as a tax refund check. It was their money in the first place,” the investor, James Fishback, wrote on X on February 14, 2025.

open image in gallery Early during his second term, Trump and Elon Musk floated the idea of a DOGE Dividend, which would be taken from the savings DOGE would accrue ( Getty Images )

Musk said he would check with Trump on the idea. A few days later, the president expressed interest, bringing it up repeatedly.

"We're considering giving 20% of the DOGE savings to American citizens and 20% to paying down the debt," he said during a Florida event. Later on Air Force One, he told reporters: “I love it. A 20% dividend, so to speak, for the money that we saving by going after the waste and fraud and abuse and all the other things that are happening.”

Musk’s DOGE experiment, which polls showed was unpopular, did not end up reducing federal spending. And the so-called DOGE Dividend never materialized.

Tariff dividends

Later in 2025, after Trump unveiled his sweeping Liberation Day tariffs, the president vowed to send back some of the revenue generated by the levies to Americans.

“We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and will soon begin paying down our ENORMOUS DEBT, $37 Trillion,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on November 9, 2025. “A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.”

open image in gallery In 2025, after Trump unveiled his sweeping Liberation Day tariffs, the president vowed to send back some of the revenue generated by the levies to Americans ( AFP via Getty Images )

Much of Trump’s tariff authority was ultimately struck down by the Supreme Court in February of this year, and the dividends have yet to appear.

A New York Times reporter asked the president about the dividends in January — before the Supreme Court’s landmark decision — and he said those payments could potentially be sent out at the end of 2026, now only a few months away.

Health care payments

In December 2025, Trump signaled his support for a GOP proposal that would have deposited checks of up to $1,500 into Americans’ health care accounts.

The proposal was unveiled by Senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, to give certain Affordable Care Act enrollees a one-time deposit of either $1,000 or $1,500. An estimated 19.2 million people are enrolled in ACA Exchange plans as of February.

“I like the concept,” Trump told reporters on December 9, 2025. “I don't want to give the insurance companies any money…They've been ripping off the public for years.”

The enhanced ACA subsidies expired a few weeks later, leading many enrolled in Obamacare health plans to see their premiums rise, and those dividends never went out.

open image in gallery ‘In honor of our nation's founding in 1776, we are sending every soldier $1,776 and the checks are already on the way,’ Trump announced in December 2025 ( Doug Mills - Pool/Getty Images )

The national debt problem

Amid Trump’s multiple proposals to send out checks to Americans, the U.S. national debt continues to balloon to record levels, topping $40 trillion for the first time last month.

The debt doubled under the watch of Trump and Joe Biden, rising by $11.6 trillion during Trump’s two terms and $8.4 trillion during Biden’s one term, according to Reuters.

Much of those increases came during the Covid pandemic, when the federal government borrowed at a feverish pace, including to dole out several rounds of stimulus checks.

UK economic growth is set to have ground to a halt in July, as consumers swapped spending in shops for drinking in pubs amid the heatwaves and Fifa World Cup, economists think.

Most economists are expecting gross domestic product (GDP) to have shown no growth in July, when the Office for National Statistics (ONS) releases its next dataset on Friday.

It would represent a downbeat start to the leadership of Andy Burnham, who was appointed Prime Minister during the month.

open image in gallery

It would also come after Chancellor John Healey insisted that there was an “optimistic story” about the UK economy that was “turning a corner”.

In June, the UK economy grew 0.3% as hospitality and leisure firms received a boost from football fever and the prolonged hot weather.

It meant GDP expanded by 0.4% during the second quarter of the year.

However, economists have predicted that activity was muted in July as other parts of the economy lagged, offsetting the continued World Cup and hot weather boost to hospitality.

In particular, retail and wholesale activity is predicted to have dipped by 0.3% for the month.

Elliott Jordan-Doak, an analyst for Pantheon Macroeconomics, said any decline was “more likely the result of consumers shifting spending to drinking in the pub than a sign of weakening in consumer spending growth”.

open image in gallery Flat GDP growth in July would represent a downbeat start to the leadership of Andy Burnham (Leon Neal/PA) ( PA Wire )

It indicates that households may have reprioritised rather than reduced overall spending, despite facing increased energy and fuel costs.

Analysts for Investec said: “After a positive first half of the year, where the UK economy actually outperformed the rest of the G7, growing by 1%, we expect the third quarter will begin with a weaker performance.

“Some evidence of this has already been seen in soft retail sales for the month, whilst we expect the rise in household utility bills due to the 13% uplift to the energy price cap would have had a dampening effect.”

Economists for Deutsche Bank said they were expecting the economy to “slow from its current torrid pace of growth”.

“The real income shock from the Middle East has yet to fully filter through the data,” they said.

“One-offs that have buoyed the economy will also likely unwind. And some budget uncertainty could put households and businesses off from spending.”

Cats have a long history with humans, going back more than 9,000 years. Attracted to human settlements by the rodents that plagued (sometimes literally) our ancestors, cats ingratiated themselves as useful mousers and slowly domesticated themselves.

Farmers began to employ them as pest controllers. It was through this arrangement that cats and milk first became acquainted.

Before the commercialisation of pet food, cats were mostly fed scraps from the family table. Not much was known about their nutritional needs. In his 1877 book on cats, Scottish doctor Gordon Stables insisted cats need two bowls – “one for water and the other for milk” – and suggested porridge and milk as an excellent feline breakfast.

From these origins, cats and milk became further embedded in the collective zeitgeist through depictions of milk-loving cats in art, books, movies and cartoons. There’s even the classic trope of the scruffy street cat being rescued from the rain to enjoy a saucer of milk from a kindly stranger.

While it’s not surprising that cats and milk have persisted as an unquestioned combination, research now tells us cats shouldn’t be drinking milk at all.

open image in gallery From these origins, cats and milk became further embedded in the collective zeitgeist through depictions of milk-loving cats in art, books, movies and cartoons ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The vast majority of cats are lactose intolerant

Like all mammals, cats begin life drinking milk from their mother. But past kittenhood, milk is a completely unnecessary part of a cat’s diet.

After weaning (around 6–12 weeks of age), kittens stop producing the enzyme lactase, required to digest lactose in milk. For the vast majority of cats, this means they are lactose intolerant.

However, just like in humans, the level of intolerance varies for each individual based on how much of the enzyme their body naturally produces.

Don’t rush to give your kitten milk, though. Just because kittens can digest lactose doesn’t mean they should be drinking cow’s milk. Cats are much smaller animals than cows and, fittingly, the amount of lactose in the milk of mother cats is much lower than in cow’s milk. It’s best to let them drink from their mother or to get them a kitten-appropriate cat formula.

Lactose intolerance isn’t the only reason not to give your cats milk. Though rare, cats can also develop an allergy to milk or dairy.

What happens to cats who drink milk?

Lactose is a type of sugar. When it can’t be broken down to be absorbed into the bloodstream, lactose travels through the intestines to the colon where the bacteria inside the body ferment it.

This fermentation breaks lactose down into acids and gases which cause unpleasant symptoms, including the passing of excessive gas, bloating, constipation, abdominal pain and occasionally nausea and vomiting. In cats, the most common symptom observed is diarrhoea.

Chronic or persistent diarrhoea can cause further complications such as dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and malnutrition. In some cases, it can even be life threatening.

Cats who consume milk or dairy regularly as part of their diet are at increased risk of these health complications.

If milk is so bad for cats, why do they love it?

We often like things that are bad for us. But to answer this question, we first have to remember cow’s milk is intended for feeding and growing a baby cow.

To achieve this feat, it contains an assortment of proteins and fats that are highly palatable, especially to cats. Cats need high levels of protein and fat for optimal health and daily functioning.

Cow’s milk, in particular, is also high in casein, a protein that is broken down by the body into alpha-casozepine. In some studies, it’s been associated with a calming effect in cats. While this wouldn’t initially make a cat want to drink milk, it may create a comforting association with milk over time.

open image in gallery Cow’s milk, in particular, is also high in casein, a protein that is broken down by the body into alpha-casozepine ( Getty Images )

Can I give milk sometimes as a treat? What about milk alternatives?

The short answer is: no.

Dairy is not a natural part of cats’ diet. While they may like the taste, milk is likely to cause your furry friend discomfort and health issues, so it’s best to avoid entirely.

And if you’re thinking your cat is one of the lucky few that isn’t lactose intolerant, think again. Cats are very good at hiding discomfort because, in the wild, showing weakness would make them a target for predators.

If you absolutely must, opt for lactose-free milk or milk formulated specifically for cats, and keep it as a very occasional treat.

About the author Julia Henning is a PhD Candidate in Feline Behaviour, School of Animal and Veterinary Science, University of Adelaide. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

While it won’t upset their stomachs in the same way as regular cow’s milk, it still won’t offer your cat any nutritional benefit.

As for milk alternatives like oat, soy or almond milk? Any unusual additions to your cat’s diet are likely to cause digestive upset, so it’s best to avoid these as well.

The bottom line? Don’t give your cat milk. They don’t need it, they probably can’t digest it and it’s likely to cause more pain than it’s worth.
