Goalkeepers: Karl Darlow, Tom Heaton, Senne Lammens, Dermot Mee. Defenders: Patrick Dorgu, Diogo Dalot, Matthijs de Ligt, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Noussair Mazraoui, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven.

Midfielders: Carlos Baleba, Bruno Fernandes, Mason Mount, Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Manuel Ugarte.

Sports.title: Premier League fixtures: Bumper festive period announced
Sports.content:
The Premier League's festive fixtures have been announced for this season - with 29 matches available to watch live on Sky Sports between Boxing Day and January 7.

England's top-flight have announced the festive fixtures more than three months in advance as it "gives supporters notice to plan and make travel arrangements for a particularly busy time of the year".

It also follows consultation with the Football Supporters' Association and representatives from club Fan Advisory Boards.

There will be seven Premier League matches on Boxing Day this year, with Hull City vs Liverpool - kicking off at 5.30pm - and Newcastle vs Man City - kicking off at 8pm - featuring as a live Sky Sports double header.

A triple header on Sky Sports then follows on Super Sunday on December 27, with Frank Lampard taking on Chelsea as Coventry boss at 2pm. That match is then followed by Manchester United vs Nottingham Forest at 4.30pm, then Crystal Palace vs Arsenal at 7pm.

Every Premier League club has been given at least 60 hours between their Christmas and New Year fixtures.

There are two festive midweek rounds of Premier League fixtures where every match will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

The first takes place between Tuesday December 29 and Wednesday December 30. The other takes place between Tuesday January 5 and Thursday January 7.

And in the weekend in between, Sky Sports will be showing Leeds vs Everton on Friday Night Football on New Year's Day, then Bournemouth vs Aston Villa on January 3 for Saturday Night Football at 5.30pm. That weekend's Super Sunday sees Chelsea vs Newcastle at 2pm, then Man City vs Tottenham at 4.30pm.

Broadcast selections for November and early December will be announced before October 19.

Sports.title: Red Roses boosted for Australia clash by returns from injury
Sports.content:
The Red Roses have named their side to face Australia on Saturday in the first match of the home leg of the WXV Global Series.

Head coach John Mitchell has made five changes from England's last match against France in May, when they secured their fifth successive Women's Six Nations Grand Slam.

World Cup winners Tatyana Heard (centre) and Natasha Hunt (scrum-half) return from injury to reclaim places in the XV.

Fly-half Holly Aitchison comes in to win her 50th international cap, May Campbell is selected at hooker and Wing Mia Venner forms the back three with Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Ellie Kildunne.

Hannah Botterman, who missed the entire Six Nations, and Morwenna Talling are also available again and are named among the replacements.

Saracens prop Kelsey Clifford has been ruled out of the entire WXV series because of a hamstring injury, with Liz Crake called up to the squad to replace her.

Saturday's match against Australia takes place at CorpAcq Stadium, the home of the Gallagher Prem's Sale Sharks.

Mitchell, who had two stints at Sale, said: "I have very fond memories of the north west from my time with Sale Sharks so it's awesome to be able to take our game to this part of the country.

"Playing in a different part of the country allows us to be present in the community and keeps the game healthy. You've not only got to be visible, but if you can actually be close to your community, I think that's even better.

Image: Ellie Kildunne forms a back three with Mia Venner and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald

"Connection is such an important part of life, but particularly in sport. The girls have worked hard in pre-season to deepen their bond and that will make us stronger on the field.

"We're excited to get our WXV Global Series under way and aim to excite and entertain."

The 2026 season is the inaugural edition of the WXV Global Series. The 12 participating nations are fixed for the 2026-2028 cycle, with no promotion or relegation.

England next play Canada in a repeat of their 2025 World Cup final clash at Sandy Park, Exeter, on September 19 before facing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on September 26.

The Red Roses tour Canada and the United States as part of the series in October.

England team to play Australia

15 Ellie Kildunne, 14 Mia Venner, 13 Megan Jones (c), 12 Tatyana Heard, 11 Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, 10 Holly Aitchison, 9 Natasha Hunt; 1 Mackenzie Carson, 2 May Campbell, 3 Sarah Bern, 4 Delaney Burns. 5 Lilli Ives Campion, 6 Abi Burton, 7 Sadia Kabeya, 8 Maddie Feaunati.

Replacements: 16 Bryony Field, 17 Hannah Botterman, 18 Maud Muir, 19 Morwenna Talling, 20 Marlie Packer, 21 Lucy Packer, 22 Zoe Harrison, 23 Helena Rowland.

Sports.title: St Leger: Big race runners guide
Sports.content:
As the United States Of America celebrates its 250th anniversary, so does the world’s oldest Classic race. How many sporting events last this long? Very few.

So, who will take Saturday's special renewal of the Betfred St Leger? First of all, it's great to see the Derby winner, Christmas Day, lining up. Not all that many do the double, a fact that I appreciated early in my racing life when even the mighty Shergar could manage only fourth. In more recent years, Camelot just missed out on his Triple Crown attempt.

Remember, the Leger is only a furlong and a half shorter than two miles but you still need speed as well as stamina to take it.

Never Say Die, St Paddy, Nijinksy and Reference Point are the last four to have backed up here after Epsom, however, so good luck to Christmas Day.

He is closely matched with stablemate Pierre Bonnard but Aidan O'Brien's hopes of a tenth Leger may be challenged by his own son, Joseph, trainer of the favourite, Enceladus.

1. Action

Jockey: TBC | Trainer: Aidan O'Brien

I feel rather sorry for Action who, being a close relative of last year's Derby winner and Leger fourth Lambourn, did little wrong in a juvenile campaign which yielded a third to Bow Echo in the Royal Lodge Stakes and then an even better second to Hawk Mountain here in the Group 1 Futurity.

Even this year's campaign didn't start too badly when he improved on a fourth in the Sandown Classic Trial to chase home the future Juddmonte hero, Item, in the Dante at York.

It all started to go wrong when he raced way too freely in first-time cheekpieces in the Derby and since then he has been sacrificed as a pacemaker in the Irish Derby, King George and the Juddmonte. In the last-named, he didn't get away anywhere quickly enough to do his job and a mid-race move still ended with him being tailed off.

It doesn't augur well for his prospects as he steps up in trip here.

I think he needs an arm around his powerful shoulders!

2. Alderman

Rossa Ryan | Richard Hannon

Many who watched this year's Derby may have gone away thinking that Alderman might end up being aimed at the Leger after he finished off rather well to take fifth (would have been fourth in another stride or two) behind Christmas Day, some two and a half lengths in front of Rebel Rocker in sixth.

Note that Pierre Bonnard, Ancient Egypt and Item were among those behind him.

However, he failed to build on that in the Bahrain Trophy at Newmarket, notably on firm going, when last of the five runners.

He remains a five-race maiden, albeit a talented one, and on the evidence of Epsom when the Derby was run on soft ground, any rain that falls this week will be a bonus.

Even then, he has way too much to do here.

3. Christmas Day

Jockey: TBC | Trainer: Aidan O'Brien

After last year's Derby winner Lambourn failed to follow up here in fourth, we still await the

first to emulate Reference Point who remains the last to win both Derby and St Leger in 1987.

Christmas Day has a bright chance of doing it, though, especially if showers arrive on Town Moor. His Derby win on soft ground was pretty emphatic, beating Arc-bound Maltese Cross by nearly three lengths and that is about the best form on offer here.

Image: Christmas Day won the 2026 Derby

He failed to back-up in the Irish Derby but went down fighting behind Benvenuto Cellini and a neck in front of Pierre Bonnard. The form-line with his stablemate was replicated in the Great Voltigeur when Pierre Bonnard reversed the placings in receipt of 5lb from the Derby winner as they were left toiling behind the upwardly mobile Maltese Cross.

Christmas Day has been a model of consistency all season and shapes as though he could just about stay the trip. I doubt he will improve for it, however, but he should be bang there.

4. Enceladus

Billy Loughnane | Joseph O'Brien

This big, long-striding colt is unbeaten as a three-year-old and gets better every time he shows up. The form of his King George V Handicap win at Royal Ascot has received multiple boosts and he did his bit in style to land the Group 3 Gordon Stakes at Goodwood next time.

There was a lot to like about the way he settled the issue with a fine turn of speed approaching the final furlong there, albeit with a tendency to edge right again, and rather more pronounced than it was at Ascot. Maybe that is why they have fitted cheekpieces for today.

Image: Enceladus heads the market for the St Leger

It is six years since Joseph O'Brien won his first Leger with Galileo Chrome and, with this vintage season yielding so much, he must be optimistic of following up with this son of Sea The Stars.

The fact that his half-brother won at a mile and six furlongs must add to the expectation, plus the fact that he arrives here fresher than most and with the chance of improvement to come.

Sadly, Dylan Brown McMonagle is still recovering from a horror fall at Bellewstown and so Billy Loughnane is booked to wear the iconic Niarchos family silks.

5. Galiyan

Danny Tudhope | Andrew Balding

Looked one to follow for Andrew Balding when winning his maiden at Chester's Boodles May Festival and was expected to take some beating in the Queen's Vase, for which he started favourite. But he could manage only sixth to Limestone.

His very decent second in the Bahrain Trophy at Newmarket was a step back in the right direction but then came a heavy defeat in the Great Voltigeur at York. Sure, he probably did too much in that race, but it is hard to see him turning that all around here, even with the newly fitted cheekpieces.

6. Golden Story

Clifford Lee | Karl Burke

One of the more unexposed runners, winning two of his four starts, including a tight verdict over Del Maro in the Listed Cocked Hat Stakes at Goodwood.

However, his progress stalled in the King Edward VII Stakes at Royal Ascot when he was way too keen and was left behind in the home straight.

His full brother Arabian Force stays a mile and six but he needs to settle down a bit to emulate him and also needs to improve a lot.

7. Hatteen

David Probert | Andrew Balding

A record of one win from six but he is steadily improving and gained his only win with a comfortable stroll here over a mile and a half in July.

He backed that up with a clear second in a valuable handicap at Goodwood but, as the lowest rated in the line-up, he does have a lot to find with some of these and even then, is not guaranteed to last out the trip.

That said, he has been quietly backed in recent days and looks the first string from a top stable enjoying one of its finest campaigns.

8. Highwayman

Saffie Osborne | Joseph O'Brien

Stablemate of Enceladus and looks the second string but is, without doubt, the most fascinating contender in the field.

He has had an incredible turnaround after showing precious little in his first three starts, ranging between six and a half furlongs and a mile. Then, on his fourth appearance, and an SP of 250-1, there was more than a glimmer at Naas, again over a mile. It was some eyecatcher!

Plenty more were watching when he then stepped up to almost a mile and a half at Killarney and duly strolled home by nine lengths. Next, he went off at 22-1 and landed the Listed Vinnie Roe Stakes over a mile and six furlongs at Leopardstown, hitting the line strongly, again with his customary high head carriage.

So, we know he stays the trip and probably has more to offer and will be ridden by Saffie Osborne. Could they make history together? Anything is possible but in truth he needs to find plenty more to steal this.

9. Pierre Bonnard

Jockey: TBC | Trainer: Aidan O'Brien

The most experienced runner in the field who looked every inch a Leger type at two when landing the Group 3 Zetland Stakes at Newmarket and Group 1 Criterium de Saint-Cloud (beating the smart A Boy Named Susie) both over a mile and a quarter. The former was on good to firm and the latter on a testing surface so the ground comes alike to him, clearly.

Had a patchy first half of the season, including when only seventh in the Derby, but has done a whole lot better in his two most recent appearances.

Image: Pierre Bonnard represents Aidan O'Brien in the St Leger

He stayed on well for third, a neck behind Christmas Day, in the Irish Derby and then, in receipt of 5lb from his Derby-winning stablemate, reversed the form in the Great Voltigeur, giving Maltese Cross something to think about until the last few yards.

I cannot have this Camelot colt failing for stamina, especially as his dam's half-sister was third in the Park Hill, and he has the form in the book to go very close.

10. Rebel Rocker

Jason Watson | Faye Bramley

A useful and relatively unexposed colt who probably has more to offer but was a well-held sixth in the Derby and ran to a similar level in the Geoffrey Freer at Newbury.

There is stamina on his dam's side that suggests he will stay well but even so, this represents a very tough ask.

11. Amelia Earhart

Jockey: TBC | Trainer: Aidan O'Brien

The only filly in the line-up who won the Listed Cheshire Oaks but has come up short in Group company since, including in the Epsom and Curragh Oaks.

She didn't seem to quite get home in the Lillie Langtry Stakes at Goodwood over a mile and six furlongs two starts back, which was a surprise as she is bred to be suited by a trip like this one. At least she shaped better in the Give Thanks Stakes back over a mile and a half at Cork last time.

Needs to find something from somewhere and I wish her well as she is named after a personal heroine of mine, who also happens to be a distant relative of my American wife!

Mike's verdict

ENCELADUS arrives here on the crest of a wave for Joseph O'Brien, who has enjoyed a marvellous season. He is on an upward curve with improvement not guaranteed, but surely very likely, and with the promise that the trip will suit.

He gets a narrow vote and could become the first European Classic winner for the Niarchos family since Study Of Man won the French Derby in 2018. It would be the second Classic of the season for Billy Loughnane.

Derby winner Christmas Day has performed at a consistent level all season but his prep at York perhaps lacked a little sparkle and I wouldn't be at all surprised if Pierre Bonnard finished ahead of him again, especially over this trip. Both are by Camelot (as is Amelia Earhart) who is a real stamina influence.

I will be intrigued to see how Highwayman goes and fancy him to grab fourth in a race that the incredible O'Brien family look set to dominate.

Sports.title: Garcia reveals why he snubbed face-off with Benn
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia offered no apologies for missing Tuesday's face-off with Conor Benn, adding it was "funny" to see the British fighter pretending to square off against his dad, Nigel.

Garcia is set to embark on the first defence of his WBC welterweight title against Benn at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn hit out at Garcia for 'bottling it' after American failed to show up for face-off in Las Vegas (Credit: @Zuffa Boxing)

Earlier in the week, the pair were due to meet at the Mandalay Bay Hotel for a media event, but the American fighter did not show up, with Benn subsequently claiming his opponent had "bottled it".

During a press conference on Wednesday, Garcia said: "I wasn't there because I didn't want to be.

"Look, we have a face-off at the press conference [Thursday], then at the weigh-ins [Friday] and then a final face-off literally in the ring when the refs give you instructions.

"I've been doing this for so long. I've had fight weeks in Vegas before. I've never had to do a face-off on [Tuesday]. So I have a routine to do, and it's just something I didn't want to do.''

"It was funny seeing him [Benn] staring at himself."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn is relishing his status as the underdog ahead of his fight against Garcia

Benn, meanwhile, believes Garcia's absence let the fans down.

"Ultimately it's disrespectful to the public because they deserve it,'' he said on Wednesday.

"The public deserves us giving you guys the best. This is what we do. This is what we're here for.''

Benn: Weight cut dragged me through the pits of hell

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn said he had been 'dragged through the pits of hell' in trying to make weight for the fight

Benn comes into this fight as the underdog after stepping up to middleweight to fight Chris Eubank Jr. He lost his first fight against his rival in April 2025, before avenging that loss later that November. He comes into this weekend's bout after beating Regis Prograis at a 150lbs catchweight in April.

Should Benn make the weight at Friday's weigh-in, this will be the first time that he has fought at the welterweight limit in over four years, with his last fight at under 147lbs coming against Chris van Heerden in April 2022.

The 29-year-old hit back at those who have doubted his ability to make the weight, but added he felt like he had been "dragged through the pits of hell and had a fight with satan" during his preparations.

"A lot of people said I couldn't make the weight, watch me do it," Benn said, adding he went through 15 weeks of dieting before the fight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The pair have exchanged a war of words in the build-up to Saturday's world title fight

"I've done it, and that's it."

Benn added that this would be his last fight at 147lbs and is hoping to move up in weight after this to 160 or 168lbs.

Garcia said he didn't want to hear any excuses from Benn after the fight regarding his weight cut.

"All we can do is go by past experience," Garcia said. "He cut back down to 150lbs to fight Regis Prograis. We have seen how he bloated up. Now he has an extra three pounds to go. I don't want to hear any excuses. He doesn't have a rehydration clause.

"I don't want to be hearing any crybaby s*** from him. He's trying to set up a narrative, because when he gets his a** whopped, he'll say: 'I was drained'. I'm about to beat his a**, it doesn't matter how much he weighs."

Sports.title: Why Kai Havertz’s dummy was perhaps more pleasing than a Lionel Messi waltz | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
During Covid, when sport was back but behind closed doors, I hosted a number of strange online shows to fill the void of real life. The highlight was chatting to Darren Gough about a lifesize bronze rhinoceros for 45 minutes to 15 small boxes on a Zoom call. I don’t recall who it was for and where the rhinoceros came from – but it might be in his garden.

I ended up doing virtual pre-match corporate Zoom calls for Heineken before Europa League games. It was the wifi version of Club Wembley: a Q&A happening on stage between a generic host and some random ex-pro while you’re trying to chat to your mate and eat an unidentified square of meat with some dauphinoise potatoes.

I’d be in my little square talking to Luis García in his little square about the ghost goal while an assorted group of faces and living rooms or kitchen tables would stare at you, perhaps interested, perhaps not. Did they even want to be there? Were we on mute while someone from marketing was filling a spare box on my laptop watching Death In Paradise on the TV behind me?

Certainly it was hard to create an amazing vibe with Mark van Bommel while his internet connection crashed and a little note on a Google doc appeared telling me to fill for 25 minutes with my favourite memories of the Europa League. Did these disembodied heads in front of me want the deep dive they got on Tony Parks’ heroics in 1984? How many of them knew about Gary Mabbutt playing centre mid and marking Enzo Scifo out of the game?

One of the guests was Dimitar Berbatov. You’d log on half an hour before the show and say hello, try to build some kind of electric rapport with a man in Bulgaria (I think) presumably looking to get in and get out and get back on with whatever social distancing life in Sofia had to offer.

He may have not had Akabusi levels of energy, and his economy of language was not unlike his playing style – why use a hundred words when one will do? But he was into it and did the job perfectly. I absolutely loved Berbatov as a player. Watching him pluck a goalkick out of the sky was more beautiful than watching a lot of other players banging one in from 25 yards. There’s a YouTube video called Dimitar Berbatov – the most underrated first touch ever? It begins with him standing like a lamp-post on the halfway line at Craven Cottage and stopping a crossfield ball stone dead like it’s an anvil.

View image in fullscreen Dimitar Berbatov, pictured scoring for Manchester United against Sunderland in 2009, could make football look easy. Photograph: Carl Recine/Action Images/Reuters

Back to the Zoom call: I welcome Dimitar, he says hello, I explain my admiration for him, and then say to him that he made football look easy. Did he find it easy? “Yes” he replied. Totally matter of fact. Not trying to impress – just explaining that football was easy.

And for someone like Berbatov, it is a different level to “good touch for a big man”. This is the ultimate type of grace on a football pitch. And perhaps it is reserved for tall, skilful players. I’ve probably used the word languid already but I can’t think of any other use of the word – reserved for players who are almost balletic.

Is it insane to say it’s more aesthetically pleasing than seeing a Messi or a Maradona waltz through a defence? It almost feels as if a low centre of gravity gives you an unfair advantage when it comes to technical skill. No flailing arms and legs to get in the way of you being naturally brilliant.

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Lionel Messi dribbles away from three Dutch players in the 2022 World Cup. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

My biased brain instantly goes to Glenn Hoddle walking through the Oxford United defence with one sway, sitting the keeper down with a movement of the leg. It’s all saying: “This is easier for me than it is for you.”

Which brings us to Kai Havertz – and that dummy against Chelsea. The more and more football becomes that David Mitchell sketch, the more surprised I am that there are still moments in a game that lead to some involuntary noise from deep within.

The ball from Christos Tzolis is definitely for him. Havertz points in front to where he wants the ball. If it’s played there he can probably get a shot away first time. But when it comes, controlling the ball would have been a sensible choice. Back to goal. He could have turned and shot, or just kept the ball. There are lots of good players to pass it to.

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard scores Arsenal’s second goal against Chelsea after Kai Havertz’s dummy. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

Even the way he lifts his left leg at the last second to let the ball run through to Martin Ødegaard is delightful. It’s easy to forget the pace of the game at this level. And when you’re watching on TV where it’s much easier to see the pass you also forget these guys don’t have that view.

Someone somewhere will have done a report on Havertz’s scanning abilities. He doesn’t appear to look behind to check where Ødegaard is. But awareness is hard to calculate. He just knows. And he does it all in a split second, not even. How wonderful that you can do so much without even touching the ball.

A lot of people do quite well out of repeatedly asking whether Arsenal need a centre-forward, so I don’t want to do them out of work. And Havertz isn’t perfect – he isn’t Robbie Fowler in the box. But he has scored in two Champions League finals. He did win the league last season. A lot of beautiful graceful players tend to be beautiful and graceful without delivering on the biggest occasions. Havertz does both. And when he gets it right, it looks easy to him. Imagine finding it easy.

Sports.title: Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be given to Spurs, says Pochettino
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino says Chelsea should be stripped of their 2016-17 Premier League title for financial rule breaches and the honour retrospectively awarded to Tottenham, who he led to second place that season.

Chelsea were fined £10m by the Football Association in July and given a suspended two-window transfer ban for multiple violations of the rules during the Roman Abramovich era. They were also fined £10.75m by the Premier League in March.

The club were found to have used unlicensed agents and sought to obscure the nature of their transfer business between 2009 and 2022. The deals that took Eden Hazard, Willian, David Luiz and Nemanja Matic to Stamford Bridge were among those found to have transgressed. Those players were central to Chelsea’s 2016-17 triumph under Antonio Conte. Many of these secret transactions, routed through Abramovich’s network of offshore companies, were revealed in an investigation published by the Guardian and international partners in 2023.

The club’s BlueCo ownership self-reported the breaches when it took over from Abramovich in 2022 in the hope of mitigating the punishment, and the club avoided a points deduction. Pochettino, who went on to manage Chelsea in 2023-24 and is in charge of the US, believes the authorities did not go nearly far enough. His Spurs team finished seven points behind Conte’s Chelsea.

“We should win one Premier League, we should have been awarded it,” Pochettino said as part of a wide-ranging interview. “If that [Chelsea’s rule-break] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure. They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second.

“We can say that they scored goals, they won games. OK. But it’s completely fair to say that we didn’t compete before the start of the season with the same card. Maybe with the same rules, we could’ve signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals.”

Between 2009 and 2022, Chelsea won three league titles, two Champions Leagues, two Europa Leagues, four FA Cups and one League Cup. It was put to Pochettino that Hazard had made a particular difference in the 2016-17 title race; the winger scored 16 goals in the competition.

“Maybe yes,” Pochettino replied. “I have no doubt and I’m not scared to say the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me. But if we were at Tottenham and broke the rules, I’d admit the same: ‘We don’t deserve the title because we broke the rules.’

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It’s impossible if only some clubs play with offside and another plays with no offside. Or one plays with VAR and another plays with no VAR. For everyone it needs to be the same rules. And then you have the capacity to create the best team.

“I don’t say that Chelsea didn’t play well, that Conte was not great. I don’t say that. I don’t want the message to be twisted. But if you broke the rules then ciao – you need to give it to another team. I don’t know why that didn’t happen. What is being promoted and incentivised is to break the rules. If you don’t punish in the way that you need to punish, I say: ‘Yeah … I lost my job [at Spurs] because we didn’t win a title.’”

Sports.title: ‘Football saved Dad’s life’: meet the coach of the England women’s Parkinson’s team
Sports.content:
When Gemma Darvill’s dad, Les, was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease aged 58, joining a walking football team stopped him from confining himself to his own home, and she believes the game saved his life.

What she could never have foreseen was that, eight years later, she would find herself coaching the first England women’s Parkinson’s team, helping transform the lives of women with the disease from all across the country. She is set to embark on a journey to Toronto to help spread awareness of the ways in which walking football can help put the brakes on the progression of Parkinson’s symptoms.

A teacher at Swallowfield primary school in Woburn Sands, in Milton Keynes, Darvill’s interest in walking football was sparked by supporting her dad. She now coaches what is believed to be the first walking football team specifically dedicated to women with Parkinson’s, the Parkinson’s Pioneers, who train in Solihull and have seen a tenfold increase in their membership in just over three years. That led to her appointment as the coach of the first England women’s national side.

There are reportedly about 166,000 people in the UK living with Parkinson’s disease. It is a progressive brain condition for which there is no cure, but known treatments can help reduce the severity of the main symptoms. Darvill, who says exercise “helped slow down the progression of the disease” for her dad, recalled: “When he was first diagnosed, it hits you hard. But football genuinely saved his life.

“At first, he didn’t want to leave the house. He used to have a season ticket at Tottenham [but] he gave that up. He didn’t tell any of his friends. He just stopped doing everything. He really struggled with life in general, [even] getting out of bed. And then we found this football session. His team’s called Fighting Fit Football [based at Watford’s training ground]. I took him along one week and he’s never looked back since.

“So, just to be able to give back a little bit, I guess that’s why I still do it: to help others who get diagnosed, to show them that there is still a life after being diagnosed with the disease and you can meet lots of incredible people, and still try to do things as normally as possible.”

View image in fullscreen Gemma Darvill’s first coaching role was with the Parkinson’s Pioneers, a team she helped set up in 2023.

Darvill, who has played football since she was 10, was spotted cheering for her dad on the sidelines of a tournament at St George’s Park and was promptly asked by Annie Booth, the founder of the Parkinson’s Pioneers, if she would be interested in helping set up the team. To Darvill, helping out felt natural: “I’ve always coached football as well as played, and I was a teacher, so I used to run football camps for kids in the school holidays.”

Booth and Darvill have seen the Parkinson’s Pioneers blossom into a flourishing community, explaining: “I remember our very first training session, it was only three of us. We now have over 40 ladies coming to the sessions. It’s incredible.

“They use it as a social network as well. So after the sessions, everyone stays for a bit of food, a conversation, and they can just discuss like their symptoms, how they’re coping. And we’re family now, really, if I’m honest. Everyone just helps each other out.

“We train at Solihull purely because the ladies come from all over the country. We have ladies from Manchester, we have myself coming from Milton Keynes, we have people in Devon.

“So it’s the most central location that we could find to try to make it as fair as possible for everyone travelling. So we try to meet up once a month and then we enter the tournaments as well.”

As well as prohibiting running, walking football includes several different rules to the mainstream game. There is no offside rule, no heading, no throw-ins and it is a non-contact game. Darvill says: “I’d say the tactics are the same [in general]. But you can’t tackle from the side or from behind in walking football – it has to be face-on.

View image in fullscreen Darvill’s first involvement with walking football for people with Parkinson’s came through helping her father after his diagnosis.

“Everyone with Parkinson’s has a very different level of the condition. The walking element just helps keep them all safe. We have a brilliant physio on board as well who is specifically a Parkinson’s physio, which is brilliant, and she helps us a lot with the warm-ups and the cool-downs and just makes sure that ladies are getting what they need. It makes their brain think about something else. [For example] I’ve got one lady who can’t walk in a straight line but if you put a sports ladder down in front of her, she can walk through it. It’s really interesting.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The growth of the Pioneers meant that Darvill was the natural pick when the Walking Football Association (WFA) was launching the first England women’s Parkinson’s team with trials last year. Then, in August this year, the WFA and the Football Association announced a new partnership that will install the FA as walking football’s governing body in England with the WFA now the delivery partner for the game. The collaboration was partly aimed at benefits such as being able to streamline the registration of referees and agree on a unified set of rules. Darvill adds: “That’s a positive, going forward, that they’re coming together a little bit more.”

Darvill’s England team play six-a-side and the players range in age from 36 to 66. They have held training sessions in Watford, Droitwich and Bedford so far, but are about to cross the Atlantic to join the England men’s Parkinson’s team on a landmark trip to Canada for an international showcase of the benefits of walking football and a series of invitational friendlies.

The team travel on Saturday for one week in Toronto. The teams have been crowdfunding to try to help cover the course of the trip. Darvill’s own fundraising page has raised over £400 and a wider fundraising page for both the men’s and women’s sides has drawn in more than £17,000. Darvill says: “We’re doing it because we want to raise awareness of Parkinson’s in Canada and help those out there with Parkinson’s. We’re trying to showcase sort of what we do, to try to reach more people.

“We’re going to play two American teams when we’re out there, an over-40s team and over-60s all women’s walking football team [non-disabled], and then we’re going to play some men’s teams as well. We’re running a Parkinson’s fundraising day too, where we will run the session ourselves, we’ll put on the coaching drills and have a bit of fun to try to get as many people in Canada interested.”

For Darvill, it is a mission with a deeply personal motivation, with her own gratitude to walking football for how it is helping her dad continuing to drive her to help others with the condition.

Sports.title: ‘That’s how it started’: Dambrauskas’ journey from Who Wants to Be a Millionaire to Champions League
Sports.content:
Valdas Dambrauskas can reel off the questions and answers without a moment’s pause. Who won the first Academy Award for best actor in 1929? It was Emil Jannings, even if someone else might have been tempted to go with Charlie Chaplin. Which country publishes the highest number of daily newspapers? India was the clear winner. Can you name the nation that produces the most electricity per capita in the world? His family, watching back home, clasped heads in hands but he was right: back then, in 2002, the answer was his native Lithuania.

It was enough to win Dambrauskas about £725 in his appearance on Six Zeros – A Million, the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? “At that time it was quite big money,” he says. “I could have bought a flat in my home town; it was a very difficult period there and they were almost free. But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started.”

More than two and a half decades later the story continues at Old Trafford where Dambrauskas will manage the Azerbaijani champions, Sabah, in their Champions League debut on Thursday night. The club’s journey is some tale in itself given Sabah, who came through a dramatic playoff with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, did not exist until 2017. But the path taken by their head coach, a 25-year-old office worker with only a modest football background when his general knowledge skills were put on display, is virtually unparalleled in the modern game.

The money he won helped Dambrauskas and his girlfriend, now wife, to move to north London and establish themselves in an alien environment. “I would have done it anyway – the show came in the middle of our planning,” he says of the move, which became an ambition after a work visit to Norway in 2000.

In Scandinavia he had grasped the extent of the Premier League’s incipient popularity. “I realised this was where real football is. There was no pathway to coaching in Lithuania if you hadn’t been a player; it was impossible. But if I could take a course in England, maybe I could get a chance to step on the ladder at home.”

Dambrauskas spent eight years in London. “The start was very, very difficult. I wasn’t speaking decent English, had no contacts, we didn’t know anyone, we lived in different places, did all kinds of jobs.” He worked in a Muswell Hill pub, delivered newspapers in the area, held down jobs in a nursery school, as a gardener, in sales, and as a self-employed handyman, often simultaneously. The hours were relentless but so was the young man’s focus.

Dambrauskas during his appearance on Lithuania’s version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Photograph: x

It was a life of an immigrant couple straining every sinew to make their way. Their first child was born in 2004; by then Dambrauskas, who had studied philosophy and social sciences in Lithuania, had enrolled on a sports science and coaching course at London Metropolitan University. From his classroom on the 10th floor he could see the Emirates Stadium sprouting up during that spell of Arsenal invincibility.

The Access to Sports Project, based in Finsbury Park, is a stone’s throw from Arsenal but galaxies away in another sense. It is where Dambrauskas landed his first coaching role, giving sessions to children on Saturday mornings and during school holidays. His next step is all the more remarkable for what has passed since. A round of interviews with Manchester United Soccer Schools brought the chance to work with youngsters around the country, and sometimes on residential trips abroad, under the banner of the then serial title winners. Despite the name it was a far cry from even academy football, but the injection of confidence was transformative.

“It was John Shiels, CEO of the Manchester United Foundation, who gave me the chance. I don’t know what he saw in me – I came in with very broken English and couldn’t express myself as I can now – but he really supported me. At the end of the year he wrote me an appraisal of what I’d done. He said that I was good and could do much more. It was a massive, massive boost for me.”

Through a friend at university, Dambrauskas became involved with the community sports organisation London Tigers. “He told me they always needed coaches.” Eventually he took charge of their semi-professional team, which played in the Spartan South Midlands League. “That was where it really started, coaching at some kind of level.” It meant managing in the FA Vase and the early rounds of the FA Cup.

Dambrauskas also undertook part-time roles at Fulham and Brentford before working as a sports activator for Central YMCA on Tottenham Court Road. He would later take a broader role as sports development manager at London Tigers and took his coaching badges at the London Football Association. “It was a time with no holidays, no days off. I’m a big reader, I read all the time and studied constantly. Sometimes I would finish my university work on the bus. I took every kind of education I could and went to every possible course for every meeting.

“Over the years I had countless interviews for coaching roles, for jobs at centres of excellency in London and outside, so many CVs and applications, but I understood early on that it’s very difficult in England to get on the ladder and that to coach at professional level there was probably impossible. If there is a story where someone is starting in the community scheme and going all the way to become a head coach, I am still to find it.”

View image in fullscreen Dambrauskas geeing up his players during his spell in charge of Hajduk Split, which ended in 2022. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

By late 2010 he felt ready to pursue what had originally been the end goal: a role in Lithuania. He had started working with their under-17s and agreed to join Ekranas, national champions at the time, as assistant manager. “I had the London Tigers job, 15 hours a week at Brentford and some other things here and there. We had a good life and people thought I was crazy going back home and earning about a fifth of what I was getting in England. But the biggest risk in life is not to take risks.

“I’m forever grateful to my wife for being behind me. We always faced questions: twenty- or thirtysomething guy always studying, trying to work in football, spending all his money on books and courses rather than buying an apartment or something for the family. But I’m very happy with how it turned out and nobody questions those decisions now.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A kaleidoscopic career bloomed. By December 2014 he had become head coach at Zalgiris Vilnius, the biggest club in Lithuania, winning two more league titles and various cups in a move that felt unthinkable during a humble upbringing in the tiny northern town Pakruojis. “My childhood was not a gift. My dad died when I was 11, and if he knew that I had the job at Zalgiris and that we won so many trophies he would be the happiest person in the world.”

Dambrauskas was not content to stop there. “You are basically nobody and suddenly you get this job. Then you have to prove yourself to everybody again and again and again. So you reached this step on the ladder but what’s next? How do you go to the next level?”

After three years he joined the upwardly mobile Latvian club RFS but harboured concerns about the prospects of leaving the small Baltic football bubble. In the event he need not have worried. Since 2020 he has managed in Croatia with Gorica and Hajduk Split – the latter are “like a tattoo you can’t ever take out, it leaves a mark on you” – in Bulgaria with Ludogorets, in Greece with OFI Crete, in Cyprus with Omonia and with the Hungarian club Diosgyor, who he describes as having “one of the biggest hidden football potentials in Europe”.

Itinerant career paths such as that are, especially in eastern and southern Europe, nothing new. But Sabah had been courting Dambrauskas for two years before he took over in 2025. Once the stars had aligned, he worked a miracle. In 2024-25, Sabah had finished 41 points behind the biggest club in Azerbaijan, Qarabag. Last season Sabah beat them to the title by nine points, earning their crack at the Champions League qualifiers. “I’m really grateful to Qarabag. Every game against them is like taking a master’s degree.”

View image in fullscreen Dambrauskas embraces a Sabah fan after presiding over a 4-1 aggregate victory against The New Saints in Champions League qualifying. Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images

He waxes lyrical about the stability and facilities available at well-backed Sabah, who were cheered on with fervour befitting a national team when they thrillingly overcame an injury-time deficit against Be’er Sheva. Their success has come with a multinational squad that plays bold, front-foot football in the style he preaches. “But if you don’t understand the human being in front of you, it’s very difficult to pass him your ideas and build trust,” he says.

“What is important in east Africa can be completely different from what someone needs in west Africa or anywhere across Europe. You need to be able to understand different cultures, different traditions, different ways of speaking or behaving. Without that it’s impossible to do anything, and I believe this is where my strength lies.”

It is a glorious piece of circularity that Dambrauskas and Sabah will be watched from the stands on Thursday by a number of his old colleagues from Manchester United Soccer Schools. He beams at the thought; none of this could have seemed remotely attainable during their time on the grass together. “But I had this belief. I had this confidence all the time that I could do it.”

He is equally delighted that the draw has also brought a January visit to Arsenal, that huge presence in his eyeline during those years studying on Holloway Road. He is 49 and would surely lever himself among Europe’s most sought-after coaching properties if he can take Sabah further. “We’re going to respect everyone but not be afraid of anyone. There’s a very nice song by the Lithuanian band Colours of Bubbles called Truth or Dare. Very soon we’re going to find out the truth about ourselves and what we can do. It will be very beneficial for us because I don’t want this club to be a one-day wonder.” As final answers go, it may be his most significant yet.

Sports.title: Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat Atlético
Sports.content:
It was the time and place for Alexis Mac Allister to do his talking on the pitch and the disgruntled Liverpool midfielder delivered on cue. “Very sad” over Liverpool’s refusal to offer him a new contract, while Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were getting theirs, Mac Allister made Anfield very happy with a match-winning display against Atlético Madrid.

The Argentina international, one of five World Cup finalists involved in an absorbing, delicately-poised contest, vented his frustrations in the best possible and most professional way – from behind an immaculate 20-yard strike into Jan Oblak’s goal rather than a microphone. Mac Allister believes he is playing for a new deal this season and promised to give “100% to my last day” at the pre-match press conference. He was true to his word to extend Atlético’s winless sequence against English opposition in the Champions League league phase to 11 matches.

For Andoni Iraola, it was the perfect start to life as a Champions League coach after an imperfect start to the game. Diego Simeone’s switch to a 3-5-2 formation caught Liverpool cold and it was only when they regrouped in the aftermath of Marcos Llorente’s latest Anfield goal, and again during the half-time interval, that their performance level improved. Mac Allister’s timely moment, Alexander Isak’s relentless industry, Florian Wirtz’s creativity and another performance of drive and intelligence from Szoboszlai ensured the Liverpool head coach had plenty to savour.

“I have to blame myself a bit for the start of the game,” Iraola said. “Atlético surprised us with the way they approached the game. They haven’t used that system too much this season and it’s difficult if you are not ready for it, but we adjusted and played better. In the second half we were the best team. We came back for the third time [this season] and that showed the players are pushing and they have character.”

It was a night of firsts. Iraola coached a Champions League game for the first time in his career – he did take charge of 12 Europa League matches with AEK Larnaca in 2018-19 – Bradley Barcola made his first Liverpool start following a £123m move from Paris Saint-Germain and Julián Álvarez was in Atlético’s starting lineup for the first time this season since his failed attempt to join Barcelona. All appeared to have been forgiven – for now at least – as his name was cheered by the small pocket of Atlético fans when the teams were announced before kick-off and he repaid them by creating the opening goal.

View image in fullscreen Dominik Szoboszlai scores Liverpool’s equaliser late in the first half. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Llorente was the scourge of Anfield yet again when Álvarez threaded a pass behind the home defence and the right wing-back raced clear on goal. The man who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice to eliminate Jürgen Klopp’s team from the competition in 2020, in the game played while Madrid was in lockdown from the Covid pandemic, lofted a confident finish beyond Alisson. It was Llorente’s fifth goal at Anfield, half of his entire total of Champions League goals. He had been kept onside by Milos Kerkez, who endured a poor night with his positioning and distribution before atoning with a key role in Liverpool’s equaliser.

Álvarez almost doubled the visitors’ lead when granted far too much time and space to take aim from almost 30 yards. Alisson, at full stretch, intervened with a superb finger-tip save. Anfield was growing restless at Liverpool’s carelessness on the ball and Atlético’s comfort on it. But the threat and control from the hosts increased.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wirtz drew a fine save from Oblak at the end of a flowing move involving Barcola and Isak. Liverpool then drew level thanks to tenacity from Kerkez, a lovely touch from Ronald Araújo and Szoboszlai’s instinctive finish. The left-back won possession with a clean, crunching challenge on Lee Kang-in before finding Barcola. The France international was denied a goal on his full debut by Oblak’s low save but Wirtz kept the pressure on and Szoboszlai, having been halted on the edge of the area, got a second bite from Araújo’s clever flick. The midfielder’s first time shot sailed into the far corner.

Barcola should have put Liverpool ahead when played through on goal by Wirtz early in the second half. The winger had time to measure the finish but pulled it wide of Oblak’s right-hand post. He would later depart with cramp. Liverpool were ahead one minute later when the lively Rio Ngumoha beat Llorente and his cross fell to Mac Allister via a deflection off Isak. Mac Allister told Szoboszlai to leave the ball and drilled home an unstoppable left-footed drive from 20 yards. Atlético remained dangerous and the introduction of Ademola Lookman added an extra dimension to the visitors’ attack but Liverpool defended impressively to secure a deserved victory.

Sports.title: Champions League roundup: Raphinha shines as Barcelona thrash Feyenoord
Sports.content:
Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.

There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.

“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” the Barcelona head coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”

Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred as Paris Saint-Germain began their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 at the Parc des Princes.

View image in fullscreen Paris Saint-Germain’s Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their fifth goal with Ousmane Dembélé. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.

Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.

Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.
