World.title: Hundreds of thousands lack adequate shelter at Sudan’s Tawila camp
World.content:
Blue tents stand in tight rows at the Daba Naira camp in Tawila, 68 kilometres west of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur in Sudan, racked by war.

The tents were set up by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), with support from the Turkish Disaster and Emergency Management Authority.

Relief teams have erected 3,000 new tents in recent months, but the number is negligible compared with the needs of more than 665,000 displaced people, the IOM said in a statement.

The most pressing question remains: how can this number of tents possibly be enough for hundreds of thousands of displaced people, especially when rainfall threatens to turn the low‑lying ground into swamps?

Promises of aid

Abdelbagi Mohamed Hamid, the minister of social welfare and humanitarian affairs coordinator in the Darfur region, told Al Jazeera Arabic that the regional government appealed to donors, including the Turkish ambassador, to provide tents for the displaced.

As a result, Turkiye allocated 30,000 tents to be distributed in Darfur and Kordofan through the IOM. Abdelbagi said 3,000 of 6,000 expected tents were erected in the Daba Naira camp in Tawila. Another 2,450 were delivered to the Salam, al‑Wihda and al‑Nakheel camps in Shaeria locality in South and East Darfur.

The minister said the Malha locality had the greatest need for humanitarian assistance in Darfur, followed by Tina, Karnoy and Um Baru areas. The Tina border crossing should be opened to allow the delivery of aid to these isolated areas, which suffer from acute shortages of food, medicine and fuel, while the war has deepened their isolation and worsened their humanitarian situation, he said.



Abdelbagi warned that providing shelter alone is not enough to confront the crisis, given the looming danger of famine, which could prove deadlier than the war itself, as humanitarian organisations struggle to reach many affected regions.

Worn‑out tents

The arrival of the new tents coincided with the beginning of the rainy season and an outbreak of fires sweeping through displacement camps, increasing the suffering of displaced people living under tattered canopies without protection from wind and rain, amid acute shortages of food, clean water and healthcare.

The IOM warned of persistent and worsening humanitarian needs in Tawila, as services deteriorate and diseases like cholera spread amid a lack of clean drinking water, resulting in watery diarrhoea and skin infections. The camps are overcrowded and lack basic sanitation.

The organisation, while continuing to expand the number of shelters in the Daba Naira camp, cannot keep up with the rapid pace of displacement.

‘Dropping like flies’

Ahmed Mousa, a displaced man from el-Fasher who is staying in the Daba Naira camp, told Al Jazeera that the new tents do not cover even a tenth of the camp’s needs, with people sleeping in the rain in the open and children falling ill without adequate care.

Fatima Ibrahim, a displaced woman in the same camp, said people fled el-Fasher in search of safety – only to find themselves exposed to the elements, hunger and disease.

“We see the new tents from afar, but they are not enough. We are dropping like flies from hunger and disease. Our children fall ill before our eyes, and we don’t even have medicine,” she said, adding that many families slept on bare ground without protection from the cold of night and the heat of day.

Famine ‘may be more dangerous than war’

The Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Darfur region, Al‑Sadiq Barango, told Al Jazeera in a statement that the famine may be more dangerous than the war, amid declining seasonal rains and the drying of agricultural lands and livestock pastures.

He says the war has driven farmers to abandon their land, while cultivated areas, particularly fruit farms and cash‑crop plantations, have been attacked and destroyed by armed groups.

Barango described the situation as “ominous signs of a looming catastrophe,” and called for urgent humanitarian intervention, as starvation threatens thousands of people across Sudan, with Darfur the most affected due to years of conflict and the collapse of agricultural infrastructure.

‘Tawila is not just numbers’

Tawila hosts about 665,000 displaced people, most of whom fled el-Fasher and its surroundings, according to the IOM’s statement. Their number had more than doubled between March and September 2025, from 238,000 to more than 652,000.



More than 70 percent of households in Tawila lack healthcare, while half of families have been unable to obtain treatment, according to the organisation’s estimates. Children under the age of five and pregnant women are the most affected, with rising rates of malnutrition and infectious diseases.

Adam Rijal, spokesperson for the Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees, told Al Jazeera that “Tawila is not just numbers,” noting that needs exceed capacities dozens of times over, and warning of more deaths, especially among children and the elderly, due to hunger, disease and the absence of basic services.

Relief challenges

Humanitarian organisations face major difficulties reaching displaced people because of rough terrain and the spread of checkpoints belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which is at war with the Sudanese government and controls vital routes in the area.

Local activists say that aid trucks are sometimes subjected to looting and extortion, which raises the cost of relief and delays its arrival to those who need it. Many displaced people – according to field reports – have been forced to walk long distances to obtain limited food rations, while others go weeks without assistance.

In Tawila, where hundreds of thousands live in worn‑out tents amid disease outbreaks and the hazards of the rainy season, the need for shelter, food and care is growing, while 3,000 tents are nowhere near enough to confront a humanitarian catastrophe that is worsening by the day.

World.title: At least 25 dead after cargo ship catches fire in China
World.content:
Fire breaks out on ship being repaired in the port of Qingdao, eastern China.

Share At least 25 dead after cargo ship catches fire in China on social media

At least 25 people have died after a foreign-flagged cargo ship caught fire while docked in a Chinese port, state media reported.

Of the 42 people on board, 12 were safely evacuated, while five were hospitalised with injuries and were in stable condition, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Thursday.

State news agency Xinhua said the fire broke out at about 11:15am (03:15 GMT) while the ship was docked for repairs at the Beihai Shipbuilding Company at the port of Qingdao, a major shipping hub on the northeastern Chinese coast.

It was unclear what had caused the fire or whether it had been extinguished.

A photo released by Xinhua identified the ship as the Ocean Melody, which sails under a Liberian flag, according to the public vessel-tracking website VesselFinder.

President Xi Jinping called for urgent search-and-rescue operations.

He “stressed the need to urgently search for missing persons … and strictly hold those responsible to account”, Xinhua reported.

Premier Li Qiang called for the search and rescue of “trapped” people, and for those injured to receive medical treatment.

He also urged authorities to “strictly prevent secondary disasters”.

Xi said “all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards.”

World.title: Trump says every adult American will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he would offer every adult American a $5,000 (Â£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November's midterm elections â a plan that would cost more than a trillion dollars.

The offer was made in a speech at the party's first-ever convention in the middle of a US presidential term.

He gave no details on how it would work or be funded â saying only that the money would have to be spent in the US. Vice-President JD Vance has linked the plan to the revenue that Trump has raised from US tariffs on imported goods.

Democrats labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was legal or feasible.

It may be the first time a US president offered such a payout to Americans, in the context of an election year plea to get out and vote.

The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.

There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.

Questions have begun to be raised about whether his plan is feasible â especially as prices rise in the US, partially as a result of the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.

Iran's retaliation has included attacks against US bases and allies in the Gulf â but crucially it has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit.

The blockage has caused fluctuations in oil prices worldwide and Trump has faced pressure from his party to end the war.

On Wednesday, the US president warned his supporters that the war would not end until after the midterms and that oil prices would not come down until then.

He made the comments ahead of his speech in Texas, repeating it at the convention where he argued that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.

World.title: Watch: Is Trump's $5,000 election pledge legal?
World.content:
Donald Trump has pledged $5,000 (Â£3,700) to every American if the Republicans win the midterm elections in November.

The US president offered no details on how the plan would work or where the money would come from.

Democrats labelled it an "empty promise" and others have questioned whether such a pledge is even legal

BBC North America editor Sarah Smith looks into whether Trump's promise - which would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion - stands up.

World.title: Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.

"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.

He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the Republican Party's first midterm election convention â and repeated them there, arguing that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons.

Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

The conflict rapidly spread across the Middle East, as Iran retaliated by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Arab states hosting US military facilities.

The price of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, has risen above the $100 (Â£74) mark three times over the past six months, with Iranian attacks forcing production stoppages in Gulf states and disrupting exports through the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway.

The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran's ports and has recently begun striking Iranian tankers in response to attacks on warships and other vessels.

"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" â an apparent reference to the Democrats â "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".

He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons and insisted its nuclear programme is solely peaceful.

At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".

In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".

Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".

The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from fuel to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings â and pressure from those within his party, including staunch supporters, to quickly end the war.

Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing control on Congress.

At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.

Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and other goods that require shipping.

The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.

There are also predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates.

World.title: Five dead and 86 missing as 'heartbreaking' fire breaks out on Philippines ferry
World.content:
At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.

The MV June Aster, which set off from Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron when it caught fire.

The blaze, which erupted at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and thick smoke were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.

A survivor said he floated in the sea for two hours before he got rescued. "It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," Roland Lerma told the BBC.

World.title: Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
World.content:
"My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.

Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".

She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.

"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.

His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.

Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.

Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.

World.title: Twenty-five dead after fire on cargo ship in eastern China
World.content:
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.

Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.

The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.

Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.

World.title: Apple's new boss starts with big gamble on £1,999 first folding iPhone
World.content:
Apple has launched its most expensive iPhone ever - a foldable handheld that costs at least Â£1,999 and marks the first major iPhone design change in almost 20 years.

The iPhone Duo is a gamble by new boss John Ternus, who took over from long-time chief executive Tim Cook this month.

Apple is entering the foldable phone market comparatively late, following the likes of South Korea's Samsung and China's Huawei.

Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters: "Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together." Apple's model, he claimed "redefine[s] the experience of using a foldable phone".

In the US, prices start at $1,999, but can go up to $3,200. It has taken eight years to develop, something Ternus was directly involved in after spending many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division.

When unfolded, it looks like a small iPad and a wider iPhone when it is folded.

Ternus said: "It's entirely new and at the same time remarkably familiar. A similar size to your passport, it feels familiar to hold and comfortable to use with one hand."

But the product is facing established competitors. "The real fight is China, where Huawei owns nearly 80% of foldables." said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for data and analytics, devices at IDC EMEA.

World.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
World.content:
Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.

The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.

On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.

SÃ¡nchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".

The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."

It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.

The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on SÃ¡nchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.

Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.

However, SÃ¡nchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.

Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".

But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.

"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester MuÃ±oz of the conservative People's Party.

Jorge BuxadÃ©, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that SÃ¡nchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".

The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.

Foreign Minister JosÃ© Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have foreseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".

A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".

Miguel Ãngel PÃ©rez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.

"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

World.title: When a black scholar becomes a symbol: The Jason Arday controversy, By Toyin Falola
World.content:
Occasionally, what a person achieves eclipses who they are. They may be allowed into an institution because of scholarship, research, intellectual contribution, or intellectual promise. But that credential can come to matter more than they do. Their appointment becomes a symbol of advancement. Their success becomes a testament to diversification. Their failure, if it ever occurs, can become something bigger than individual disappointment. It can become justification as to why people like them shouldn’t have been there to fail in the first place. This is just one of many tough questions raised during a panel discussion about Jason Arday. When Jason Arday was appointed Professor of Sociology at the University of Cambridge in 2023, he was thrust into the spotlight as the youngest black professor at Cambridge, and his research involves race, inequality, higher education and mental health. His ascent was symbolic of more than just individual achievement. It took place during hundreds of years of racial exclusion in UK academia and alongside universities’ modern attempts to brand themselves as inclusive.

But visibility also has a price often left out of conversations about diversity. The more visible a person’s presence becomes at an institution, the more unusual that presence is thought to be, the easier it is for that person to become symbolic of that institution. Jason Arday was no longer just Jason Arday the scholar, researcher, and teacher. His presence on that faculty was used as proof that Cambridge was changing. It can also be used as proof, by those against such changes, that Cambridge has reduced its standards or changed them. This is what I called the “representational burden”. Representational burden occurs when a scholar becomes more than just themselves in the eyes of an institution. Their success is now symbolic of a whole group of people. And if they fail, they also fail as that representative body. The burden starts when we value or deplore a scholar not only for their own actions and successes, but for what their presence means about the wider institution. Do universities praise that scholar’s success as a successful scholar or as proof of diversity? Do critics judge that scholar as an individual or as a “representational body”?

Which brings me to the issue of academic scrutiny. Scrutiny is not the problem. Universities require it. Scholarly activity requires criticism, evidence, and even questioning of claims. If a scholar comes from a historically oppressed minority, he or she cannot rightfully claim protection from legitimate criticism just because they claim marginalization. However, just because there are legitimate standards does not mean they are always applied with equal vigor, nor that they don’t harbor biases. The tough part, then, is not deciding if academic integrity should be protected. It’s deciding if it is protected fairly, without double standards, and by means that can differentiate an allegation from fact.

That mattered particularly in relation to discussion about Arday’s academic record and the subsequent investigation of his background. Professor Lester split the discussion about Arday’s academic conduct from the later scrutiny of his personal history. He confirmed errors had been made in Arday’s academic attributions but said claims relating to Arday’s PhD thesis had already been investigated by the awarding body. According to Prof. Lester’s account, that investigation identified citation errors but considered them excusable. Prof. Lester also argued that some of the extraordinary claims associated with Arday’s life story had subsequently acquired evidence, while others remained difficult to substantiate. His larger point was that questions surrounding a person’s biography should not automatically be transformed into evidence about the integrity of that person’s academic publications.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This distinction is more than a technical one. It invites us to consider what happens when the biography of a public figure becomes part of the process through which that person’s intellectual credibility is judged. A scholar may have an imperfect biography. The individual might distort the event in his mind, exaggerate the situation, misconstrue the occurrence, make statements that will not be easy to verify later, or recount his life story in accordance with the memoir format. In itself, none of this invalidates the individual’s scholarship. Academic claims and autobiographical claims belong to different categories and require different forms of evaluation. Once those categories are collapsed, however, suspicion begins to accumulate. A question about citation can become a question about biography; a question about biography can become a question about character; and a question about character can then be used to cast doubt upon professional achievement. Individual allegations begin to reinforce one another even when they do not possess the same evidentiary basis.

The media becomes particularly important at this point because public scrutiny does not remain within the university. According to Professor Lester’s account during the discussion, after Nathan Cofnas published a blog accusing Arday of plagiarism, 274 British press articles appeared within 22 days. Professor Lester further stated that 23 of these were connected in some way to the Free-Speech Union network associated with Toby Young, that 19 appeared after Arday’s resignation, and that 21 were published in The Spectator. He argued that the initial plagiarism allegations had not been proven and that the scrutiny subsequently expanded into Arday’s character and life story. These figures and interpretations are Professor Lester’s account of the media campaign and should therefore be understood as part of his argument about the controversy.

Yet the larger media question remains significant beyond the accuracy of any individual figure. When an allegation is being reiterated frequently to become the primary narrative associated with an individual, what does happen? Repetition has its own peculiar effect. When an allegation starts off as a claim that needs to be backed up with evidence, frequent iteration of that allegation in newspapers, on websites, on social media, and in analysis could transform it into a familiar piece of information; familiarity could then easily take the place of proof. It is more likely for the audience to recall the allegation rather than the qualification made in it. That does not mean that the act of scrutiny by the media is itself an illegitimate act. The media plays a crucial role in raising questions regarding powerful organisations. Yet, the frequency of scrutiny does become relevant when an identifiable individual is being scrutinised.

This raises another question that emerged from the discussion: who has the authority to judge an academic? A university has procedures for investigating misconduct. External examiners possess disciplinary expertise. Academic colleagues understand the conventions of their fields. Journalists may investigate matters of legitimate public interest, while the wider public has an interest in institutions that receive public legitimacy and resources. But these forms of authority are not interchangeable. A newspaper allegation is not a university finding. A social-media campaign is not a disciplinary investigation. Public suspicion is not the same thing as academic judgment. Once these distinctions disappear, the authority to judge becomes dispersed among actors who do not necessarily possess the same evidence, expertise, or responsibility.

Professor Shose Kessi pushed this question further by drawing attention to the way institutional processes operate. She did not argue against investigation. Instead, she emphasized the need to examine the process through which investigations are conducted: who sits on committees, what criteria are used, how complaints are handled and how conclusions are reached. A procedure can appear neutral while containing less visible practices that produce different outcomes for different groups. When multiple complaints repeatedly concern a particular demographic, the institution, she argued, has a responsibility to examine its own practices rather than treating every case as an isolated problem.

This changes the question from whether rules exist to how rules operate. Institutions can possess formally neutral procedures while applying those procedures unevenly. The existence of a rule does not by itself establish equality. What matters is how the rule is interpreted, who is subjected to it, who is protected by it, and whose circumstances are considered relevant when judgment is made. This is particularly important in academic institutions because universities do not simply judge scholarship. They also judge people. They determine who is appointed, promoted, funded, supported and recognized as authoritative. The procedures through which these decisions are made therefore become part of the production of academic legitimacy itself.

The distinction between critique and attack becomes important for the same reason. Sabelo McInziba argued that there is a difference between engaging critically with a scholar’s work and turning criticism into personal attack and slander. He suggested that the engagement with Arday had moved beyond ordinary scholarly criticism and involved deeper, organized interests. Yet his argument also returned to the importance of process. Different groups may contribute to testing allegations, but their participation must be grounded in the integrity of the process. The integrity of the process is as important as the outcome. The issue, therefore, is not whether criticism should be permitted. An academy without criticism would cease to be one. The issue is whether criticism remains connected to evidence and proportionality. Academic integrity cannot be defended by abandoning the procedures through which integrity is established. If the process becomes detached from evidence, consistency, and fairness, then academic integrity itself becomes vulnerable. What begins as an effort to protect standards can become an exercise in institutional power. The distinction between critique and attack is consequently not merely semantic. It is a distinction between challenging knowledge and discrediting a person.

There is another difficulty that becomes visible when a Black scholar achieves an extraordinary position. As the story grows more extraordinary, the easier it will be for the institution and society to turn that individual into an inspirational icon. The life of Arday had already been constructed in the discourse of human potential: an individual who has faced many difficulties in his early life, yet has managed to reach one of the most prestigious positions within British academia. There is something powerful about such a story. But there is also a danger in making the inspirational narrative the primary meaning of the person. Once a scholar becomes a symbol of possibility, the individual may be denied the ordinary human permission to be imperfect.

This is when the idea of Black excellence raises its complications. Excellent achievement is important, but the requirement of outstanding work hides an unpleasant truth. If Black academics have to prove their exceptional talent in order to be accepted in an institution, then the glorification of such exceptionalism might actually reinforce the obstacles they had to overcome. An exceptional individual becomes proof of how well the system works, while the structures that have made this success exceptional stay unnoticed. One succeeded, and the institution used that success to claim that it was open. The question of how many equally capable people were never given the opportunity to succeed remains unanswered.

To be clear, the story should not be reduced to a simple narrative of triumph over adversity because such a reading can obscure the structures that determine whose potential is recognised, cultivated, funded, and encouraged. The remarkable individual can become the centre of the story while the institutional conditions surrounding that individual disappear from view. The more useful question is therefore not simply how one person overcame barriers, but how many people with potential never received the opportunity to demonstrate what they could become.

Professor Christine Vogt-William approached the problem through the related ideas of invisibility and hyper-surveillance. For black and minority ethnic academics, there can exist an awkward balance whereby they are not being recognised enough as intellectual subjects but are seen very much indeed when things go awry. Good news may be seen as an exception and lucky coincidence, whereas bad news becomes inflated. The result is a paradoxical form of visibility: the scholar can be visible as a representative of diversity without necessarily being fully recognised as an intellectual individual. This helps explain why the Arday controversy cannot simply be collapsed into the question of whether racism existed or whether academic misconduct should be investigated. These questions must remain conceptually distinct while still allowing us to examine the conditions under which they interact.

Professor Vogt-William’s intervention also introduced the question of consistency. Her question revolved around how universities like Cambridge and Ghent can hire academics for whom she felt her views of race realism and scientific racism applied, whereas there is a great deal of focus on the hiring and research of Arday. She raised this question on the grounds of consistency within institutions: If academic legitimacy is argued so strongly in one case, then is it not reasonable to raise similar questions in another? Rather, it raises the larger issue of whether principles such as merit, academic integrity, and institutional standards retain the same meaning when applied to different people.

This is where the individual case begins to open into a structural question. Jason Arday’s story matters not only because of what happened to one scholar but because it forces us to examine the conditions under which certain people enter institutions of authority. Who is believed to possess intellectual potential? Who receives the resources necessary to develop that potential? Who is encouraged when they struggle? Who is scrutinized when they succeed? Who is permitted to make mistakes without those mistakes becoming evidence against an entire category of people? These questions move the discussion away from the individual and toward the institution that determines how individuals are recognised in the first place.

The academy requires standards and criticism. Accountability is also required here, although in a way that does not confuse the issue of fairness about whom the accountability applies to, what evidence is, who gets to judge, and how judgment is carried out. In the absence of such clarification, accountability turns into a form of performance, scrutiny becomes a form of punishment, and academic integrity turns into a language through which institutional power is exerted. The real question is, of course, not whether Jason Arday was perfect. He was human. The question is whether an academy committed to equality can allow its Black scholars to be human while still holding them to serious intellectual standards. An equal academy is not one in which Black scholars are protected from criticism. It is a criticism that is moderated by the same rules of evidence, balance, and proportion as criticism of anyone else. It is not an institution where Black intellectuals are celebrated because they are Black, or where their Blackness makes them even more subject to skepticism. It is an academy in which they are allowed to be scholars first.

The controversy surrounding Jason Arday therefore leaves us with a difficult proposition. And perhaps it is not only about who gets accepted in the academy, but about what happens to them after they join. Because inclusion cannot be measured in terms of how many Black scholars are occupying positions of power. One must take into account the nature of the kind of scrutiny they face, the kind of flaws they can commit, and the kind of support they receive, as well as whether they are allowed to lead their lives as individuals or as symbols. Once one asks the question in such a way, the issue becomes not only about the life story of a particular person. The issue becomes about what the academy does. How an institution recognises intelligence and makes opportunities available to certain individuals, and how it constructs notions of merit in response to people who were previously marginalised moving to the position of power.

The Arday question therefore does not end with the controversy surrounding Jason Arday. It begins there. His story forces us to look beyond the individual and examine the institutional environment into which he entered. The reason we have to ask ourselves why some academics come loaded with representation, why some need to be exceptional in order to be seen as ordinary, and how criteria for determining academic legitimacy might themselves become problematic in light of concerns around race and power. The second question is therefore inescapable: In that the Arday affair was not just about one person’s conduct but also about the processes through which academic authority is constructed, assessed and defended, then how are those processes determined? What constitutes the appearance of neutrality in a university that produces inequalities of recognition, scrutiny and opportunity?

Toyin Falola, a professor of History, University Distinguished Teaching Professor, and Jacob and Frances Sanger Mossiker Chair in the Humanities at The University of Texas at Austin, is the Bobapitan of Ibadanland.

World.title: Police, ADC supporters clash in Kaduna as 2027 campaigns begin
World.content:
Tension erupted in Kaduna on Wednesday as security operatives and supporters of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) clashed during a solidarity walk for the party’s governorship candidate, Isa Ashiru, in the state capital.

The confrontation occurred at or around Murtala Square as ADC supporters gathered for a solidarity march to signal the beginning of the party’s campaign activities ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

The ADC accused the police and the state government of using security operatives and alleged political thugs to disrupt what it described as a peaceful gathering.

The party said tear gas was fired at its supporters, leaving some injured and forcing participants to disperse.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But a government official, who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES, offered a different account, saying the police intervened to prevent a breakdown of law and order and to protect residents and property.

Efforts by PREMIUM TIMES to obtain the police’s version of the incident were unsuccessful as calls to the command’s spokesperson did not go through.

ADC accuses police of disrupting peaceful march

In a statement signed by Mr Ashiru, the ADC governorship candidate, the party described the gathering as a peaceful demonstration by “thousands” of its supporters.

The party said the protesters had gathered “not with weapons, not with stones, not with incitement” but to express support for the ADC and demand what it called a better Kaduna.

The ADC alleged that the APC-led government deployed security operatives and “hired thugs” to disrupt the walk.

It also accused the police of firing tear gas at unarmed supporters.

The party cited Sections 39 and 40 of the 1999 Constitution, which protect freedom of expression and peaceful assembly and association, arguing that the use of force against its supporters amounted to a violation of their constitutional rights.

“The people of Kaduna are not children to be scattered with canisters. They are not subjects to be cowed by hired muscle. They are citizens,” Mr Ashiru said in the statement.

The ADC also referred to a previous Kaduna High Court ruling which it said declared attempts by the police to suspend political gatherings unconstitutional.

The party vowed to continue its political activities despite the incident.

“We will continue to assemble. We will continue to speak. We will continue to organise. We will continue to walk,” Mr Ashiru said.

Government says police intervened to prevent breakdown of law and order

The government official, who doesn’t want his name to be mentioned because he was not authorised to speak on the matter, however, said the police intervened to prevent violence and protect members of the public.

The official said the security agencies acted because of concerns that hoodlums could take advantage of the gathering to destroy the property of innocent residents and disrupt normal activities in the city.

Some people who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES also said several supporters were injured during the confrontation and that tear gas was used to disperse the crowd.

The accounts could not immediately be independently verified.

The incident comes at a politically sensitive moment for Kaduna, with campaigns for the 2027 governorship and State House of Assembly elections officially beginning on 9 September.

Kaduna enters a heated 2027 contest

The confrontation comes as Kaduna enters what is expected to be one of the most competitive governorship contests in northern Nigeria.

Governor Uba Sani of the All Progressives Congress (APC) is seeking a second term, while Mr Ashiru is running again after unsuccessful bids in 2019 and 2023.

Mr Ashiru contested the 2023 election for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and finished second to Mr Sani.

He later moved to the ADC and won its governorship primary in May 2026 with 86,113 votes.

The ADC has since moved to strengthen its campaign organisation.

Mr Ashiru appointed John Ayuba, a former Kaduna commissioner and university lecturer, as Director-General of his campaign council, alongside other officials responsible for operations and administration.

He has also selected former Kaduna State lawmaker, Irimiya Kantitok, as his running mate.

The party’s campaign is also drawing strength from the political realignment involving former Governor Nasir El-Rufai, who has left the APC and joined the ADC.

APC relies on incumbency

Mr Sani, meanwhile, enters the contest with the advantage of incumbency and the political structure of the ruling APC.

He secured the APC governorship ticket through an affirmation process in which he received 459,393 votes.

The governor’s camp has also attracted several politicians who were previously associated with opposition parties, strengthening the APC’s structure ahead of the election.

On Wednesday, the Kaduna APC announced the commencement of its governorship and State House of Assembly campaign, saying it would focus on the achievements of the Sani administration rather than personal attacks on opposition candidates.

World.title: Diphtheria deaths rise to 27 as suspected cases hit 303 in Plateau
World.content:
Twenty-seven people have died from a suspected diphtheria outbreak in Plateau State, while suspected cases have increased to 303, a state health official has said.

The State Epidemiologist, Maren Damulak, disclosed the figures while speaking with journalists in Jos on Wednesday.

He said most of the suspected cases were recorded in Jos North Local Government Area.

Mr Damulak said 99 per cent of the suspected cases were recorded in Jos North, with Rikkos community among the worst-affected areas.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“As of today, the cases have increased from 149 to 303. The death has also increased from 23 to 27. The high cases of the disease are in Jos North. Ninety-nine per cent of the cases are in Jos North,” he said.

He attributed a significant proportion of the cases to people who had not received diphtheria vaccination and said children constituted a substantial number of those affected.

“Most of the people that were affected were those that did not take diphtheria vaccine. Apart from Jos North, we also have few cases from other LGAs. Children account for a significant proportion of those affected,” he said.

Schools remain closed

The latest figures come days after the Plateau State Government ordered the temporary closure of all public and private primary and secondary schools across the state.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on September 5 that the government directed schools to close from Monday, September 7, following suspected diphtheria cases in Jos North, Jos South, Bassa and Wase local government areas.

The Commissioner for Information and Communication, Joyce Ramnap, said the measure was intended to prevent further transmission and protect pupils, students and teaching and non-teaching staff.

Schools that had already resumed academic activities were also directed to close and remain shut until further notice.

The government asked school proprietors, administrators, teachers, parents and guardians to comply with the directive and ensure that pupils and students remained at home while health authorities strengthened surveillance and response efforts.

Response intensified

The state government has also increased efforts to provide treatment and strengthen disease surveillance in affected communities.

Some patients are receiving treatment at the Jos University Teaching Hospital and Plateau State Specialist Hospital, where isolation facilities have been provided.

In Jos North, the local government council has deployed additional logistics, including motorcycles, to support contact tracing, field surveillance and community mobilisation.

Governor Caleb Mutfwang also directed the immediate mobilisation of drugs and other medical commodities to health facilities to support the response.

The Director-General of the Plateau State Drug and Medical Commodity Management Agency, Kim Bot, said government intervention was already ongoing at JUTH and PSSH and would be extended to other affected facilities.

Mr Bot said the state government responded after receiving reports of the outbreak and was working to ensure that affected health facilities received the necessary medical supplies.

READ ALSO: Plateau buses make face masks compulsory as diphtheria outbreak worsens

Meanwhile, the Chairman of Jos North Local Government, John Christopher, has urged residents to maintain personal and environmental hygiene to reduce the spread of the disease.

Mr Christopher made the call on Wednesday during an assessment of affected communities and a visit to suspected patients receiving treatment at the Primary Healthcare Clinic in Abba Na Shehu Ward.

The rising figures come amid continued efforts by health authorities to contain the outbreak, increase surveillance and encourage residents to seek prompt medical attention and vaccination.

World.title: NSCIA alleges bias in El-Rufai’s prosecution, demands fair trial
World.content:
The Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA) has broken its silence on the legal battles of former Kaduna State Governor, Nasir El-Rufai, alleging that extraneous religious interests appear to be influencing his trial.

In a press statement signed by its secretary-general, Is-haq Oloyede, the Nigerian apex Islamic body urged the government and the Judiciary to prevent individuals with sectarian agendas from weaponising public institutions against the former governor.

The council stated that it refrained from commenting on the matter, viewing the legal proceedings as a standard judicial process, and trusting the court system to uphold justice.

“The restraint was because the Council hitherto considered the prosecution as a standard judicial process, and that the Judiciary has inherent capacity to uphold justice.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“However, recent developments in the public domain have raised serious concerns that strongly suggest an extraneous involvement of an underlying religious bias against the former Governor.

“Consequently, the Council calls upon the Federal Government of Nigeria and the Judiciary to ensure that individuals with vested religious interests are strictly prevented from weaponising public institutions or the legal system to execute a sectarian agenda against him.

“Furthermore, the Council appeals to the general public to refrain from incendiary comments that could prejudice the fair trial of Mallam El-Rufai or exacerbate the security situation in our nation,” the statement read.

Background

The prosecution of Mr El-Rufai by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) stems primarily from recommendations made in a 2024 Kaduna State House of Assembly probe report, which accused his 2015–2023 administration of mismanaging public funds.

The ICPC has filed multiple charges against the former governor across both Federal and State courts,s including one in which he was accused of tapping the phone calls of National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu.

Mr El-Rufai has pleaded not guilty to all charges, maintaining that his prosecution is politically motivated.

He remains in ICPC custody under court-authorised remand orders while his legal team challenges his continued detention.

World.title: Two arrested over murder of Kano social media influencer
World.content:
The police have arrested two suspects in the violent murder of social media influencier, Ibrahim Khalil, at his residence in Gaida Quarters, Kumbotso Local Government Area of Kano State.

Mr Khalil, also known as Danshagamu, was attacked with sharp objects after hoodlums forced their way into his home on Monday at 11:30 p.m.

According to a press statement from the police command’s spokesperson, Abdullahi Kiyawa, officers from the Kumbotso Police Division responded after receiving a distress call from the commander of the quarters vigilante group.

“Upon arriving at the scene, police officers rushed the severely injured victim to the Murtala Mohammad Specialist Hospital in Kano for emergency medical care, where he was pronounced dead on arrival by the attending physician,” the police said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said an investigation later led to the arrest of the two suspects.

“The suspects are currently in custody undergoing interrogation,” Mr Kiyawa stated.

He said the police have intensified search efforts to track down the accomplices in the incident.

“The Kano State Police Command will not relent in its mandate to protect lives and property. We assure the good people of Kano that justice will be pursued to its logical conclusion,” the commissioner warned.

Meanwhile, he said the police have deployed patrol units and intelligence personnel throughout Gaida and adjacent communities to uphold public safety.

World.title: The “Daily Times” we wish for, but can’t have, By Azu Ishiekwene
World.content:
Repossession is never as easy as it seems. Once a privatised enterprise has passed through mortgages, receivership, asset sales and successive owners, “taking it back” is no longer a simple reversal of the original sale. It can lead to years of litigation without restoring the original productive capacity of the firm.

The piece by columnist and former Managing Director/Editor-In-Chief of The Guardian, Martins Oloja, entitled “Why Should We Celebrate Daily Times @ 100, FRCN @ 75?” published on 5 September, was an angry one. And Oloja has many good reasons to be angry.

Daily Times, Nigeria’s newspaper of record, was 100 years old on 1 June, and the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria (FRCN), the legacy successor to the Nigerian Broadcasting Service (NBS), was 75 in April. The anniversaries of these institutional brands evoked mixed feelings, especially regret, because they have not grown into what their founders intended.

What it Used To Be…

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Oloja narrated the decline of Daily Times, from the newspaper that produced some of Nigeria’s most outstanding journalists and was a formidable, professional, commercial, and asset powerhouse in its heyday, to a scrap of memory, struggling for its future.

Among the many golden assets of the newspaper was, for example, a 60 per cent equity interest in Naira Properties Limited, the company that was the majority shareholder in the Nigerian Stock Exchange house.

And that, of course, was apart from having many other valuable landed properties in Nigeria and London, and a content repository that was a treasure trove of Nigeria’s history. Its training arm, the Times Journalism Institute, was also one of its eight subsidiaries.

Yet, today, the brainchild of Richard Barrow, Adeyemo Alakija, and VR Osborne could use help from the Salvation Army. It’s more of a cautionary tale than the monument it once was.

Whose Radio Now?

The odyssey of the FRCN has not been significantly different, and Oloja’s agony and frustration over what might have been poured into his article in a bitter, relentless wave of nostalgia.

The problem, however, is that while nostalgia can sometimes provide relief, it is impotent to face the future. Not many would disagree that the transfer of the Daily Times was fraught with controversy, from disputes over the purchase price, relative to the property portfolio to financing, share ownership, the purchaser’s obligations, and post-sale asset management.

But the way forward is not in the past. The suggestion that Daily Times should be retrieved from Folio Communications 22 years after the sale and handed over to what is no doubt an accomplished group of media managers is like chasing the train long after it has left the station. It will only end in grief.

But regret is a waste of time. For me, it’s not very important who bought Daily Times – whether it was sold to a group of journalists or to some fishermen on Ekeremo waterside. We have seen journalists manage media houses successfully and others fail disastrously. We have also seen non-journalists turn around ailing media houses, the most obvious example being The PUNCH‘s Chairman Emeritus, Chief Ajibola Ogunshola.

A Litany of Sales

We’ve seen this before. After President Olusegun Obasanjo’s government sold the Port Harcourt and Kaduna Refineries to Bluestar in 2007, Obasanjo’s successor, Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, reversed the sale under pressure from labour and other interest groups, who didn’t want “our national patrimony” disposed of so casually.

Of course, that was a convenient scam that has now cost the country billions of dollars in futile promises to fix the refineries. Ajaokuta Steel and the Aluminium Smelter Company of Nigeria (ALSCON) tell similar stories of well-intentioned government repossession that ended in deeper misery for all parties, except the predators.

Repossession is never as easy as it seems. Once a privatised enterprise has passed through mortgages, receivership, asset sales and successive owners, “taking it back” is no longer a simple reversal of the original sale. It can lead to years of litigation without restoring the original productive capacity of the firm.

There are several examples of privatisations that worked, such as Eleme Petrochemicals, Ashaka Cement, and the Nigerian Aviation Handling Company, as well as those that have partly succeeded and others that have been catastrophic failures. The reasons could range from technical competence to the availability of new capital post-acquisition, and from the freedom to price and operate commercially to the regulatory environment. No one-size-fits-all.

Regret As Medicine

But regret is a waste of time. For me, it’s not very important who bought Daily Times – whether it was sold to a group of journalists or to some fishermen on Ekeremo waterside. We have seen journalists manage media houses successfully and others fail disastrously. We have also seen non-journalists turn around ailing media houses, the most obvious example being The PUNCH‘s Chairman Emeritus, Chief Ajibola Ogunshola.

From a business point of view, the question is not whether the enterprise has become what one thinks the founders wanted it to be, but about how it is innovating, adapting and creating value sustainably. We may romanticise the past, but no business is immortal, as we have seen from the examples of Blackberry and Kodak. In a relatively free market, mortality is not necessarily a bad thing; out of the ashes of a badly run business may arise another to take its place, sometimes offering even better value.

And it doesn’t matter whether such businesses are a bequeathed legacy, a contested sale, or a start-up. This applies to the Daily Times as it does to over 314 news platforms – from the legacy media to digital natives – in Nigeria’s existentially challenging media landscape today. Nature hates a vacuum.

Oloja may be right. Daily Times’ influence has attracted vectors, the first of which was the Murtala/Obasanjo government. If the takeover and subsequent privatisation had not happened, perhaps Daily Times might have been all we hoped for and more. But that will remain in the realm of probability. And in that realm, things may also have been worse had the sale not happened.

Apples and Oranges

Let me now say a word about FRCN. Oloja’s comparison of FRCN with public broadcasters such as the BBC and the SABC may not be entirely accurate. There are fundamental differences between state-owned/controlled broadcasters, such as the FRCN, and public broadcasters, such as the BBC or the SABC, whose legacies Oloja highlighted.

While all three – FRCN, the BBC, and the SABC – are publicly owned or constituted, there are material differences in appointments, finance, editorial authority, and regulation.

The legal foundation of each one, its corporate character, ownership, and editorial freedom, affect the quality of its content and programming as a whole.

It’s inconceivable, for example, that the fragmentation by fiat which the writer referred to in Radio Nigeria will happen in the BBC or SABC. What the piper in the Nigerian government cannot undo with businesses in its control does not exist.

The Market As Teacher

Yet, in a world where even established services like the BBC are losing captive audiences due to licence-fee evasion, as more and more households access on-demand channels, and with fewer public resources available, the existential challenges might compel broadcasters of all shades to innovate or be left behind. No one needs to count the years for failing businesses. That’s a job the ever-changing consumer market does so well.

Oloja may be right. Daily Times’ influence has attracted vectors, the first of which was the Murtala/Obasanjo government. If the takeover and subsequent privatisation had not happened, perhaps Daily Times might have been all we hoped for and more. But that will remain in the realm of probability. And in that realm, things may also have been worse had the sale not happened.

Or has the New Nigerian, the regional equivalent of Daily Times and relic of the 19 Northern state governments, done significantly better?

The best tribute to Daily Times and Radio Nigeria is not to recover their past. It is to recover the standards they represented and build institutions capable of meeting them in the future.

Azu Ishiekwene is Editor-In-Chief of LEADERSHIP and author of the book,Writing for Media and Monetising It.

World.title: Trump offers to pay each American $5,000 if Republicans win midterm elections
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has promised to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

He said this at the party’s convention on Wednesday in the middle of a US presidential term and ahead of the midterms, expected to be held on 3 November.

The proposal will cost over $1 trillion and has raised ethical concerns. Mr Trump’s proposal aims to induce US citizens to vote for Republicans, with a direct financial reward conditioned on his party winning.

His statement also made Republicans’ concerned about their prospects in the November elections obvious.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” he told the crowd of supporters present at the convention.

“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country. We will defeat communism in America,” he went on.

He also urged them to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” despite his growing unpopularity among Americans.

Reports and polls show his approval rating hovering around 38 per cent.

The Guardian reported that many Republican candidates skipped the two-day convention because of Mr Trump’s deep unpopularity, driven by discontent over inflation and high consumer and gas prices. This has been linked to the trade war with China and Canada. There are also concerns about the US war with Iran.

Mr Trump also discussed the war in his lengthy speech, explaining that he needed to start the war because Iran was perhaps “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon,” a claim that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) already identified as untrue.

The president also devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about the implications of losing to the Democrats.

“If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said

“If we hand America’s future to the radical-left Democrats, our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet. Vote Republican, and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come.”

World.title: UK increases Ebola response funding to £78.7m
World.content:
The United Kingdom has increased its support for the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), bringing its total commitment to £78.7 million, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

Africa CDC announced the development in a statement on its website, following a meeting in Addis Ababa between its Director-General, Jean Kaseya, and UK Minister for International Development, Kirsty McNeill.

The discussions focused on the Ebola response, regional coordination and the need for sustained support to affected countries.

According to Ms McNeill, the government had earlier allocated £26.9 million for the immediate response in the DRC and Uganda, as well as for regional coordination.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Africa CDC noted that “the additional UK funding will support the response in the DRC and Uganda, as well as wider regional coordination and preparedness.”

The increased support comes as the Ebola outbreak continues to spread across the DRC.

As of 6 September, the country had recorded 6,686 confirmed Ebola cases and 3,226 deaths, according to the latest WHO Africa situation report.

The outbreak is now affecting six provinces and 60 health zones.

How outbreak began

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus different from the Zaire species responsible for several previous Ebola outbreaks.

The first alerts were received in early May after an unexplained illness with high mortality was reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone in Ituri Province.

Laboratory testing subsequently confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease, and DRC officially declared its 17th Ebola outbreak on 15 May.

Uganda subsequently confirmed imported cases linked to the outbreak, prompting WHO to declare the situation a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 16 May.

What UK funding will support

Africa CDC said the additional UK support will strengthen several areas of the response, including surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management, community engagement and cross-border preparedness.

The announcement also comes as African health authorities and international partners seek to strengthen coordination across borders and improve the speed with which suspected cases can be identified, tested and treated.

Africa CDC said it would continue working with member states and partners to strengthen surveillance, laboratory systems, patient care, infection prevention and control, community engagement and preparedness along borders.

Speaking on the latest funding, Mr Kaseya welcomed the UK’s support for the African-led response.

“This support comes at an important time. We are working closely with the DRC, neighbouring countries and partners to stop transmission, protect communities and support health workers on the front line,” he said.

He said strong international partnerships aligned with the priorities of affected countries and African institutions is essential to bringing the outbreak under control.

READ ALSO: Uganda declares Ebola outbreak over after 42 days without a new case

Shortage of health workers

WHO has warned that about 5,000 additional health workers are needed for Ebola treatment centres in the DRC as the outbreak expands.

Nearly 4,000 health workers are already working in treatment centres, but more are needed as treatment capacity increases.

WHO has also reported that nearly 1,400 treatment beds are available across 59 treatment centres, while another 1,600 beds are needed to meet the projected demand.

World.title: List of 10 youngest billionaires in Africa
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

Africa’s billionaire class is dominated by older business leaders, but a handful of younger billionaires have also earned fortunes running businesses across sectors including manufacturing, telecommunications, energy, mining and diversified investments.

This makes them stand out on Forbes’ 2026 Africa Billionaires list.

The ranking below reorders Forbes’ 23 African billionaires by age rather than wealth. Where billionaires share the same age, their position on Forbes’ original 2026 Africa ranking is used as the tie-breaker.

Here are the 10 youngest billionaires in Africa, according to Forbes’ 2026 Africa Billionaires ranking:

1. Mohammed Dewji — 51 — $2.1bn

Tanzanian businessman Mohammed Dewji is the youngest billionaire on Forbes’ 2026 Africa list at 51.

Dewji is the CEO of METL, a conglomerate founded by his father in the 1970s. Forbes says the company operates across textile manufacturing, flour milling, beverages and edible oils in eastern, southern and central Africa, with operations in 10 African countries.

Dewji, Tanzania’s only billionaire, signed the Giving Pledge in 2016, committing to donate at least half of his fortune to philanthropic causes.

2. Femi Otedola — 63 — $1.3bn

Nigerian businessman Femi Otedola ranks second among Africa’s youngest billionaires at 63, with a Forbes 2026 fortune of $1.3 billion.

Forbes says Otedola built his initial fortune in commodities before selling his shares in Forte Oil and moving into energy investments. In 2025, he sold a majority stake in Geregu Power, while retaining a 5% interest.

His other investments include stakes in Zenith Bank and FBN Holdings, according to Forbes.

3. Patrice Motsepe — 64 — $4.3bn

South African mining billionaire Patrice Motsepe is 64 and has a Forbes-estimated net worth of $4.3 billion.

He founded African Rainbow Minerals and became a billionaire in 2008, becoming the first Black African to appear on the Forbes billionaires list.

Forbes also identifies Motsepe’s interests in African Rainbow Capital, Sanlam and football club Mamelodi Sundowns. He has served as president of the Confederation of African Football since 2021.

4. Nassef Sawiris — 65 — $9.6bn

Egyptian billionaire Nassef Sawiris, 65, is the wealthiest among the five billionaires aged 65 on this list, with a Forbes 2026 fortune of $9.6 billion.

Sawiris runs OCI, one of the world’s major nitrogen fertiliser producers, while also holding interests in Orascom Construction and Adidas.

Forbes says he also teamed up with Wes Edens and Fortress to acquire English Premier League club Aston Villa and holds a stake in Madison Square Garden Sports, which owns the NBA’s New York Knicks and NHL’s New York Rangers.

5. Strive Masiyiwa — 65 — $2.1bn

Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa is 65 and has a Forbes 2026 net worth of $2.1 billion.

Forbes says Masiyiwa overcame government opposition to establish Econet Wireless Zimbabwe in 1998. He owns a 38% stake in the publicly traded company and about 33% of EcoCash.

His interests also include Liquid Intelligent Technologies, fintech and power-distribution investments. Forbes notes that Masiyiwa has served on Netflix’s board since December 2020.

6. Aziz Akhannouch — 65 — $1.6bn

Moroccan businessman and Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch is 65, with Forbes valuing his fortune at $1.6 billion.

Akhannouch is the majority owner of Akwa Group, a conglomerate founded by his father and his father’s business partner in 1932.

Forbes says the group has interests in petroleum, gas and chemicals, including through publicly traded Afriquia Gaz and Maghreb Oxygene. Akhannouch became Morocco’s prime minister in September 2021.

7. Yasseen Mansour — 65 — $1.4bn

Egyptian businessman Yasseen Mansour, 65, has a Forbes 2026 fortune of $1.4 billion.

He is a shareholder in the family-owned Mansour Group, which was founded by his father, Loutfy Mansour, in 1952. Forbes says the group is the exclusive distributor of General Motors vehicles and Caterpillar equipment in Egypt and several other countries.

Mansour is also chairman of Palm Hills Developments, one of Egypt’s major real estate developers. His brothers, Mohamed and Youssef Mansour, are also billionaires.

8. Abdulsamad Rabiu — 66 — $11.2bn

Nigerian industrialist Abdulsamad Rabiu is 66 and has a Forbes 2026 net worth of $11.2 billion.

Rabiu founded BUA Group, a Nigerian conglomerate with interests in cement production, sugar refining and real estate.

Forbes says Rabiu owns 98.2% of BUA Cement and 95% of BUA Foods. He began his own business in 1988, importing iron, steel and chemicals, before building the BUA empire.

9. Aliko Dangote — 69 — $28.5bn

Africa’s richest person, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, is 69 and has a Forbes 2026 net worth of $28.5 billion.

Dangote founded and chairs Dangote Cement, which Forbes describes as Africa’s largest cement producer. The company has annual capacity of 48.6 million metric tonnes and operates in 10 African countries.

His business interests have also expanded into fertiliser and refining, with his fertiliser plant beginning operations in 2022 and the Dangote Refinery beginning refining operations in 2024.

10. Samih Sawiris — 69 — $1.4bn

Egyptian businessman Samih Sawiris, 69, rounds out the list with a Forbes 2026 fortune of $1.4 billion.

Sawiris is the founder and chairman of Orascom Development Holding, which develops and operates resorts in Egypt, Montenegro and Switzerland.

Forbes says he and his brothers, Nassef and Naguib Sawiris, also hold stakes in publicly traded Orascom Construction, a company established by their father. Sawiris is also a founder and board member of the Sawiris Foundation for Social Development, which focuses on creating sustainable jobs for Egyptians.
