Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. Transcript text may be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio on npr.org may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

World.title: Conductor Julian Wachner receives suspended sentence for possession of child sex abuse material
World.content:
Conductor Julian Wachner receives suspended sentence for possession of child sex abuse material

toggle caption Hiroyuki Ito/Getty Images/Hulton Archive

This report includes mentions of sexual violence.

The formerly prominent conductor Julian Wachner has been sentenced to nearly six years of probation after having pleaded guilty in July to five counts of possession of child sex abuse material and one count of possession of cocaine. Wachner must also register as a sex offender. He will receive credit for five days he spent in jail, according to the sentencing order.

The sentencing took place Wednesday afternoon in Indiana's Marion Superior Court.

Sponsor Message

At the time of his arrest in August 2025, Wachner, who had formerly been based in New York City, had been working as a fourth-grade math teacher at an Indianapolis charter school after his career as an internationally known conductor and composer had disintegrated in recent years. The school, Invent Learning Hub, told NPR at the time that it had not been aware that Wachner had been under police investigation, and that it had conducted thorough background checks. Wachner was fired after his arrest.

In charging documents issued in 2025, the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department said that Wachner had admitted to using cryptocurrency "hundreds of times" over several years to purchase videos of children "ranging in age from approximately 1 to 16 years old," and that Wachner disclosed to police that "his specific preference was for material involving children between the ages of 6 and 13."

Wachner was initially charged with 10 counts of possession of child sex abuse material depicting children younger than 12 years old and one count of possession of cocaine. On July 15, as part of a plea agreement with the state of Indiana, Wachner pleaded guilty to five of the child sexual abuse material charges and the cocaine possession charge, and waived his right to appeal the court's sentence.

Sponsor Message

Wachner had been once highly lauded as a musician who recorded over a dozen albums of his own and other composers' music, and had been twice-nominated for Grammy Awards as a conductor. He conducted major orchestras across the globe, including the Philadelphia Orchestra and the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, and until 2022, he was the director of music and the arts at Trinity Church Wall Street, one of New York's wealthiest churches and a staple presence in the city's arts community. It is particularly well known for its youth chorus, which draws child singers from across the city.

He was dismissed from his job at Trinity in 2022, after The New York Times published a report that said that a woman had accused him of groping her and kissing her against her will at a Juilliard School residency program in Aiken, S.C., in 2014. Wachner denied the allegations, and no criminal charges were filed against him.

Wachner later filed a civil suit against Juilliard, accusing the school of defamation. That case was dismissed with prejudice by the New York Supreme Court in June 2023.

World.title: Canadian bank CEOs can't stop bragging about AI. Are job cuts next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scotiabank CEO Scott Thomson says artificial intelligence saved his bank roughly 24,000 days' worth of work over about four and a half months. At TD Bank, CEO Raymond Chun recently said AI has reduced the time it takes to pre-process mortgages from about 15 hours to three minutes.

Canada's Big Five banks employ nearly 400,000 full-time-equivalent workers. That's more than double the number of employees in Canada's auto assembly and parts manufacturing industry. TD Bank workers alone outnumber Canada's active military force.

According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. That's far higher, they say, than the 56 per cent estimated for the Canadian workforce overall.

Last month, the Bank of Canada estimated that one‑third of jobs may "undergo substantial changes" because of AI integration, given today's capabilities. The central bank found that banking, insurance and other financial clerks are among the most exposed.

"AI is a big opportunity for us, a transformational opportunity both from an effectiveness, and an efficiency perspective," Thomson said on Wednesday at the annual Scotiabank Financials Summit in Toronto.

RBC CEO Dave McKay, who has led the bank since 2014, says AI is affecting every part of its business and that he uses it each morning to generate custom reports from RBC's internal data. (Kevin Van Paassen/Bloomberg)

His enthusiasm is shared by his C-suite peers.

"There isn't a part of our business that's not being impacted by AI," RBC CEO Dave McKay told an audience at an industry conference hosted by his bank earlier this year. At an event in June, he spoke about using AI every morning to generate custom reports based on RBC's internal data.

Last month, BMO CEO Darryl White said predictive AI modelling in his bank's insurance business can make underwriting decisions in as little as 10 seconds. The industry standard is at least 28 days, he noted.

Stock market analyst John Aiken covers the banking industry for New York-based Jefferies Financial Group. He sees top executives at Canada's Big Five — Royal Bank, TD Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, and CIBC — brimming with excitement over the billions of dollars they've invested in AI in recent years.

What's unclear, he said, is how rank-and-file bank employees will feel the impact.

"This isn't a little pet project," Aiken told CBC News. "The funny thing is, it's the CEOs themselves that are bringing it up unprompted.

"Strangely enough, we're not seeing head count reductions from the banks. You're presumably going to see lesser demand for lower skilled workers ... the front-line staff at the branches."

OpenAI and Anthropic logos are seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo)

Questions about how AI will affect some of Canada's largest private employers come amid a much broader debate over how the technology could shape humanity as a whole.

Earlier this week, an artificial intelligence researcher quit his job at Anthropic, accusing the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of irresponsibly "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence."

On Tuesday, another Anthropic employee wrote on the social media platform X that, "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."

On Wednesday, federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said "there are real concerns" at the frontier of AI development

WATCH | AI Minister Evan Solomon says AI safety a top priority: Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says | Duration 5:23 AI Minister Evan Solomon said 'there are real concerns' at the frontier of AI development, when asked about an Anthropic researcher who quit the firm, citing existential safety risks. 'Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,' Solomon said.

Jon Pinkus, a partner at Samfiru Tamakin LLP who specializes in employment law, sees jobs at risk throughout the white-collar world because of AI. However, he said he has yet to see a clear-cut instance of humans being replaced.

"I have real generational anxieties for the incoming workforce. Not just this generation, but for generations to come," he said.

"I think there are going to be certain positions that just don't exist, particularly more junior positions, entry-level positions.

"A lot of those entry level tasks are the ones now being done by AI ... [it does] them well enough for many organizations to say, 'Why are we going to pay this person $80,000 per year?'"

Jeff Lanthier, director of media relations at RBC, told CBC News in response to questions about AI's impact on staffing levels that people and relationships would always be at the core of the bank's strategy.

"We see AI as an enhancement, not a replacement," Lanthier said.

The other Big Five banks did not respond to requests for comment in time for publication.

At its investor day last year, RBC announced plans to generate $700 million to $1 billion in enterprise value through AI-driven benefits by 2027. TD Bank is similarly targeting $1 billion in annual value from its artificial intelligence initiatives. Both banks have in-house AI research labs, called RBC Borealis and Layer 6, respectively.

CIBC president and CEO Harry Culham, left, greets German Vice-Chancellor and Federal Minister of Finance Lars Klingbeil before a CIBC roundtable with the German-Canadian Chamber of Industry and Commerce in Toronto, on Friday, May 8, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Sammy Kogan)

CIBC CEO sees staff levels rising

CIBC CEO Harry Culham said his bank's new AI workspace is more like a "co-worker" than a chatbot. Even so, he predicts the bank will add employees overall.

"We actually see head count growth over the next five years," CIBC CEO Harry Culham said on his bank's Aug. 27 earnings call with stock market analysts. "We're using it all over the entire organization, and we've got thousands and thousands of people being educated."

Kiridaran Kanagaretnam, an associate dean at York University's Schulich School of Business in Toronto, sees the Canadian banking industry's overall employee numbers drifting higher, absent a major financial crisis.

He recommends students pursue professional designations in accounting and finance to boost their value to employers.

"Everything is changing at a rapid rate," he said. "But that doesn't mean things are bleak."

World.title: Trump's 9/11 statements come under scrutiny again
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump this week recounted an incident in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in downtown Manhattan that was long on descriptive detail but not easily verified.

At a Tuesday event in Washington, D.C., organized by a Sept. 11 foundation, Trump recalled being near Ground Zero after the attacks, when the main building at One Liberty Plaza was under stress.

"The United States Steel building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down because it creaked a lot. It creaked. It still creaks. But it never came down," Trump said.

"I will never forget ... we thought it was coming down on top of us and two firemen, big strong guys — and I'm not the smallest guy in the world — they grabbed me under the arms and said, 'Gotta get out of here,' and they literally lifted me up."

Trump offered a somewhat similar description of the incident on the presidential campaign trail in New Hampshire in early 2016, though he stressed he wasn't inside the building.

"I must tell you, honestly, I never knew I could run that fast," he said at the time.

'A small and sick man'

It is one of at least four claims Trump has made surrounding the Sept. 11 attacks in New York City that have come under scrutiny over time.

As well, between the immediate aftermath of the attacks and when Trump launched his first presidential campaign — a period of about 13 years spanning many media interviews and news conferences — he made few such claims.

WATCH | The ongoing work to identify the victims: This lab is still trying to identify 9/11 victims. Not everyone wants to know | Duration 10:52 25 years after the September 11 attacks, a team of forensic experts continues the monumental task of identifying remains from the World Trade Center debris. CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault goes inside the lab using cutting-edge DNA science to bring closure to families — and explores the difficult reality that not everyone wants to know.

As a result, Trump has been accused by some liberal commentators, as well as former Republican congressman (now an anti-MAGA pundit) Joe Walsh of "stolen valour," the term usually used for ex-military who exaggerate their service careers.

Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, who served in the U.S. army in Afghanistan and Iraq after Sept. 11, 2001, also condemned Trump's latest comments.

"This solemn day is not about Trump. It never was, and it never will be," Crowe said on social media. "Our president is a small and sick man to make a day of remembrance and service about himself."

'I have a lot of men down here'

During the 2015-16 presidential campaign, Trump received pushback for claiming that "thousands and thousands of people were cheering" the attacks at an unspecified setting in New Jersey, including a "heavy Arab population."

Trump also said that he had lost "hundreds of friends" in the attacks, a remarkable claim given that just under 3,000 died in the attacks which designated terrorist organization al-Qaeda claimed responsibility for. Trump didn't widely repeat either statement, or provide names to media outlets in the latter example, after they received substantial news coverage.

LISTEN | Author and reporter Spencer Akerman on how 9/11 influenced U.S. immigration policy: Front Burner 31:57 Trump, ICE and the impact of 9/11

At Tuesday's event in D.C., Trump said he was "building a big building" in Manhattan at the time of the incident with firefighters. He didn't specify, but it's a possible reference to the Trump World Tower, completed in October 2001 about 40 blocks away from Ground Zero.

What is known is that on Sept. 13, 2001, Trump told a reporter from Germany's Deutsche Welle near Ground Zero that, "I have a lot of men down here right now, we have over 100 or we have about 125 coming, so we'll have a couple of hundred people down here."

A report the next day in the suburban-based New York paper Newsday mentions Trump's presence near Ground Zero, though not any crew affiliated with the longtime real estate developer.

"The workers are so worn out that they barely glance at the sight of Donald Trump, every hair in place and impeccably dressed in a black suit, pressed white shirt and red tie, walking into the plaza with his cellular phone to his ear," the paper reported.

That November, Trump told Newsday he "sent 225 of my workers and a great deal of excavating equipment to the site."

WATCH | How Sept. 11, 2001, unfolded in CBC's newsrooms: Reporting on 9/11: The day the world changed | Duration 24:36 Sept. 11, 2001 started like any other work day in the CBC newsrooms — and then the world changed. Correspondents Adrienne Arsenault, Ioanna Roumeliotis, Paul Hunter and David Common reflect on the chaos and shock of covering 9/11, 25 years later.

Failed WTC proposal

Curiously, there is a paucity of such statements between 2002 and mid-2015, when Trump announced his first presidential campaign. He made multiple appearances on Fox News where Sept. 11 is mentioned, including on anniversaries of the attacks, and program transcripts from those appearances reveal no such claims.

This also holds true for two occasions when Trump inserted himself in major post-Sept. 11 developments — in 2005, sponsoring a new tower proposal as he bashed the winning One World Center proposal as a "piece of junk," and a few years later when he offered to buy out the investors of a nearby project that included an Islamic centre.

Trump speaks to reporters next to a model of his proposed World Trade Center project, which he called the 'Twin Towers II,' on May 18, 2005. (Mary Altaffer/The Associated Press)

By the time of the 2016 campaign, Trump was again retrospectively back at the Ground Zero scene, telling a rally in Buffalo, N.Y, that he "h elped a little bit."

At a 2019 White House event during this first term as president, he told a gathering that included first responders that he "spent a lot of time down there with you."

"He was a private citizen at the time. I don't know what kind of role he could have possibly played," Richard Alles, who held a supervisory role at Ground Zero, told the New York Times, while separately telling Politifact he didn't see Trump in his months on duty.

It is possible that Trump is claiming ownership on tenuous grounds, much like he did after the death of Aretha Franklin, when he said the legendary soul singer "worked for me on numerous occasions." Franklin had performed concerts at Trump-owned casinos.

Bovis Lend Lease, a contractor for the Trump World Tower project that subcontracted work to other companies, also had a presence in Ground Zero recovery efforts. It's not clear if any workers were involved in both settings.

WATCH | Gander, N.L., to welcome thousands to commemorate 9/11 anniversary: Once more, the Town of Gander is getting ready to welcome thousands of people | Duration 3:01 On September 11, 2001, the people of Gander in central Newfoundland responded with open arms in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks in New York. This week, the town is expected to welcome about 2,000 people for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.

Trump, in a Truth Social post late Tuesday, lashed out at the media reports questioning his claims.

"Well, I don’t think I would be the first thing on anyone’s mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of construction workers," he said.

Trump is scheduled to speak at a 25th anniversary event at the Pentagon, the site of one of the 2001 attacks, on Friday.

World.title: Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Prime Minister Mark Carney gathered leaders of the world's foremost economies in Kananaskis Country's picturesque mountainside last spring for the G7, it was fresh off his election win, a wind seemingly at his back as he met with U.S. President Donald Trump to talk trade, and the threat of the province's separation from Canada was a remote hypothetical.

"Our primary focus will be on trade and trade with Canada," said Trump at the time, standing side by side with Carney in his first visit to this country since 2018. "I'm sure we can work something out."

A little more than a year later, Carney is once again holding high-level meetings in the Rocky Mountains of the province where he grew up, this time to plan the upcoming parliamentary sitting with his cabinet, fresh off three byelections where his governing Liberals cleaned up.

But there is little else in common with the optimistic outlook of 2025.

Trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. only continue to intensify, while the danger of Alberta's departure from federation has become much more real.

While Abacus Data founder and CEO David Coletto said there's little indication Canadians are blaming the prime minister for the trouble facing the country at this time, they are still looking for answers on the way forward.

"I think there's always risk when the impact might be job losses or the cost of things going up because we are in the midst of a cost of living crisis, you know, the No. 1 issue for most Canadians right across the country," Coletto told CBC News.

WATCH | Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas: Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas | Duration 1:48 In an excerpt from a 15-minute explanatory video released by Prime Minister Mark Carney's office on Tuesday, Carney says U.S. trade negotiators wanted Canada 'to become even more reliant on them, not less.'

The prime minister continues to defend his decision to reject the proposed new trade agreement with the U.S. in order to protect Canada’s sovereignty, as officials from the Trump administration try to convince the public that Carney walked away for political reasons.

Carney is close to peak popularity, with poll numbers stronger than his predecessor Justin Trudeau at this point in his mandate, according to Coletto, who says there’s no sign personal attacks from the White House are going to change that anytime soon.

"The likelihood that Canadians would trust what Donald Trump says over Mark Carney is very low," Coletto said.

"I think we’ve always assumed that there would be a best-before date on the public’s patience and I now question that because I think as long as people overwhelmingly believe that the greatest threat to their quality of life is coming from Washington and not from policy out of Ottawa that that’s going to continue to buy the prime minister and the government time."

Pivot away from U.S., national unity on the agenda

As the two-day cabinet planning forum with cabinet ministers and secretaries of state kicks off, there’s no announcement yet on whether Ottawa will match the Trump administration’s latest retaliation.

The White House is adding more Canadian products to its list of those subject to tariffs of 50 per cent, including mattresses and motorboats, and also planning to ban certain Canadian goods, including most alcoholic drinks, some dairy products and motorcycles by the end of the month.

That itself is a response to Ottawa imposing retaliatory tariffs on more than $27 billion worth of U.S. imports – a counter to 50 per cent levies the Trump administration placed on an equivalent amount of Canadian goods last month, after Carney called off trade talks.

WATCH | Ottawa considers next moves in U.S. trade war: Government assesses U.S. trade war damage, says Canada in 'a position of strength' | Duration 4:57 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada is still assessing the damage from the escalating trade with the U.S., but it's doing so from 'a position of strength.' Meanwhile Conservatives repeated calls to reconvene Parliament early.

The cabinet planning forum will focus on the pivot Carney says he is trying to lead, steering Canada away from its over-reliance on the U.S. — its largest trading partner — shoring up the economy and strengthening partnerships with other countries.

It’s expected that ministers and secretaries of state will arrive prepared to defend their performance on their files and propose solutions as the country deals with what Carney describes as an unprecedented crisis.

The forum will also tackle separatism, coming as it does a little more than a month ahead of a referendum where Albertans will answer, among other questions, whether they want to stay part of Canada or have an eventual vote on secession.

Some of Carney's top ministers fanned throughout the province ahead of the cabinet meeting, including Natural Resources Minister Timothy Hodgson, who was in Clive to break ground on a carbon-capture project.

"We are in a trade war, a trade war that we did not ask for, but that we must win," he said. "Canada didn't ask for a world where energy security equals economic security, equals national security. But that's the world we're in today."

WATCH | Canada faces more U.S. trade war escalation: At Issue | Canada faces more U.S. trade war escalation | Duration 22:33 At Issue this week: With Canada's $28 billion tit-for-tat counter-tariffs sparking further U.S. tariffs and outright bans on some Canadian products, the At Issue panel breaks down Canada's strategy, what it might do next, and what all the trade chaos means for politics and national unity.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, at an armchair discussion hosted by the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, was asked about the possibility of restarting talks with the U.S.

"At the right time, there will be further engagement with respect," Champagne said. "Canada's a big nation, Canada's a G7 country, Canada's a NATO country … and Canada is a big customer. We buy more from the United States than Japan, England and Germany combined."

"Any action taken will affect both sides of the border."

Guests scheduled to brief cabinet reflect the concerns about both the trade war and Alberta separatism.

The list includes the mayors of Calgary and Red Deer, pollsters including Janet Brown — known for her insights into the Alberta political landscape — and Ian Bremmer, the founding political scientist of Eurasia Group.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who landed in Calgary Wednesday, will also briefly address cabinet in Banff.

Missing from the list is any expert on affordability or pocketbook issues, unlike in January 2026, when Carney and his ministers heard from Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley.

An apparent ambivalence toward pocketbook issues might become a weakness for Carney in the long term, Coletto said.

"I think that thing that Canadians are looking for more than anything is reassurance," Coletto said. "Reassurance that their government understands the risks seized by them and is doing everything it can to mitigate them at the same time as finding ways of looking long term to how to strengthen Canada."

World.title: Police did not intervene as Canada's most prolific voyeur was 'looking for more victims,' court records show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saanich police watched but did not intervene for over a month as Canada's most prolific voyeur strode through businesses with a phone in hand in breach of bail conditions.

According to court records obtained by CBC News, a Crown lawyer claimed Yin Yeung Derek Chan was under police observation as the voyeur hunted for victims in locations like Fitness World and Value Village, where Chan had previously recorded hundreds of women and girls.

Chan, who filmed at least 652 women and girls in Greater Victoria in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada, was later sentenced to four and a half years in jail after being convicted of voyeurism and child pornography charges.

CBC News has listened to courtroom submissions in the case, which cast light on the Saanich Police Department investigation. Those records, along with victim impact statements and interviews with victims, raise questions about why police did not act to stop the voyeur sooner.

Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News for this story, but said in a statement that the department's decisions took a trauma-informed approach to avoid "actions that could contribute to further victimization."

Businesses Chan visited while violating bail conditions say they were never contacted by police.

"We are deeply concerned by the reported conduct and the impact it had on those affected," said Value Village in a statement.

Police found thousands of images and more than 100 hours of videos of women and children in Chan's home prior to the voyeur's arrest in April 2024. Chan was released on bail that month, with a condition not to use a cellphone outside of the home.

Despite that condition, Saanich police observed Chan using multiple cellphones in public on at least three occasions over a month before Chan was re-arrested on Jan. 30, 2025.

On Dec. 27, 2024, police observed Chan using a cellphone at Uptown shopping centre, entering a Fitness World gym, and using the phone inside the gym.

Police watched as Chan returned to the gym on Jan. 7, 2025, and used a phone in the gym again.

On Jan. 9, Chan used two cellphones in a Tim Hortons parking lot and was seen on a phone at Fitness World. Then, police followed Chan to Value Village in Victoria where the voyeur spent an hour and a half with a cellphone in hand.

The majority of Chan's victims prior to his initial arrest — more than 400 women and children — were secretly recorded while at Value Village, according to statements made in court by Crown lawyer Paul Cheeseman.

"That's exactly where his offending behaviour was, at these gyms and at Value Village, so the circumstances of the breach was that he was … out looking for more victims," Cheeseman told the judge.

For years prior to arrest, Chan found ways to thwart court orders aimed at preventing further voyeurism. The voyeur secretly recorded hundreds of women while on bail following an arrest for voyeurism in 2019 .

Chan served 60 days in jail for that offence in 2022. During that same year, Chan filmed more than one video every other day, breaching probation and failing to complete court-ordered counselling.

Police have responsibility to prevent harm, former IIO head says

Ashley Dryburgh, executive director of the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre, which has been helping victims impacted by Chan's crimes, believes the police didn't do enough to alert and protect the community from the risks Chan posed.

"I am deeply disappointed to hear that the perpetrator was on bail [for months] and police seemingly had evidence of his continuation of committing crimes and violating his bail conditions, and it took a month to re-arrest the perpetrator," she said.

"Were people being used as bait to build a case to support this person?"

Saanich police did not respond to specific questions from CBC News for this story, including how many people Chan recorded while out on bail.

But Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that the department shared information with the public where it could, but based decisions on what to release on an intention to protect victims' privacy and avoid causing them further harm.

"Throughout the investigation, our priorities were to identify victims, support those affected, protect their privacy, hold the offender accountable, and take reasonable steps to reduce the risk of further victimization," wrote Kowalewich.

"We recognized from the outset that these were deeply personal and intrusive offences, and our approach was guided by a trauma-informed commitment to minimizing further harm while supporting victims through the criminal justice process."

Police headquarters in Saanich, B.C. (Kathryn Marlow/CBC)

Police have a responsibility to prevent harm if they believe the public is at risk, said Ron MacDonald, the former chief civilian director of B.C.'s Independent Investigations Office, which is a civilian-led police oversight agency. In this case, he says voyeurism poses a "serious psychological harm."

"One could certainly make an argument that he ought to have been arrested as soon as he was seen outside of the home with a cellphone, because that's a clear violation of his court order," said MacDonald, who added that without full details from police it is difficult to know why they did not take this action.

Outstanding questions remain

As Chan's crimes came to light publicly for the first time in the wake of the sentencing, community group chats and social media comments bubbled with anxiety.

Women and girls across southern Vancouver Island wondered the same thing: am I or is someone I know a victim?

One victim, whose identity is protected by a publication ban, told CBC News it's a concern.

"I feel like every single woman and girl in Victoria, like anywhere, could have been a victim at any time during those years, and like, how are you supposed to know?" she said.

A Victoria-area woman who was unknowingly videoed by a voyeur is pictured in a park. Her identity cannot be divulged due to a court publication ban. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

About 40 victims were identified by police prior to the sentencing. Police will not say how many more victims they have confirmed since.

Officers uploaded images of women and girls to an AI model earlier this year to help find victims and additional videos created by Chan, according to a police report read at the sentencing hearing.

From this, one officer found a site where six videos, featuring known victims and one unknown victim, had garnered more than 100,000 views.

In the statement provided by Kowalewich, the deputy chief constable wrote that he understands Chan's crimes will continue to have effects long after the sentencing.

"We understand that some victims may still be seeking answers, information, or support as they continue to process the impact of these offences," he wrote.

"Our commitment to those affected remains ongoing, and support remains available for those who may require it."

World.title: Canadian citizenship certificate applications now facing nearly 3-year delays
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Less than nine months after Parliament allowed those with Canadian ancestors to be recognized as Canadian citizens, the backlog of applications has soared to a new high.

More than 136,000 applications for citizenship certificates are now waiting for a decision — many of them from Americans. Those who apply today face an estimated wait of 33 months, according to figures posted on Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC)'s website.

That is a 32 per cent jump in wait time and an 11 per cent rise in the number of applications since the previous update on Aug. 10.

In May 2025, prior to Bill C-3 going into effect, the estimated processing time for citizenship certificate applications was five months.

Christine Beltempo, president of the Canadian Bar Association's immigration section and a lawyer with McCarthy Tétrault, said her members are concerned about the "exponential increase" of processing times for citizenship certificate applications.

"We have known since the first drafts of Bill C-3 that this would cause a lot of uptake in the number of applications for proof of citizenship," Beltempo said.

Beltempo said IRCC needs to assign more people to process the applications, and that she expects the volume to further increase next year.

"I think it would be nice to see the department devoting more resources to this business line so that processing times can go back to what I would consider to be normal standards for people who are presumably Canadians," she said.

IRCC spokesperson Briannah Dale said the increase is influenced by a range of factors — not just Bill C-3.

"The department is continuing to monitor application trends and volumes and is implementing operational measures to respond to increased demand, including triaging applications, enhancing intake processes, training and onboarding additional staff and refining workload management practices," Dale said.

The spokesperson said processing times can vary and the 33-month estimate reflects the increased volume and "complexity of many applications" that "often require substantial documentary evidence and additional verification."

Prior to Bill C-3, Canadian citizenship by descent was limited to the first generation born or adopted outside Canada to a Canadian citizen. However, that limitation on citizenship for those who became known as "lost Canadians" was struck down by the courts as unconstitutional.

Under Bill C-3, which went into effect Dec. 15, people living in other countries who can trace their lineage from Canadian ancestors can qualify for Canadian citizenship even if their Canadian ancestor left Canada several generations back.

Diab told a parliamentary committee in October 2025 that the impact of Bill C-3 would be limited.

"We anticipate volumes in the tens of thousands over time," she said. "We do not expect any surge."

However, since the adoption of Bill C-3, Canada's archives have been deluged with requests for the documents needed to prove lineage to a Canadian ancestor — sometimes going back seven or eight generations — as the number of applications soared.

As of May 31, the most recent data provided by IRCC, half of those who have been recognized as Canadian citizens as a result of Bill C-3 were born in the United States.

Citizenship certificates granted between Dec. 15 and June under all categories — including Bill C-3, first generation or replacement certificates — were divided fairly evenly when it came to gender. IRCC said 16,250 were granted to male applicants, 16,285 to female applicants and 45 to applicants who listed their gender as "other." The gender of another 55 applicants was unknown.

While discussion on social media has speculated that older Americans are applying for Canadian citizenship to move to Canada and qualify for universal health care, the numbers show only 3,650 certificates of all types went to people over age 55. The largest age demographic was applicants under age 14 with 16,435 certificates. Many of those may have been issued for babies born to Canadians abroad.

The IRCC stats show 2,880 certificate recipients were between the ages of 14 and 17 while 18-54-year-olds accounted for 9,670 certificates.

A citizenship certificate allows you to do things like move to Canada or get a Canadian passport. However, Elections Canada says it doesn't allow someone to vote in a Canadian election unless they have lived in Canada at some point in their life.

It would also not allow them to cast a ballot in things like Alberta's upcoming sovereignty referendum unless they moved to that province. Elections Alberta says expats and Canadian citizens not ordinarily residing in Alberta aren't eligible to vote in provincial election events.

Immigration lawyer Colin Singer says IRCC's failure to deal with the growing backlog could end up in court, and that the delays could violate the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

"For professionals seeking cross-border employment, students applying to universities and families trying to relocate, these delays are severe economic roadblocks," Singer wrote.

Singer said applicants stuck in the backlog could eventually apply to Federal Court for a writ of mandamus, asking the court to set a deadline for IRCC to process their application.

NDP immigration critic Jenny Kwan said Prime Minister Mark Carney's government needs to ensure that IRCC has the resources to address the "growing crisis," pointing out that the government's last budget called for 3,300 positions to be cut by 2028-29.

"It is completely unacceptable that people who have a legitimate claim to Canadian citizenship, passed in legislation by Parliament, are being left in limbo," she said in a statement.

"Families [are] facing enormous disruption to their ability to travel, work, study, access services and plan their lives."

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said members of her party warned the government about the issues that citizenship by descent could raise.

"The Liberals assured us that there would be processes in place to help deal with the surge of applications that came alongside citizenship by descent," she wrote in a statement. "This was clearly untrue."

But Rempel Garner said "the absolute worst thing" the government could do is "mass approve" the backlogged applications.

World.title: N.L. residents helped Muslims feel safe amid post-9/11 prejudice, says association leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the anniversary of 9/11 marking 25 years, many are remembering the events that shook the world that morning in New York. For Muslims living in Newfoundland and Labrador, one says that September day brought out the best and the worst in people. But in the years that followed, Haseen Khan — the president of the Muslim Association of Newfoundland and Labrador — says the province’s Muslim community was supported by their neighbours. The CBC’s Adam Walsh reports.

When Haseen Khan looks back on his memories around the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, he often begins on the shock it brought.

It's a "grave wound" that is still open for many.

"It was beyond imagination. It was beyond anyone's imagination, that humanity can fall that low," Khan told CBC News Wednesday.

"A loss of one innocent life is loss of the entire humanity. And that's a very strong reminder, and that's what was going through our minds at that time."

But Khan also looks back on how it impacted Newfoundland and Labrador's Muslim community at the time.

Twenty-five years after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Khan is president of the Muslim Association of Newfoundland and Labrador. Back then, he was part of a growing population in the province — one that has grown from 50 people in 1989 to more than 4,000 residents as of the 2021 census.

He said he remembers the tragedy bringing out both the best and worst in people. It rallied the world closer together, he said, but it also changed how Muslims were viewed globally.

"These perpetrators, they associated themselves with Islamic faith. And that created lots of anxiety and fear among Muslims and, unfortunately, the entire community," Khan said.

"Sometimes, you see people react to the situation and they don't, kind of, respond to the situation. That kind of had some lasting impact that led to Islamophobia. And that resulted in, kind of, fear, injustice, and [a] sense of insecurity."

The attacks stoked fear across parts of Canada, which led to Muslims being targeted in some parts of the country.

A 2003 report from the Canadian Islamic Congress showed more than 170 anti-Muslim hate crimes were reported to the group in 2002 — a 1,600 per cent increase from the just 11 reports made in 2000.

In the days that followed Sept. 11, then-prime minister Jean Chretien publicly condemned the attacks while visiting a mosque in Ottawa, saying he turned his back on Canadians who took part in shaming or attacks.

Muslim people who spoke with CBC News in the years that followed shared they often faced threats while in the United States, questioning their safety, security and voicing a desire to find a new home where they could freely embrace their Muslim identity.

WATCH | Three Muslim people spoke with CBC News in 2021 about life as a Muslim post-9/11: Muslims in Canada on why they left the U.S. after 9/11 | Duration 6:06 The rise in Islamophobia in the U.S. after 9/11 prompted these three Muslims to move to Canada. Now after two decades, they see worrying signs emerging here.

But Khan said he also remembers the support that came from Newfoundlanders and Labradorians in the years that followed.

He's felt residents have historically been quick to support the community in times of need. He specifically cited support following a shooting at a mosque in Quebec City on Jan. 29, 2017, when residents formed a human chain around the St. John's mosque during prayers in the following days.

"Our fellow Newfoundlanders and Labradorians showed a very strong, kind of, support that, 'We are with you. You should not feel, you should not have any type of concern," Khan said.

"The support of local people and their welcoming attitude, I think that has been a source of reassurance and confidence."

The Suleman Dawood Mosque was opened in St. John's in 2025. What began as a community of around 50 people in the late-1980s has blossomed into a Muslim population upwards of 10,000 residents across Newfoundland and Labrador. (Katie Breen/CBC)

Looking ahead to Friday, Khan said he believes his thoughts will be on the response following the tragedy.

He encouraged other spiritual leaders to think the same, hoping the community can continue to invest in interfaith community building.

"In order to understand and respect our differences, and to find common ground for collaboration, [we have] to build a stronger, safer and united community so that future generations will inherit a world defined by unity. Not division."

World.title: TIFF's at a turning point — but how will the film festival's new focus on dealmaking affect fans?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For years, the Toronto International Festival has prided itself as a tastemaker. Toronto was the place movie stars flocked to for the unofficial start of their Oscar campaigns.

But as major films and A-list stars increasingly look to other festivals as launchpads, TIFF is reinventing itself with a new focus on the business of buying and packaging movies.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, this transformation could help keep TIFF in the conversation, but as ticket prices rise, what does it all mean for the heart of this festival: the filmgoing public?

Here's a look at TIFF's very own movie makeover moment — plus a few choice films you may want to catch yourself.

Shifting the spotlight to dealmaking

Continuing a post-pandemic trend, many of the season's buzziest titles, including Primetime starring Robert Pattinson and You Can See Everything from Canada's own Nathan Fielder, chose Venice or Telluride over TIFF for their world premieres.

So, like the nerdy girl in a rom-com who takes off her glasses, TIFF is trying to transform itself, pivoting to embrace the dealmaking and caffeine-fuelled strategy sessions that populate many major festivals.

Launching with a $23 million boost from Ottawa, TIFF: The Market features 70 sessions and events exploring film, television and interactive content.

A sci-fi film with Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra, a rom-com featuring Colin Firth and Halle Berry and a new instalment of the Air Bud franchise are just a few of the projects being shopped around town.

But just like the cutthroat competition for red carpet premieres, TIFF will be facing competition from other industry players.

Diego Calva, left, and director Jordan Firstman pose at the photo call for Firstman's film Club Kid during the 79th Cannes Film Festival in May. (John Locher/The Associated Press)

First, there's the Cannes marketplace, the biggest and best known showcase that sets the tempo for the year.

Case in point, it was on La Croisette, the famous boulevard at the centre of Cannes, where the buzz began for Jordan Firstman's Club Kid, resulting in a frenzied bidding war. That film's Canadian premiere takes place at TIFF Sunday.

The Trump factor

While TIFF is trying to position itself as a fall alternative to spring's Cannes, it's also competing with the American Film Market (AFM), which takes place in November in Los Angeles .

While AFM generally caters to more mainstream films, TIFF, which has always touted international cinema, will be highlighting emerging markets in Africa and Asia as part of The Market programming.

And as U.S. President Donald Trump talks up new national incentives to reshore American film production, international buyers wary of engaging with Hollywood or even looking to avoid hassles at the border, may see TIFF as an attractive alternative.

TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey speaks at a media event for the film festival last month. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Tickets and tastemakers

As TIFF's star wattage continues to diminish and the festival evolves to become more business-facing, questions remain about what that means for the heart of the TIFF experience: the film fans. The ones who camp out in long lines, wait for hours to watch stars walk red carpets and scream like pirates at midnight screenings.

Director Guillermo del Toro greets fans at the premiere of his film Frankenstein at the Toronto International Film Festival last September. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Every year TIFF rightly boasts about its track record of predicting best picture winners, touting the People's Choice Award as a barometer of Oscar worthiness.

But as ticket prices climb higher (regular screenings now begin at $30 and up), fewer members of the public who make the festival one big, beautiful focus group end up populating those screenings.

Speaking to the Toronto Star recently, TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey acknowledged that glitzy premieres with stars and filmmakers in attendance command higher ticket prices, but he also argued that they still cost less than a ticket to pro sports games in the city.

At a time when Canadians want to support the home team, that means some film fans could find themselves priced out of a seat.

Must-see movies

While the number of A-listers coming to TIFF may be shrinking, there's still a number of the upcoming fall season's most buzzworthy films making the rounds in Toronto.

WATCH | Trailer for director Danny Boyle's Ink:

Ink finds Trainspotting director Danny Boyle returning to Britain to explore the rise of The Sun tabloid newspaper, with rumoured James Bond contender Jack O'Connell as a rapacious editor in chief.

WATCH | Trailer for The Debut starring Julianne Moore:

Then there's The Debut, a love letter to community theatre written and directed by actor Jesse Eisenberg. In 2025 Eisenberg's A Real Pain helped Kieran Culkin bring home Oscar gold. Already, some are seeing a golden hue in Julianne Moore's performance as a harried housewife who abandons herself in a role.

Primetime programming

Increasingly, TIFF has embraced both the small and big screen in its programming and this year a number of TV series are showcased in the Primetime program. That includes Apple TV's Slow Horses, which is bringing its sixth season premiere to Toronto with star Gary Oldman, who will also be interviewed on stage.

WATCH | Teaser trailer for Yaga:

With shooting already underway for the second season of Heated Rivalry, another hot title is the upcoming Crave series Yaga, starring Hudson Williams as an heir to a powerful fishery and The Matrix's Carrie-Anne Moss as a university professor. Riffing on the fearsome fairy tale character Baba Yaga, the show promises a steamy mix of mischief and malevolence.

Oh Canada

It's worth remembering that, before the trade war escalated, the Canadian film industry was riding high, based on the success of films like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, Mile End Kicks, undertone and more.

To capitalize on the moment, there's a broad swath of Canadian titles at TIFF this year. Can't get enough of Jay Baruchel and love Canadian hosers who perform incredible feats? From FUBAR director Michael Dowse comes The Stunt Driver, which explores the true story of Canadian stuntman Ken Carter.

WATCH | Trailer for The Stunt Driver:

Music fans can check out Neil Peart: No One's Disciple, a 106 minute documentary exploring the life of the late Rush drummer with the help of Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith and Stewart Copeland of The Police.

If you'd like a less conventional film, Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney promises an unhinged look at the former prime minister. Director Matthew Rankin, who also helmed Universal Language, has conjured what TIFF describes as a "retro-pop fever dream," which will be premiering in the always raucous Midnight Madness category.

In Smudge the Blades, director and writer Cody Lightning, centre, also plays the coach of the Treaty 6 Blades in a movie the tells the story of an Indigenous hockey team fighting for a place in Alberta's northern league. (Liam Mitchell)

Not content to let Heated Rivalry steal all the hockey shenanigans, Smudge the Blades is a scrappy sports story about an Indigenous hockey team based in Northern Alberta.

Triple threat Cree director/writer/star Cody Lightning plays the team's beleaguered coach alongside an all-star team of Indigenous talent including Jana Schmieding and Paulina Alexis.

World.title: 25 people killed in commercial ship fire in China
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twenty-five people died in a fire aboard a foreign cargo vessel undergoing repairs at a state-owned ‌shipyard in the eastern Chinese city of Qingdao on Thursday, state media reported.

The fire broke out ​at about 11:15 a.m. local time at the ​Qingdao Beihai shipyard during repair and inspection works, state-run Xinhua said. Of the 42 people ​onboard, 12 were evacuated safely and five were ⁠injured and hospitalized.

The ⁠blaze was extinguished ‌by early afternoon, state media said.

Chinese President ​Xi Jinping called for intensified search and rescue efforts, a swift ⁠investigation and accountability measures, according to Xinhua.

A picture of the scene released by Xinhua showed the vessel involved to be the Ocean Melody. LSEG ship-tracking ⁠data identified it as a 20-year-old Liberia-flagged dry bulk carrier managed by Yuyangkunpeng Shanghai Shp Mgm, with Huili Shipping Co. Ltd. ‌listed as its registered owner.

A drone view shows ships and containers at the port in Qingdao, China, in this Oct. 20, 2025 file photo. (China Daily/Reuters)

The vessel arrived at the Qingdao shipyard on Aug. 31 and has remained there since, LSEG data showed.

The shipyard is controlled ⁠by state-owned China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the ⁠world's ⁠largest shipbuilders.

CSSC describes itself ​as China's principal naval shipbuilder and the country's largest designer ​and builder of ⁠ships and offshore equipment.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.

World.title: Far-right political marketing in Colombia
World.content:
A deep dive into the murky world of far-right propaganda and political marketing in Colombia and Latin America.

The surge of the peso, which went up roughly 25% over the past year, put Colombia Reports in acute financial trouble. If you can, please donate or become a patron.

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.
