The Wider Reading

Brazil’s iron ore economics have been squeezed from both directions this year. Chinese steel demand has been soft, and the freight leg has been repricing on geopolitical risk that has nothing to do with either producer or customer.

A mine that idles because of freight rather than because of ore price is a different signal from one that idles on demand. Freight can reverse quickly. Whether Samambaia restarts is therefore a question about the Red Sea and the Gulf as much as about Minas Gerais.

Why Freight Moves the Margin So Much

Iron ore is a low-value, high-bulk commodity. At roughly US$100 a tonne delivered, a freight cost of US$35 rather than US$22 is not a rounding error. It is a substantial share of the delivered price.

That is the structural difference between iron ore and almost every other traded commodity. For copper concentrate or for gold, shipping is a small fraction of value. For ore it is a controlling variable.

It is also why Australian producers have a permanent structural advantage over Brazilian ones in the Chinese market. The sailing distance from Port Hedland to Qingdao is a fraction of the distance from Brazilian ports, and no operational improvement in Minas Gerais closes it.

Brazil competes on ore quality rather than on distance. When the price of that quality premium falls below the freight penalty, Brazilian tonnes stop moving.

Where Samambaia Sits

Mineração Usiminas is a comparatively small producer by Brazilian standards, operating in the Iron Quadrangle of Minas Gerais rather than in the northern Carajás systems where Vale’s highest-grade ore comes from.

Iron Quadrangle ore is generally lower grade and requires more processing. The deposits have been worked for a century and the easiest material is long gone.

It is also further from a port. Minas Gerais ore travels several hundred kilometres by rail to the Atlantic before it is loaded, which adds cost that a coastal or northern operation does not carry.

A producer with those characteristics is the first to stop when delivered economics tighten and the last to restart when they loosen.

What Restart Depends On

Two variables, and neither is Brazilian. The first is Chinese steel demand, which has been soft through 2026 as the property sector continues to work through its adjustment.

The second is shipping. The freight spike is attributed in part to disruption connected to the conflict involving Iran, which affects vessel routing, insurance and available tonnage across the whole dry bulk market rather than the Brazil-China route specifically.

Freight can normalise quickly once the disruption ends, and a mine idled on freight is easier to restart than one idled on ore price. The 300 workers reported locally will be watching the second variable more closely than the first.

Usiminas has not published a restart condition or a timeline.

Iron ore fell to US$99.34 a tonne while freight to China rose to US$35 to US$38, from US$22 to US$23.

Is this a steel plant?

World.title: The Ibovespa Will Make Room for Depositary Receipts
World.content:
BRAZIL · MARKETS

Key Facts — The change B3 announced on 8 September that Brazilian depositary receipts will become eligible for the Ibovespa.

— The cap Their combined weight in the theoretical portfolio is limited to 10 percent.

— The current rule BDRs are not eligible for Ibovespa inclusion at all today.

— When First half of 2027.

— The conditions Standard liquidity and representativeness criteria still apply.

— Who it affects Brazilian companies listed abroad whose Brazilian exposure reaches investors through receipts rather than ordinary shares.

Brazil’s benchmark index has never contained a depositary receipt. From 2027 it can be one tenth of it.

The Ibovespa Will Make Room for Depositary Receipts

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

B3 said on 8 September that Brazilian depositary receipts issued by Brazilian companies will become eligible for inclusion in the Ibovespa from the first half of 2027, capped at 10 percent of the index.

What Changes

Today BDRs are not eligible for the Ibovespa at any weight. From the first half of 2027 they will be, subject to the same liquidity and representativeness tests every other constituent must pass.

The joint participation of all BDRs in the theoretical portfolio is capped at 10 percent. That is a ceiling on the category, not on any one issuer.

Why the Rule Existed

The Ibovespa is a measure of the Brazilian equity market. A depositary receipt is a claim on a share listed somewhere else, and including one has always raised the question of whether the index is measuring Brazil or measuring Brazilian exposure wherever it happens to be listed.

That distinction has become harder to hold. A growing number of Brazilian companies have their primary listing abroad, with Brazilian investors reaching them through receipts. Excluding those receipts means the benchmark increasingly excludes companies that are, in every commercial sense, Brazilian.

The 10 percent cap is the compromise. It admits the category without letting it define the index.

What to Watch

Which receipts actually qualify. Eligibility is not automatic and the liquidity and representativeness thresholds do real work in the Ibovespa methodology.

And what index-tracking money does about it. Passive funds benchmarked to the Ibovespa will have to buy whatever enters, which makes the first inclusion window in 2027 a mechanical flow event as much as a methodological one.

What a BDR Is

A Brazilian Depositary Receipt is a certificate traded on the B3 that represents shares held by a custodian in another market. The holder gets economic exposure to the foreign share without owning it directly and without needing an offshore account.

The instrument exists because Brazilian capital controls and custody rules historically made direct foreign holdings awkward for retail investors and impossible for many domestic funds. A receipt solves the plumbing problem.

The category that matters here is narrower than the general BDR market. This rule change concerns receipts issued by Brazilian companies whose primary listing sits abroad, not receipts over Apple or Nvidia.

The Companies This Was Written For

A meaningful group of Brazilian businesses now lists in New York rather than São Paulo. StoneCo, PagSeguro, XP, Nu Holdings and Vinci Partners all built their businesses almost entirely in Brazil and chose United States listings for valuation, liquidity and governance reasons.

From the index’s point of view they simply disappeared. A benchmark meant to represent the Brazilian equity market excluded some of the largest Brazilian companies created in the past decade, purely on the basis of where the primary listing sat.

That is a measurement problem rather than a policy one, and it gets worse as the trend continues. Each new offshore listing makes the Ibovespa a slightly less accurate description of Brazilian corporate value.

Whether individual names actually qualify under the new rule depends on their BDR liquidity on the B3, which for several of them is thin. Eligibility is not the same as inclusion.

The Cap Is the Compromise

Ten percent is not an arbitrary number. It is large enough to admit the category meaningfully and small enough that the index cannot become a proxy for a handful of Nasdaq listings.

It also caps the mechanical flow. Passive money tracking the Ibovespa will have to buy whatever is included at whatever weight the methodology assigns, and a category ceiling puts a bound on how much of that flow leaves the domestic market for receipts.

The unresolved question is what happens if BDR-eligible companies keep growing. A cap that binds is a cap that distorts, and at that point B3 will face the same choice again with less room to compromise.

What did B3 announce?

That Brazilian depositary receipts will become eligible for the Ibovespa from the first half of 2027, capped at 10 percent of the index.

What is the rule today?

BDRs are not eligible for Ibovespa inclusion at all.

Is the 10 percent per issuer?

No. It is a cap on the combined weight of all BDRs in the theoretical portfolio.

Do the usual criteria still apply?

Yes. Liquidity and representativeness thresholds still have to be met.

When was it announced?

8 September 2026.

World.title: Light Reaches the End of a Three-Year Judicial Recovery
World.content:
BRAZIL · UTILITIES

Key Facts — The decision Rio de Janeiro’s 3rd Business Court declared on 9 September that Light had fulfilled the obligations of its recovery plan.

— How long The distributor filed for judicial recovery on 12 May 2023. That is three years and four months.

— The size Around R$11 billion of debt was restructured.

— Who signed off The judicial administrator and the Rio de Janeiro public prosecutor both gave favourable opinions.

— The caveat The court must still accept the petition and formally order closure. Light is the party asking for it.

— What it means A distributor serving Rio de Janeiro comes out of court protection with its concession intact.

Light went into judicial recovery in May 2023 with R$11 billion of debt and a concession nobody was sure it would keep. It is coming out with both settled.

Light Reaches the End of a Three-Year Judicial Recovery

Rio de Janeiro’s 3rd Business Court declared on Wednesday that Light had met the main obligations of its judicial recovery plan, clearing the way for the electricity distributor to exit court protection after more than three years.

What the Court Decided

The 3ª Vara Empresarial do Rio de Janeiro declared the plan’s obligations fulfilled on 9 September, following favourable opinions from the judicial administrator and from Rio de Janeiro’s public prosecutor.

One point deserves care. The declaration that obligations are fulfilled is not identical to the formal closure of the process. The judge must still accept the petition and order the recovery terminated. Light is the party petitioning for that.

Coverage describing the exit as complete is ahead of the paperwork, if not by much.

The Numbers

Light filed for recuperação judicial on 12 May 2023. From filing to Wednesday’s declaration is three years and four months.

Around R$11 billion of debt was restructured through the process.

For context on how unusual completion is: Brazilian judicial recoveries frequently run longer, convert into bankruptcy, or end with the operating assets sold to somebody else. Light kept its concession and its operations through the whole period.

Why It Matters Beyond Light

Light distributes electricity in Rio de Janeiro. A distribution concession is not an asset that can be quietly wound down, because the service has to continue regardless of who owns the company or what state its balance sheet is in.

That constraint is exactly what makes distributor insolvencies difficult, and it is why the regulator and the court both had to be satisfied at each stage.

The precedent now on the record is that a large Brazilian distributor can restructure R$11 billion inside the judicial recovery framework and come out the other side still holding its concession.

How Light Got There

Light distributes electricity across Rio de Janeiro city and part of the surrounding state, one of the most difficult distribution territories in Brazil.

Its central operating problem is non-technical loss, which is the industry term for electricity that is delivered and not paid for. In Light’s concession area a large share of that is theft through irregular connections in territories where the company’s employees cannot safely enter.

Non-technical losses in parts of the network have run at multiples of what regulators consider manageable, and the regulatory tariff only recognises a portion of them. The difference is absorbed by the company.

Layered on top were the cost of capital during a period of high Brazilian rates and a concession renewal question that was unresolved for years. The May 2023 filing followed from all of it.

What Distributor Insolvency Actually Involves

A judicial recovery normally works by giving a company breathing room while it decides what to keep and what to shut. A distribution concession removes that option, because the service is a legal obligation and the network cannot be turned off.

That means the restructuring has to happen while the operation continues at full capacity, with the regulator supervising service quality throughout and with the power to intervene if it deteriorates.

ANEEL has the authority to take over a failing concession and appoint an intervenor. That possibility hung over the entire process and shaped what creditors were prepared to accept, because a concession lost to intervention is worth nothing to them.

The bargaining therefore ran between creditors who needed the concession preserved and a regulator whose obligation was to consumers rather than to creditors.

What the Precedent Establishes

The result is a template Brazil did not previously have: R$11 billion restructured inside the ordinary judicial recovery framework, service maintained, concession retained.

That matters beyond Light because Brazilian distribution has other stressed operators, and because the sector faces a decade of capital expenditure on grid modernisation and distributed generation that will be funded by companies with varying balance sheet strength.

A creditor now has a worked example of what recovery looks like in a regulated utility. That should, at the margin, lower the cost of lending to the sector.

The remaining step is procedural. Light has petitioned for formal closure and the judge must accept it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the court decide?

Rio’s 3rd Business Court declared on 9 September 2026 that Light had fulfilled the obligations of its judicial recovery plan.

Is the recovery formally over?

Not quite. The judge must still accept the petition and order closure. Light is the party requesting it.

How long did it take?

Light filed on 12 May 2023, so three years and four months to the declaration.

How much debt was restructured?

Around R$11 billion.

Does Light keep its concession?

Yes. The distributor came through the process with its Rio de Janeiro concession and operations intact.

Sources: Atlas Público, Canal Solar.

World.title: Argentina’s Real Debt Record Is Arrears, Not Borrowing
World.content:
ARGENTINA · HOUSEHOLDS

Key Facts — The headline figure 58.7 percent of urban households used some form of credit or financing in the first quarter of 2026.

— Not a record That is below the fourth quarter of 2019, when the share reached 61.6 percent.

— The record that is real Arrears among debtors rose from 13.6 percent in October 2024 to 27.8 percent in June 2026.

— The source Fundación Encuentro, drawing on INDEC household survey data and the central bank’s debtor register.

— A narrower measure A separate central bank indicator puts delinquency at 12.9 percent in July 2026, also described as a record on its own basis.

— Who borrows Higher-income households borrow the most, which complicates the reading.

Nearly six in ten Argentine households borrowed. Just over one in four borrowers is behind. Those are two different statistics and they are being merged.

Argentina’s Real Debt Record Is Arrears, Not Borrowing

A report published on 9 September by Fundación Encuentro puts household credit use at 58.7 percent of urban households in the first quarter of 2026, and delinquency among debtors at a record 27.8 percent by June.

Two Numbers, Two Meanings

The first figure counts households that resorted to some form of financing during the quarter. At 58.7 percent that is high, and it is not a record. The fourth quarter of 2019 was higher, at 61.6 percent.

The second figure counts arrears among people who already owe. It rose from 13.6 percent in October 2024 to 27.8 percent in June 2026, roughly one debtor in four, and press coverage describes that as a record.

Summaries circulating this week have combined the two into a claim that more than half of Argentine households are in arrears. That is not what either number says, and the difference between 58 percent borrowing and 28 percent defaulting is the whole story.

What the Trend Actually Shows

Doubling the delinquency rate in twenty months is the finding that matters. It happened during a period of disinflation, which is not when arrears normally accelerate.

The report draws on INDEC’s permanent household survey and on the central bank’s Central de Deudores. A separate, narrower central bank measure puts delinquency at 12.9 percent in July 2026, also a record on its own basis. The two measures count different populations and should not be used interchangeably.

One detail cuts against the simplest reading: higher-income households are the ones borrowing most. That points at credit being used for consumption smoothing and durable purchases across the income distribution, rather than only at distress borrowing at the bottom.

Why It Matters Now

Argentina’s macroeconomic story in 2026 has been about stabilisation at the aggregate level. Household balance sheets are where that story is tested, because they absorb the adjustment before the statistics register it.

A delinquency rate that doubles while inflation falls suggests real incomes have not recovered at the pace the headline numbers imply, or that the debt taken on during the high-inflation period is now being serviced out of smaller nominal gains.

Neither conclusion is established by this report. What it establishes is that more Argentine borrowers are behind than at any point the series covers.

How the Two Measures Are Built

The 58.7 percent figure comes from INDEC’s permanent household survey, which asks households directly whether they used credit during the reference period. It counts anyone who took on any obligation, from a credit card instalment plan to a family loan.

The 27.8 percent figure comes from the central bank’s Central de Deudores, which records the payment status of every registered borrower in the formal financial system. It counts people already in the register who are behind on payments.

The denominators are different. One is all urban households. The other is registered debtors. A household that used no credit cannot be in arrears, and a debtor who is not a household head may not appear in the first measure.

Merging them produces a number that describes nothing. This is the specific error in the summaries circulating this week.

What Doubling Delinquency in Twenty Months Implies

Delinquency rising from 13.6 to 27.8 percent is a very large move for a credit indicator. Rates like that are usually associated with recessions or with sudden interest rate shocks.

Argentina had neither in the conventional form. What it had was a rapid disinflation, which changes the arithmetic of household debt in a way that is easy to miss.

During high inflation, nominal debt erodes quickly. A fixed instalment that felt heavy in January is trivial by December. Households borrowed accordingly, and the erosion did the repayment for them.

When inflation falls, that stops. The instalment stays real, and a household that sized its borrowing against the old dynamic finds itself servicing debt out of income that is no longer inflating to meet it.

That mechanism explains a delinquency surge during stabilisation better than any story about falling incomes does, and it is a known cost of every successful disinflation.

Why Higher-Income Households Borrow Most

The finding that higher-income households account for the most borrowing runs against the intuitive reading of a debt-stress story, and it has a mundane explanation.

Access to formal credit in Argentina is rationed by income and by formal employment status. A household in the informal economy, which is roughly forty percent of Argentine employment, largely cannot borrow from a bank at all.

So the borrowing statistics measure who has access, not who needs money. The households under the most pressure are frequently absent from the data entirely, financing themselves through family, employers or informal lenders that no register captures.

That is worth holding in mind when reading any Argentine household credit series. The measured population is the one with options.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are most Argentine households in arrears?

No. About 58.7 percent used some form of credit in the first quarter of 2026. Arrears among debtors are about 27.8 percent.

Is the borrowing figure a record?

No. The fourth quarter of 2019 was higher at 61.6 percent.

What is the record?

Delinquency among debtors, which rose from 13.6 percent in October 2024 to 27.8 percent in June 2026.

Who produced the report?

Fundación Encuentro, using INDEC household survey data and the central bank’s debtor register.

Who is borrowing most?

Higher-income households, according to the report.

Sources: Infobae, Noticias Argentinas, Economis.

World.title: YPF Borrows US$1.2 Billion, the Largest Argentine Issue in Eleven Years
World.content:
ARGENTINA · ENERGY

Key Facts — The issue YPF placed US$1.2 billion of international debt on 9 September.

— The terms A 7.55 percent coupon, an effective yield of 7.85 percent, maturing June 2035.

— The record The largest international placement by an Argentine company in eleven years.

— The plan behind it YPF chief executive Horacio Marín announced a US$154.1 billion multi-year investment programme on 8 September.

— What is in it An oil hub at around US$25 billion, Argentina LNG at 12 million tonnes a year for around US$51 billion, a further liquefaction train at around US$25 billion.

— The target Operated production from 400,000 barrels a day to 2 million, and sixth place among world LNG exporters.

A company that defaulted inside living memory just borrowed US$1.2 billion for nine years at 7.55 percent. That number is the story.

YPF Borrows US$1.2 Billion, the Largest Argentine Issue in Eleven Years

YPF placed US$1.2 billion of international debt on Tuesday, the largest bond sale by an Argentine corporate issuer since 2015, a day after unveiling an investment programme it prices at US$154.1 billion.

The Terms

The notes carry a 7.55 percent coupon and priced to an effective yield of 7.85 percent, maturing in June 2035 for a nine-year term.

Argentine financial press describes it as the largest international issue by an Argentine company in the past eleven years. For a sovereign whose corporates have spent much of the past decade locked out of international markets or paying punitive spreads, the coupon is the more meaningful figure than the size.

The Programme It Funds

On 8 September, chief executive Horacio Marín set out a multi-year investment plan totalling US$154.1 billion across projects registered under Argentina’s RIGI incentive regime.

The components include an oil hub at roughly US$25 billion, Argentina LNG at 12 million tonnes a year for roughly US$51 billion, and an additional liquefaction train at roughly US$25 billion, with further Vaca Muerta projects on top.

The stated ambition is to lift YPF’s operated production from 400,000 barrels a day to 2 million, and to make Argentina the world’s sixth largest LNG exporter.

This is YPF’s own plan, not a national investment programme, a distinction that is easy to lose in the headline figure. A final investment decision on the LNG element is expected in November, and the plan does not carry a stated completion date.

It is involved in the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbon fields and production of…

What to Hold Against It

US$154 billion is more than a third of Argentina’s annual GDP. Announced investment plans in Argentine energy have a long history of arriving late, arriving smaller, or not arriving.

The bond is different in kind. It is money actually raised at a rate actually agreed, from investors who priced nine years of Argentine corporate risk at under 8 percent. That is a market judgment rather than a corporate ambition.

The two are related but they are not the same fact, and the second is the one that can be checked.

Why Eleven Years

The last comparable Argentine corporate issue was in 2015, before the sovereign default of 2014 had been resolved and before the country’s corporates lost practical access to international markets.

What followed was a decade of interruptions. The 2018 currency crisis, the 2020 sovereign restructuring, and the exchange controls that ran through much of the period all closed the window at various points, and reopened it only at prices that made issuance uneconomic.

YPF itself restructured bond obligations in 2021 in a transaction that bondholders accepted reluctantly. That history is in the price of everything the company has issued since.

A 7.55 percent coupon for nine years is therefore not a low number in absolute terms. It is a low number for this issuer, from this country, given that history.

What the Money Is Actually For

Argentina’s energy story has changed in a way the financing had not yet caught up with. Vaca Muerta production has grown steadily, the country became a net energy exporter, and the constraint moved from geology to infrastructure.

Pipelines, processing and export terminals are what the capital is needed for. The Vaca Muerta Sur pipeline and the associated Atlantic export facilities are the projects that convert reserves into cash flow.

LNG is the larger ambition and the harder one. Liquefaction capacity is capital-intensive, requires long-term offtake contracts to finance, and puts Argentina into competition with Qatar, the United States and Australia for Asian buyers.

A final investment decision on that element is expected in November, and it is the real test of whether the announced programme becomes a built one.

The Gap Between Plan and Delivery

US$154.1 billion is a very large number for a company with YPF’s balance sheet, and it is spread across projects at very different stages of maturity.

The RIGI incentive regime, which grants tax, customs and currency guarantees to large investments, is designed to make exactly these projects financeable. Whether it survives changes of government is the risk every foreign partner is pricing.

Argentina has announced transformative energy investment before. The distinguishing feature this time is that Vaca Muerta is already producing at scale, so the projects are about moving and monetising output that exists rather than about finding it.

That is a materially better position than any previous announcement was made from, and it is still an announcement.

A 7.55 percent coupon and a 7.85 percent effective yield, maturing June 2035.

Why does it matter?

What is the production target?

World.title: Britain Says Relentless, Argentina Names the Executives
World.content:
ARGENTINA · SOUTH ATLANTIC

Key Facts — The word UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the Commons on 9 September his government would be relentless in defending the islanders’ choice.

— The quote We will always respect the rights of the Falkland Islanders to choose to be British. That will never change under this Government and we will be relentless in defending that.

— The escalation Argentina announced on 9 September it will extend its criminal complaints to name individual directors, managers and legal representatives personally.

— Who announced it Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, with Treasury Attorney Sebastián Amerio.

— The first wave Five companies were denounced on 7 September before the Federal Chamber in Buenos Aires.

— On the islands The Falkland Islands Defence Force opened recruitment for drone operators on 9 September.

The language has moved from implacable to relentless in a week. Argentina’s response is to stop suing companies and start naming the people who run them.

Britain Says Relentless, Argentina Names the Executives

Britain’s prime minister hardened his language on the Falklands at Wednesday’s Commons questions, hours before Argentina announced it would extend its criminal complaints over hydrocarbon activity to individual company officers.

What Burnham Said

Andy Burnham, who became prime minister on 20 July 2026, was asked about the islands at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday 9 September.

His answer: we will always respect the rights of the Falkland Islanders to choose to be British, that will never change under this Government, and we will be relentless in defending that.

The shift is small and deliberate. Earlier in the week the framing attributed to unnamed British officials was implacable. Relentless, said by the prime minister on the floor of the Commons, is a different order of commitment.

Argentina Widens the Target

On 7 September the Argentine government filed criminal complaints before the Federal Chamber in Buenos Aires against five companies engaged in hydrocarbon activity near the islands. Infobae listed them as Navitas Petroleum Development and Production, Navitas Petroleum Atlantic United, Navitas Petroleum LP, JHI Associates and Eco Atlantic Oil and Gas.

Company names have varied between outlets covering the same actions in the same week, and The Rio Times reports that list as Infobae’s rather than as a confirmed government roster.

On 9 September Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, supported by Treasury Attorney Sebastián Amerio, announced the complaints would be extended to name directors, managers, statutory auditors and authorised representatives in their own right.

That is the genuinely new element. An earlier action listing 45 people and entities was administrative, handled through the foreign ministry as sanctions. This is criminal, and it reaches individuals.

The government’s communiqué did not specify which court or prosecutor would receive the new filings.

Drone Operators

Recruitment for drone operators based in the islands opened on 9 September. It is being run by the Falkland Islands Defence Force, the locally recruited part-time volunteer unit, not by the regular British Army.

The postings are part-time and seek candidates with unmanned-systems experience and local navigational knowledge. That combination points at maritime and coastal surveillance rather than at anything expeditionary.

The Scale Argument

Argentine commentary is increasingly framing the dispute by comparison. YPF issued US$1.2 billion of international debt on 9 September and has announced a multi-year investment plan it puts at US$154.1 billion, almost all of it tied to Vaca Muerta and to liquefied natural gas.

Set against that, the Sea Lion field north of the islands is small. The implicit argument is that Argentina does not need the disputed acreage and is objecting on sovereignty rather than on resources.

It is a reasonable line and it does not settle anything. The complaints are being filed regardless of what Vaca Muerta produces.

The Legal Theory Argentina Is Using

Argentina’s domestic law treats hydrocarbon activity on the continental shelf around the islands as taking place on Argentine territory. Operating there without an Argentine permit is therefore, in Argentine law, illegal exploitation of national resources.

Law 26.659 sets out the framework and the penalties, which include criminal liability, exclusion from activity in Argentina for twenty years, and asset seizure.

The obvious limitation is enforcement. Companies operating from Britain with no Argentine assets and no Argentine directors are not reachable by an Argentine court in any practical sense.

Naming individuals changes the calculation slightly. A criminal complaint against a named director creates a personal exposure that follows the individual, and it complicates travel, banking and directorships in ways a complaint against a company does not.

Why This Is Escalating Now

The trigger is Sea Lion, the field north of the islands that Rockhopper and Navitas have been working toward development on for more than a decade. It has moved from a permanently deferred project to one with financing and a timetable.

A field that never gets built imposes no cost on Argentina. One that starts producing establishes a fact on the water and generates revenue for the islands’ government, which strengthens the self-determination argument Britain rests its position on.

That is why the Argentine response has intensified in step with the project’s progress rather than in step with any diplomatic event.

It is also why the government has moved from administrative sanctions, which are largely symbolic, to criminal complaints against individuals, which are not.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the UK prime minister say?

Andy Burnham told the Commons on 9 September that his government would be relentless in defending the Falkland Islanders’ right to choose to be British.

What is new in Argentina’s legal action?

The complaints will now name individual directors, managers, statutory auditors and legal representatives personally, not only the companies.

Which companies were denounced?

Infobae listed three Navitas Petroleum entities, JHI Associates and Eco Atlantic Oil and Gas in the 7 September filing. Company lists have varied between outlets.

Who is recruiting drone operators?

The Falkland Islands Defence Force, the locally recruited volunteer unit, not the regular British Army.

Who announced the escalation?

Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, with Treasury Attorney Sebastián Amerio.

World.title: A Month After Colombia’s Earthquake, 321 Dead and 1,300 Aftershocks
World.content:
COLOMBIA · RECONSTRUCTION

Key Facts — One month The 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck on 10 August with its epicentre at San José del Palmar, Chocó.

— The toll 321 dead, according to the national disaster agency.

— Still moving More than 1,300 aftershocks recorded by the Servicio Geológico Colombiano since 10 August.

— The reach 16 departments and 498 municipalities affected, with major damage in Pereira, Quibdó, Cali and Manizales.

— The response Eleven decrees for reconstruction, including a Fondo Patria Milagro and energy-continuity measures through FONDES.

— The pension route Affected territories authorised to draw exceptionally on the national territorial pension fund for emergency needs.

A month after the ground moved, Colombia has counted 321 dead and written eleven decrees. The aftershocks have not stopped.

A Month After Colombia’s Earthquake, 321 Dead and 1,300 Aftershocks

Colombia marked one month since the Chocó earthquake on Thursday with a death toll of 321, more than 1,300 recorded aftershocks and a reconstruction programme now running to eleven decrees.

The Scale

The earthquake registered magnitude 7.4 with its epicentre at San José del Palmar in Chocó, on 10 August 2026.

Sixteen departments and 498 municipalities were affected. The heaviest structural damage was recorded in Pereira, Quibdó, Cali and Manizales.

The national disaster management agency puts the death toll at 321 as of the one-month mark. The Servicio Geológico Colombiano has recorded more than 1,300 aftershocks since the main event.

The Eleven Decrees

The reconstruction package announced by the president includes a Fondo Patria Milagro, energy-continuity measures channelled through FONDES, an obras por impuestos mechanism allowing companies to discharge tax obligations through reconstruction works, rules for investment across jurisdictional boundaries, exceptional access to DANE data, and measures to keep schools running.

Separately, affected territories were authorised to draw exceptionally on the Fondo Nacional de Pensiones de las Entidades Territoriales for emergency needs. That is a significant instrument: it converts municipal pension reserves into immediate liquidity.

It is also a decision with a cost that arrives later. Money taken out of a territorial pension fund is money a municipality will have to replace.

Outside Help

Qatar delivered 23 tonnes of humanitarian aid and a fully equipped field hospital, sent through the Qatar Fund for Development and flown in by Qatari Armed Forces aircraft. The delivery was announced on 9 September.

Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar acknowledged the contribution publicly.

What the Next Month Looks Like

The immediate phase is over. What follows is the harder part: housing for displaced families, structural assessment of buildings that survived, and the reconstruction of a road and power network across terrain that was difficult before the earthquake.

Chocó is among Colombia’s poorest departments and among its least connected. The recovery there will be slower than in Pereira or Cali, and the eleven decrees do not change that.

Why Chocó Was the Worst Place for It

Chocó is Colombia’s poorest department by most measures and among its least connected. Much of it is reachable only by river or air, road density is minimal, and the terrain is dense rainforest cut by rivers.

That geography shaped the first month of the response. Aid moved slowly because the routes to move it along did not exist, and assessment teams could not reach some affected communities for days.

It will shape the second year more. Rebuilding housing and public buildings in a place where every sack of cement arrives by boat costs several times what it costs in Pereira, and takes longer.

The epicentre at San José del Palmar sits in exactly this terrain, on the western cordillera between Chocó and Valle del Cauca.

The Damage Outside the Epicentre

The heaviest structural damage was recorded not at the epicentre but in the cities. Pereira, Quibdó, Cali and Manizales all took significant losses, and between them they hold several million people.

That pattern is normal for a large earthquake in the Andes. Energy propagates along the mountain chain, and the losses concentrate wherever the building stock is weakest relative to the shaking it receives.

Colombia has had seismic building codes since 1984 and strengthened them after the 1999 Armenia earthquake, which killed around a thousand people in the coffee region. Buildings constructed since then generally performed. Older ones did not.

Sixteen departments and 498 municipalities recorded effects, which is roughly half the country by administrative area.

What the Aftershock Count Means

More than 1,300 aftershocks in a month is not unusual for a magnitude 7.4 event. Aftershock sequences decay on a well-understood curve, with frequency falling roughly in inverse proportion to the time since the main shock.

The practical consequence is for damaged buildings. A structure weakened by the main shock but still standing can fail in an aftershock a fraction of its size, which is why structural assessment before reoccupation matters more than the headline magnitude.

It also has a human cost that does not appear in the damage statistics. Populations living through a month of continuing tremors do not return to normal routines, and displacement extends well beyond the buildings actually destroyed.

The sequence will continue at declining frequency for months.

Magnitude 7.4, epicentre at San José del Palmar in Chocó, on 10 August 2026.

What is being done?

Who has sent aid?

World.title: International News: Mexico expands efforts to transform and manage Sargassum
World.content:
International News: Mexico expands efforts to transform and manage Sargassum

By Zoila Palma: Mexico is expanding efforts to manage the growing accumulation of sargassum along its Caribbean coast, with authorities promoting sustainable uses of the macroalgae while advancing the restoration of coastal ecosystems.

Through the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (SEMARNAT), the government is supporting circular-economy projects aimed at transforming sargassum into bioinputs and water-treatment systems.

SEMARNAT Deputy Minister of Biodiversity and Environmental Restoration Marina Robles recently visited the Center for Water and Algae Technologies and Sciences at the Yucatán Scientific and Technological Park and the Marine Strategic Implementations Plant.

The facilities have the capacity to process up to 20,000 tonnes of sargassum and other organic materials into products such as bioinputs and water-treatment systems.

Robles proposed greater cooperation among SEMARNAT, the Ministry of the Navy and local communities, including increased involvement from the fishing sector in developing sargassum harvesting strategies.

She also suggested financing mechanisms, including potential preferential loans from public or private banks, to support sargassum-processing projects and new value chains. So far this year, 83,137 tonnes of sargassum have been collected along Mexico’s Caribbean coast, including 30,021 tonnes in Playa del Carmen and 20,469 tonnes in Cancún.

The continuing influx of sargassum has created challenges for tourism destinations, as decomposing algae can discolor seawater and produce strong odors.

World.title: Union says SmartStream restrictions cut off the very access that exposed scandals
World.content:
Union says SmartStream restrictions cut off the very access that exposed scandals

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Public Service Union is demanding the immediate reversal of a decision restricting Finance Officers’ access to the SmartStream financial management system.

According to the PSU, Finance Officers throughout the public service can now view transactions only within the ministry where they are posted. The ability to view payments and transactions in other ministries, and across Government as a whole, has been withdrawn.

SmartStream leaks generated a string of major stories earlier this year, providing the public with its first insight into the Mira Millions and later the Kukulkan matter.

Those disclosures led to the exposure of thousands of related party supply payments in the Ministry of Defence, 99% of them falling below the $10,000 threshold.

The revelations ultimately contributed to the suspension of two ministers from Cabinet and triggered an emergency audit from the Auditor General’s Office.

“Restricting Finance Officers to their own ministry therefore does not simply reduce transparency in the abstract, it removes the very line of sight that exposed the conduct now under investigation,” the union said.

“Finance Officers do not work for ministers. They work for the people of Belize, and the money they account for is not the Government’s money. Restore the access.”

World.title: Police find 900 grams of suspected crack cocaine in San Pablo area
World.content:
Police find 900 grams of suspected crack cocaine in San Pablo area

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in San Pedro recovered 900 grams of suspected crack cocaine during an operation in the San Pablo area on Wednesday evening.

According to police information, officers acted on intelligence suggesting that illegal drugs may have been stashed at an abandoned lot in the area.

At around 5:30 p.m., officers searched through garbage at the location. During the operation, police reportedly noticed a black vegetable crate near a tree.

Inside the crate was a white sack containing a green plastic bag. Police say that bag held three transparent plastic bags with hard white substances suspected to be crack cocaine.

No one was in the immediate area when the suspected drugs were found.

The items were taken to the San Pedro Police Station for further inspection.

Police say the three suspected crack cocaine parcels weighed a combined 900 grams.

The drugs were then sealed, labelled and deposited as found property.

No arrests have been reported in connection with the discovery.

World.title: Police find 58 grams of suspected crack cocaine hidden in sewage tank north of San Pedro
World.content:
Police find 58 grams of suspected crack cocaine hidden in sewage tank north of San Pedro

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in San Pedro recovered 58 grams of suspected crack cocaine after searching an abandoned building four miles north of the town.

According to police, officers were conducting mobile patrol when they received information that led them to search the abandoned structure.

During the search, police reportedly found a transparent plastic bag hidden inside a sewage tank.

When officers opened the bag, they discovered a white buff coloured substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

No one was in the immediate area when the suspected drugs were found.

The substance was taken to the San Pedro Police Station, where it was weighed and amounted to 58 grams.

Police packaged, sealed and labelled the suspected crack cocaine before handing it over to the exhibit keeper as found property.

No arrests were reported in connection with the discovery.

World.title: Special Envoy calls for hope and action on World Suicide Prevention Day
World.content:
Special Envoy calls for hope and action on World Suicide Prevention Day

By Zoila Palma: Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children, Rossana Briceño, is calling on Belizeans to help change the narrative surrounding suicide as the country observes World Suicide Prevention Day today, September 10.

This year’s observance is being held under the theme “Changing the Narrative on Suicide,” with Briceño emphasizing that every life is precious and that no one should feel they have to face their struggles alone.

She said the day is an opportunity to honor lives lost to suicide while raising awareness, offering support, breaking the stigma surrounding mental health and inspiring hope.

The Special Envoy highlighted Belize’s ongoing efforts to strengthen suicide prevention through the National Suicide Prevention Plan 2024–2030, which is supported by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO).

The plan focuses on strengthening prevention measures, expanding crisis support, reducing stigma and encouraging people to seek help at an early stage.

She also stressed the importance of collaboration among government agencies, civil society organizations and healthcare providers in addressing suicide and promoting mental well-being across the country.

“When we pass hope from one person to another, we are reminded that every life matters,” Briceño said.

“Let us pass the hope, Belize,” she urged.

World.title: Police find 600 grams of suspected cannabis in Boca Del Rio mangrove
World.content:
Police find 600 grams of suspected cannabis in Boca Del Rio mangrove

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in San Pedro recovered 600 grams of suspected cannabis during an intelligence led operation in the Boca Del Rio area on Wednesday morning.

According to police information, officers from several units were conducting an operation around San Pedro Town at about 8:05 a.m. when they searched a mangrove area along the lagoon side.

During the search, police found a green plastic bag among garbage. Inside was a parcel wrapped in plastic containing a green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis.

No one was in the immediate area at the time of the discovery.

The suspected cannabis was taken to the San Pedro Police Station, where it was weighed on a digital scale and amounted to 600 grams.

Police later sealed and labelled the substance before handing it over to the exhibit keeper as found property.

No arrests were reported.

World.title: Belize takes Tourism spotlight in Mexico, strengthening travel industry ties
World.content:
Belize takes Tourism spotlight in Mexico, strengthening travel industry ties

By Zoila Palma: Belize was proudly showcased in Mexico during a networking cocktail reception hosted by Anthony Mahler, Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations, at the Embassy of Belize.

The reception brought together members of the Mexican media and travel trade wholesalers for an evening focused on building relationships, strengthening partnerships, and promoting Belize’s diverse tourism offerings to the Mexican market.

Also in attendance were Devin Daly, Minister of State for Youth and Sports; Nicole Usher, Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations; Mohit Budhrani, Vice Chair of the Belize Tourism Board’s Board of Directors; Evan Tillett, Director of Tourism; and other officials from the Belize Tourism Board, National Sports Council, and Football Federation of Belize.

The networking event followed the participation of Minister Mahler and the Belizean delegation in the 4th UN World Sports Tourism Congress in Mexico, which provided an additional platform to highlight Belize as a tourism destination and explore opportunities to strengthen ties with Mexico’s travel industry.

World.title: Honduran man charged for smoking cannabis in public on Caye Caulker
World.content:
Honduran man charged for smoking cannabis in public on Caye Caulker

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police on Caye Caulker have charged a 28 year old Honduran man for smoking cannabis in public.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol in the Bahia area of Caye Caulker Village at around 7:30 a.m. on Wednesday, September 9, when they noticed a man riding a bicycle while smoking what appeared to be a brown cigarette.

Police say officers could smell a strong aroma of cannabis and observed smoke coming from the cigarette.

The man was stopped and the cigarette was retrieved. Police say it contained a green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis and the tip had been burned.

The man was identified as Brayan Sosa, 28, a Honduran labourer residing in the Bahia area.

Sosa was taken to the Caye Caulker Police Station and formally charged with smoking cannabis in public.

He was granted station bail and is scheduled to appear in the San Pedro Magistrate Court on Tuesday, September 15.

World.title: Privy Council introduces free visa process for parties attending London appeals
World.content:
Visa

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Commonwealth citizens travelling to London to attend Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) proceedings can now access a free, streamlined visa application process.

The initiative, developed by the JCPC in collaboration with the United Kingdom (UK) Home Office and Ministry of Justice, is available to appellants, respondents and members of their legal teams who are attending appeals in person.

The process does not extend to wider family members, the JCPC said in a statement on Thursday.

Once a hearing date has been confirmed, counsel must use the JCPC portal to indicate who will attend the hearing in person and whether they require a visa.

The JCPC will then verify the applicant’s connection to the case before issuing an invitation letter and providing further guidance on the visa application process.

Visa applications will continue to undergo the UK’s usual database checks, and the Home Office may request additional information in some cases, the JCPC said.

JCPC Registrar Laura Angus said the new process reflects the committee’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continuous improvement.

“The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is very pleased to be able to confirm the UK Government’s offer of this service to parties attending appeals in London. We listen to our users’ feedback and this decision underlines the JCPC’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continual improvement. We also routinely offer hybrid hearings for parties who prefer to take part in appeal hearings virtually,” Angus said.

World.title: CASINO CAUTION
World.content:
AS the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) shores up its anti-money laundering defences ahead of the planned opening of Jamaica’s first casino at Princess Grande Jamaica Resort in Hanover early next year, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has issued a warning on key red flags to look out for.

FATF, the global illicit-finance watchdog, published a list of new gaming scams in a report on Wednesday, which it said was based on surveys conducted and included contributions from more than 80 jurisdictions.

The document titled ‘Red Flag Risk Indicators, Risks of Gaming and Gambling’, stated that the industries have changed significantly over recent years and continue to evolve through the expansion of online, cross-border, multi-product, and multi-payment platforms.

FATF said the work offers an updated analysis of money laundering risks posed by the casino sector as well as risks posed by the broader gambling and gaming sectors.

Red flag indicators in customer behaviour at brick-and-mortar casinos included attempts to influence or bribe venue staff to ignore their activities or bypass thorough customer due diligence checks and offering tips and other incentives.

Some casino customers were found to only want to deal with one staff member and avoid other staffers. These schemers use third parties to place cash into redemption terminals and purchase gaming chips, or place bets in an attempt to anonymise gambling.

The report outlined that the schemers also tend to request that winnings be paid in cash up to the threshold amount, but they never return to collect the balance. They also make purchases or attempts to purchase winning claim instruments from another customer and then present it as their own.

The report warned that eyebrows should raise if a player attempts to present a casino value instrument from an unknown source or if they are behaving in an unusual way on premises. It also warned of players acting on behalf of a third party and taking instructions from mobile phones or other customers on the premises.

Other red flags include customers who are reluctant or refuse to provide up-to-date identification documents or inconsistencies in personal information.

The report pointed out that some casino customers also opt to produce documents that are unclear or doctored and prove difficult to authenticate.

Where betting patterns are concerned, some customers were flagged for inconsistent spending that do not match their customer profile, including their known income and background.

In the report, FATF said it examined the scope of the risks associated with brick-and-mortar casinos, sports and novelty betting, other non-casino gambling — including scratch cards, arcades, bingo, lotteries, and slot machines outside of casinos.

“Findings indicate that certain payment methods associated with gaming and gambling activity such as cash, e-wallets, mobile money, and virtual assets are vulnerable to a range of money laundering risks. The variety of payment methods accepted by online gaming and gambling operators increasingly allows rapid, anonymous, cross-border transactions and conversion of value into different forms,” read page two of the 10-page document.

The operators and platforms covered in the report varied in nature and most of the risk indicators provided were related to land-based and online casinos and, to a lesser extent, betting. It was found that land-based operators have similar indicators as do online platforms.

In a statement on Wednesday, Giles Thomas, the president of FATF, said without robust safeguards, these sectors can attract gateways for fraudsters, professional money launderers, and organised criminal networks.

“I urge all governments to take note of the risk factors we have set out today, and put in place appropriate risk-based responses — from strengthening oversight and cracking down on illegal and offshore operators to boosting international co-operation and deepening public-private collaboration,” the FATF president said.

At a recent Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange officials of the CGC declared that they have been engaging in training with the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency (MOCA), the Financial Investigations Division (FID), and the Jamaica Customs Agency in an effort to ensure that strong anti-money laundering guardrails linked to casino gaming are in place when Jamaica gears up to claim its stake in an industry that generated more than US$320 billion worldwide last year.

The partnership with MOCA and FID is one based on capacity-building and information-sharing, support, and investigations.

Damion McKenzie, senior director of enforcement and investigations at the CGC, told Observer editors and reporters the entity recognises that, “Casino gaming is unique here, so some of the typologies and some of the crimes that happen in casinos, they might not be familiar with them. Our initiatives are to ensure that they are aware of those types of instances that can happen in a casino,” said McKenzie as he pointed out that the training of the law enforcement agents included them acquiring an understanding of the workings of slot machines and vulnerabilities.

The commission’s Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen emphasised that the entity is committed to properly regulating the casino gaming industry by ensuring that a multi-pronged approach is taken towards monitoring the sector in order to better protect the financial ecosystem.

“We operate in a space where we don’t have all the resources and all the knowledge, but remember, we operate in a large financial ecosystem. Our approach is focused on keeping us off the blacklist and on the right side of FATF,” Allen said.

He underscored that with Jamaica no longer being on the FATF list of countries that are assessed as having strategic deficiencies in their anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) regimes, dubbed a grey list, the CGC is prepared to do all in its powers to help to ensure Jamaica does not find itself back on that list.

In June 2024, then Minister of Finance Dr Nigel Clarke said he was proud to share that FATF, at its plenary in Singapore, welcomed Jamaica’s significant progress in improving its AML/CFT regimes.

As a result, FATF said that Jamaica was no longer subject to an increased monitoring process. With the island acknowledging the importance of remaining off the grey list, the CGC said it plans to ensure there are tight guardrails to protect Jamaica’s good standing with FATF.

Jamaica was placed on the FATF grey list in 2020, which signalled to international financial institutions to take special care when transacting with entities and individuals from the island.

One of the drawbacks of this is that it is more expensive to carry out transactions with countries on the list.

Other red flag indicators to look out for at casinos and other gaming establishments:

*Sudden changes in customer’s betting patterns.

*Co-ordinated or unusual betting activity, including hedged bets, betting on all outcomes and consistent losses to other players in peer-to-peer settings.

*Structuring of deposits into smaller amounts to fall under reporting thresholds.

*Use of short-odds bets and other low-risk mechanisms to justify withdrawals.

*Players making numerous large withdrawals without engaging in significant gambling activity.

*Customers appear to play frequently together, with one always winning and the other always losing.

*Suspected collusion in gambling activities, including gambling on both likely outcomes.

*Customer tries to circumvent note insertion limits by playing multiple machines simultaneously.

*Customer frequently plays games with low returns but with lower risks and a higher chance of winning.

*Customer repeatedly collects winnings just below a customer identification threshold.

*Non-genuine play patterns – wagers are low while large sums are deposited and withdrawn.

World.title: Gov’t looking to add speed to school repairs
World.content:
This file photos shows some of the damage Hurricane Melissa did to Edwin Allen High School last year.

THE Government could look overseas for contractors to speed up the repair and rebuilding of schools devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October.

More than 600 educational institutions sustained damage from the Category 5 storm with 309 severely damaged and ranked priority one for repairs and reconstruction.

At a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday officials of the Ministry of Education said 57 of those severely damaged institutions were fully repaired when the new school year began on Monday. The ministry said another 95 schools will be fully repaired by the end of September, and another 34 repaired by the end of December.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon told the media briefing that school repairs were hampered by a shortage of grade one contractors and the ministry will, among other things, explore hiring external contractors to fill gaps while ramping up efforts to upskill local contractors.

Morris Dixon admitted that the current situation is far from perfect and argued that the need for contractors was even more imperative given the mandate placed on the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) — the specialised body established to coordinate and accelerate post-disaster rebuilding and long-term infrastructure resilience after Hurricane Melissa.

She pointed out that while the Administration is committed to continue the work to rebuild schools it has been constrained by the number of grade one contractors available in Jamaica.

“When the budget for the project is above a particular amount, you have to use a grade one contractor, and we’re limited with the number of grade one contractors, so that’s a constraint,” Morris Dixon explained.

“We need those contractors for the schools, we need them for the homes, we need them for the businesses, we need them for that beautiful vision that Prime Minister [Dr Andrew Holness] laid out in his budget presentation. And so, one of the things that we are working on, separately, in a different part of the ministry on the skills side, is an initiative between HEART NSTA/Trust and the Development Bank of Jamaica (DBJ)…we have to work to get those who are at grade two up to grade one through financing and otherwise, because that’s a key element of it. And so DBJ is at the table with us, trying to work through that, because our goal is to give the money to the Jamaicans,” Morris Dixon disclosed.

“What we’re looking at is, how we can work with young people who want to be contractors, put them in groupings, provide funding, and provide incubation to them so that we can get more in the pipeline of grade one contractors. Using external sources is something that we’ll have to look at. For example, for the STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) schools, we have done international tenders, and so in some of the big projects, we’ll have to do some international tendering. We’ll see what comes out of that…but right now, our commitment is to our local contractors using them. But of course, they have to show that they can deliver,” Morris Dixon said further.

The education minister, in the meantime, said work was continuing apace to rehabilitate schools listed as priority one which were severely damaged by Melissa with almost continuous afternoon rain in Westmoreland slowing down the process.

“It’s not perfect. Where we are now is not perfect, and we have a lot of people working. We have many contractors. For our very severely damaged schools, which is about 309 schools that were severely damaged… the bills are high. A lot of them are over $100 million, $200 million, $300 million, a billion dollars almost in some instances,” Morris Dixon said.

According to Morris Dixon, the hurricane is being used as an opportunity “to get better school plants, at least in the west”.

Meanwhile, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education Dr Kasan Troupe said the new school year got off to a fair start on Monday with 92 per cent of schools having all students while two per cent of schools will have to be augmented with temporary learning spaces and utilise some amount of rotation.

“That’s tremendous given what we have been through, and I want to thank all my principals, all my chairmen and board members, and of course, all the teachers,” Troupe said.

She told the media briefing that the ministry has ensured that all schools have been given their operational funds along with furniture and other resources.

“We sent out 30 per cent of the increased grants into our schools in June. The second tranche of that is due in September, the first Friday in September and two weeks ago, we ensured that all the funds were out in all our schools, so we are ahead of time because we understand what it means for our principals to have monies to get the work done. That amounted to $3.05 billion that we have disbursed to our schools, and that will treat with the operations, that will treat with the nutritional support for the learners, and of course, an additional $75 million we sent out to our schools to impact 275 schools to treat with canteen repairs,” Troupe said.

“As it relates to furniture, 41 schools indicated that they need additional support. We are responding to that, but in preparation for this year, we spent $300 million to get furniture out into our schools. So before we started, we distributed over 17,000 pieces, and whilst we were wrapping up on the last weekend, there were 8,000 pieces that we were distributing across our schools,” added Troupe.

According to the permanent secretary, another 20,000 pieces of furniture are being prepared for distribution to the system.

She said the ministry is spending more than $700 million in resourcing high schools with books and more than $300 million in primary schools, making that approximately $1.1 billion of expenditure in providing books for public schools.

World.title: 450 set for Caribbean Music Awards performance
World.content:
450...preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right.

Dancehall artiste 450 is gearing up to make his debut performance at the highly anticipated Caribbean Music Awards (CMA).

The fourth annual ceremony and showcase will take place on Saturday, September 19 at the National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago.

For 450, the opportunity to perform on the regional stage represents another significant moment in his career.

“It feels like a big moment for me. The CMA is a major platform for Caribbean music, so it feels like another chapter of the story that my team and I are grateful for,” 450, who is also nominated for Album of the Year, told the Jamaica Observer.

V’ghn, Freetown Collective, Jah Mason, 1T1, and Theomaa are among the artistes slated to perform. The line-up represents a cross section of Caribbean music, spanning soca, reggae, dancehall, bouyon, and contemporary Caribbean sounds.

After three years of staging the awards in New York City, organisers are bringing CMA to the Caribbean for the first time since its inception. The move will also see the celebration expand beyond a single awards night into an immersive weekend of activities.

The weekend is expected to feature networking opportunities, industry discussions, cultural showcases, and opportunities for fans to interact more closely with artistes and other players in the Caribbean music industry.

450 said preparations are well under way for his performance, with his team focused on ensuring his CMA debut makes an impact.

“Preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right,” he shared.

While not revealing too much about what he has planned, the entertainer promised a high-energy performance featuring some of the songs that have connected with his fan base.

“Energy, good vibes, and some of the songs they know and love. I’m representing Jamaica and dancehall music,” 450 said.

The appearance comes during what the artiste describes as a strong year of career growth, particularly as he continues to introduce his music to audiences outside Jamaica.

“It’s been a really good year. I’ve been able to reach new audiences, perform on bigger international stages, and continue growing the music. There’s still more to accomplish, so mi nah slow down,” he said.

With the final quarter of 2026 under way, 450 has no plans to ease the pace. Beyond his upcoming CMA performance, the dancehall artiste is working on new material and further expanding his international presence.

“I’m working on new music, more visuals, and some exciting international projects. More to come soon,” he added.

World.title: Contractor says all his 7 school jobs almost complete
World.content:
Inside a newly completed grade six classroom with a new roof, ceiling, lighting and ceiling fans at Petersfield Primary School in Westmoreland..

PETERSFIELD, Westmoreland — While several schools in western Jamaica still have a long way to go to repair damage inflicted by last October’s Hurricane Melissa, Petersfield Primary in Westmoreland is now 98 per cent complete. There are only a few doors and windows left to be installed.

The Petersfield project is one of seven being undertaken by Archistruct Limited. Others include William Knibb High in Trelawny and five schools in St Ann. According to owner and managing director of the 14-year-old company Chadwick Lawrence, all the schools are almost 100 per cent repaired.

“The minister [of education] did say she’s holding us accountable, so I take that one seriously. I couldn’t afford to disappoint her,” he told the Jamaica Observer Wednesday.

With a degree in engineering and a master’s in construction project management, Lawrence is supported by a team of qualified construction professionals.

“It is no secret sauce; it’s just a matter of management and execution of tasks based on schedule and procuring materials on time. That is what I do. We use a lot of people from the area, as well as people from different areas, as needed. At Petersfield, we did a lot of night and day work to get it finished,” Lawrence explained when asked the secret to his success in having the schools ready for September.

“It boils down to one expression: Construction is about the joy of creating. It is nice to just see the students inside the classroom; it’s a genuinely nice feeling to see the students in the classroom learning and the teachers teaching in a comfortable space. When you talk with the teachers and the principals and they tell you that they are happy with the product they have received because it’s better than it was before… that really brings the joy of creating,” he said.

The company has been strategic in its approach.

“In terms of the scheduling and procurement of materials, we had ensured that we did that beforehand as we went along. We were doing seven schools, so we were able to buy in bulk and to get everything on spot before we needed it. Now we are at 98 per cent complete and we are happy to say that it is a good September morning. All the kids are out and about, parents and teachers are happy, and we’re just glad to see a satisfied customer,” Lawrence told the Observer.

School board chairman and Custos of Westmoreland Reverend Hartley Perrin, who had initial concerns, is among those pleased with the results at Petersfield Primary.

“I had my doubts. I was very concerned about the progress, or lack thereof… But then, all of a sudden, it started to pick up as if they stepped on the accelerator. They were working longer hours and they seemed to have employed more people. I’m pleased to see the work that has been done and the quality of it. Even the painting is of good standard,” the Custos beamed.

But it has not all been smooth sailing. The type of windows needed for the school projects is not available in Jamaica. The original structures had aluminum window blades.

“We’re doing some… we discussed with the principals and they have agreed to other options for the type of windows,” said Lawrence.

At all seven schools, his team is now adding little touches that make a world of difference.

“We work closely with the principals and teachers. Even now, we are at different locations doing what we call commissioning. There are little things that might be needed — a teacher may need a nail there or a piece of board there for a pin-up board [to place teaching aids] — and we’re there now putting those things in place to make the space as comfortable as possible,” said Lawrence.

At Petersfield, his company has a separate contract to build a new administrative and classroom block. Lawrence confirmed that all materials are on-site and the bending of steel began Wednesday morning.

World.title: THE ULTIMATE TEST
World.content:
World 100m champion Oblique Seville headlines Jamaica’s team for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Technical Leader Maurice Wilson says Jamaica’s athletes will be ready for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships which starts tomorrow at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary.

A 32-member team, with 27 athletes set to contest individual events for Jamaica, was named by World Athletics on Monday, based on world rankings for the first of what is set to be an annual end-of-season all-star competition.

Wilson described the event as “a fantastic initiative”, which he said has the potential to take the sport to another level.

“There are changes to the arrangements,” he told the Jamaica Observer, where athletes’ representatives will have “a more hands-on” duty, as national federations such as the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) will only be responsible for naming relay coaches.

Wilson and Michael Frater have been named by the JAAA to take charge of the mixed 4x100m and 4x400m teams, with the athletes being able to have their personal coaches with them.

“Every major professional sport has annual championships,” Wilson said. “So track and field should not be an exception, and this is something we need.”

Winners of the individual events will receive a bye to the 2027 World Championships as well as US$150,000 (over $23 million) while winning relay teams will share US$80,000 (just over $12 million). Just about every participant will take home a cash prize.

There will also be a US$100,000 ($15.5 million) bonus for breaking a world record, while the champions will get a trophy rather than the traditional gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Newly crowned Diamond League 100m champions Oblique Seville and Tina Clayton have been included in Jamaica’s 32-member team that will compete at the three-day event.

In addition to Seville on the men’s side, Commonwealth Games champions Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, and Demario Prince were also named.

Commonwealth Games champion Sanique Walker and women’s 4x100m relay gold medallists Jodean Williams and Lavanya Williams were also named.

Team Jamaica

Men



Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, Orlando Bennett, Ackeem Blake, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince, Oblique Seville, Christopher Taylor

Women

Rushell Clayton, Tina Clayton, Lamara Distin, Brianna Lyston, Ashanti Moore, Ackera Nugent, Nickisha Pryce, Demisha Roswell, Shiann Salmon, Megan Simmonds, Ackelia Smith, Jonielle Smith, Sanique Walker, Danielle Williams, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams

Relays

Zandrion Barnes, Kadrion Goldson, Rohan Watson, Assinie Wilson, Shana Kaye Anderson

World.content:
