World.title: ‘My heart broke’: Education minister orders probe after student denied restroom
World.content:
Minister of Education, Skills, Youth and Information, Senator Dr. the Hon. Dana Morris Dixon, addresses the post-Cabinet press briefing held on September 9 at Jamaica House. (Photo: JIS)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information is to receive an official report from the school where a student was denied the opportunity to use the restroom and soiled herself.

Portfolio Minister, Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, made the disclosure during the post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday at Jamaica House.

“When I saw that story, of course, as many Jamaicans did, my heart broke,” Morris Dixon said. “My heart was breaking for that student when I heard the story, and so I understand the outrage. I understand how Jamaicans feel and how they feel it as if it were their child, because I felt similarly that that was my child.”

“As minister, I have to have all the facts, and it’s for that reason that I’ve asked for an investigation of what took place, so that I can get an official report on it with all the facts on the table. And then we will take action after that,” she added.

The minister said she spoke with the child’s father on Wednesday, noting that the ministry will provide the necessary support needed.

“I had a good conversation [and] noted that all of Jamaica feels concerned and that we’re worried about his daughter. We conveyed our love for her and that at the ministry we’ll provide whatever support she may need. There was indication that there may be need for some emotional support and some counselling support,” Morris Dixon said.

“In the ministry we’ll do that. We have psychologists on retainer, so any child in our system that needs support, we in the ministry, we pay for the psychologist or if they need a psychiatrist, we also pay for it. So, we’ll provide whatever support that child needs, and the children of Jamaica are at the centre of our decision-making,” she added.

The minister also revealed that she spoke with the principal of the school on Wednesday, adding that it was important to listen to all sides.

“I had a good conversation with the principal, and she assured me that the children are at the centre of all of her policies. And that everything she does is with them in mind. She also went through what happened on the day. She’s indicated we will get the official report from the school, and as I said, we’ll meet with the Board, we’ll meet with the parent, with the school, and in the ministry we’ll get to the bottom of it, and we will take action that is needed,” she added.

Morris Dixon pointed out that many schools have a difficult balancing act, noting that “out of safety for the children and out of other incidents that may have happened, you have to make a call as a teacher”.

“So, I understand the difficulty in that call. But when there are emergencies, we have to act differently. So even when we have the set bathroom breaks, if a child is ill between those bathroom breaks, we have to give them the time to go to the bathroom. And the good thing is when I spoke to the principal, the official rules at the school match with the ministry’s expectations and so what we have to do as a ministry, is to check if the rules were broken,” she said.

— JIS

World.title: German foreign minister urges voters to back Ukraine, NATO as far right surges
World.content:
The call comes after the AfD won 43.8% in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result and leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats a distant second at 17.2 %.

Wadephul argued Thursday that the way forward was not to retreat from Germany’s commitments, but to do a better job of explaining why they matter.

He cast the challenge in stark historical terms, invoking the collapse of Germany’s democracy between the two World Wars. “Germany knows from the Weimar Republic what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system,” he said. “We have to show that we have learned our lesson.”

The Weimar Republic, Germany’s first parliamentary democracy, was progressively hollowed out amid economic crisis, political paralysis and growing support for anti-democratic forces before Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in 1933.

As for the results of Sunday's vote, they were not only the AfD’s strongest-ever showing, but the highest vote share won by any party in the state since German reunification.

During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund repeatedly presented spending abroad as money missing at home. He told regional broadcaster MDR that Germany was “giving away money all over the world” and pointed specifically to support for Kyiv: “Every minute, €20,000 goes to Ukraine. That is all money we are missing.”

World.title: UK Foreign Office gets first female leader
World.content:
Cameron was chosen by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband over Karen Pierce, the former U.S. ambassador with ties to Donald Trump, and Deputy National Security Adviser Barbara Woodward.

Miliband said in a statement: “Lindy brings enormous experience across the fields of diplomacy, development and national security, and a reputation for dynamic leadership in postings across the world.”

The outgoing high commissioner previously served as chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre, and has held senior roles in the Northern Ireland Office and the Department for International Development (DfID).

One U.K. diplomat, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said they believe Cameron had been chosen partly because of her background in international development, which “fits neatly” with Miliband’s priorities for British diplomacy.

A second British official said Pierce was the candidate with the strongest connections in Washington and they suspect Pierce was seen as “too big a figure” for the job — someone who would make their views known and attract media attention in their own right.

Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at Chatham House think tank, said the new director will “inherit a department that has been through a bruising restructure, not long after the merger between the FCDO and DFID” and “her first job might be restoring morale.”

She added that navigating a potential shift in the U.K.’s approach to the U.S. and realizing Burnham’s aim to be bolder on the EU-U.K. relationship would be among the key challenges facing Cameron, as well as trying to boost climate and aid diplomacy on a reduced budget.

World.title: France pushes back against English-first EU trade deals
World.content:
“We want to ensure equal treatment of all the European Union’s official languages, including French, of course, in the context of the agreements with Indonesia and India,” said a French official, granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door discussions.

The European Commission estimates that prioritizing the English version would cut almost a year off the time it takes to get those trade deals over the line.

The dispute is particularly sensitive for Paris, where defending the French language — once the principal language of international diplomacy — has been a core tenet of its foreign policy. France is meanwhile headed into a presidential election cycle where Euroskeptic and protectionist voices are increasingly shaping the political debate, making concessions on trade or national prestige especially explosive.

“However procedural it may appear, this measure touches on highly sensitive issues surrounding trade, language and French national prestige — handing powerful political ammunition to populist parties that polls repeatedly show are already standing at the gates of power,” said François Chimits, head of the Europe Program at the Paris-based Institut Montaigne.

Italy initially joined France in expressing concern, with Rome and Paris warning that the fast-track procedure would set a democratic and legal precedent. But it dropped its opposition on Thursday according to one of the people familiar.

“France isn’t dragging its feet; France cannot commit to an international document — such as a trade agreement — that is drafted in a language other than French,” a second French official said, citing constitutional obligations. “Voting on an English-only version would be a violation of the EU’s principle of multilingualism.”

World.title: Sánchez’s release of declassified Ceuta files turns into ‘own goal’
World.content:
One day before the influx, Spain’s National Intelligence Service warned the Civil Guard and the Government Delegation in Ceuta — the office representing the Sánchez government in the city — that it had detected messages calling for a mass crossing the following day.

“There is a call on social media for an assault by fence and sea tomorrow,” an intelligence agent wrote in a WhatsApp message to the delegation’s chief of staff, adding that the groups discussing the surge had 180,000 followers.

Hours later, the intelligence service sent an urgent message to its Moroccan counterparts warning of the planned incursion and thanking Rabat for its “invaluable and continued collaboration in this matter.”

The documents also include 18 reports noting an increase in unauthorized entries into Ceuta earlier in the summer, and a July 8 letter from the Civil Guard proposing border security be reinforced.

The Spanish government insists the documents show there was no way of preventing the migrant surge. The reports did not predict “the scale, nature, or probability” of what happened afterward, Sánchez said in a post on X.

Government Delegate in Ceuta Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano on Thursday downplayed the warnings received by his office, arguing that they could not be considered to be formal alerts because they were relayed by WhatsApp instead of official channels.

World.title: EU watchdog probes von der Leyen’s AI envoy pick
World.content:
Snabe will serve in the unpaid role until the end of March 2027 and is expected to produce a report on issues including AI infrastructure, frontier AI technologies and industrial AI adoption.

But the appointment came under fire because of Siemens’ recent role in lobbying to loosen the AI rules now shaping Europe’s industrial strategy.

Siemens was one of the main proponents of exempting products covered by the EU’s machinery rules from the bloc’s flagship AI law — a tweak EU legislators agreed to in the summer and which is now part of the law.

Siemens is also part of European Tech Creators, a new lobbying force in Brussels that also includes SAP, ASML, Mistral, Airbus, Ericsson, Nokia and BMW. The group has met with von der Leyen and plans to seek meetings with the Commission president once a quarter.

The Ombudsman has told the Commission to reply to the concerns raised by the complainants by Sept. 29.

The Commission has defended Snabe’s appointment by saying that he will produce a publicly available report that is “subject to public scrutiny”, and that his advice will be “visible and accessible to all.”

The Commission denied access to a series of documents around Snabe’s appointment — both to European Parliament lawmakers and to POLITICO.

World.title: Russia ‘trafficking’ foreigners to Ukraine’s front line, Amnesty says
World.content:
A Sri Lankan national named as Dinesh said he was approached about joining the army after his Russian work visa had expired. After the two weeks of training, Dinesh was sent to the front line, where he was captured by the Ukrainian army two months later, the report reads.

Others say they were lured into joining the army from abroad under the pretext of doing a different kind of job. A Brazilian man referred to as Pedro in the report told Amnesty he thought he was signing a contract for a well-paid IT job in Russia, and was in fact taken to a military training center and later sent to the front line.

The Kremlin’s tactics to recruit foreign nationals have been the subject of multiple reports and have triggered diplomatic disputes. Countries such as Kenya and Ghana have demanded that Russia stop recruiting their citizens to fight in the war.

Ukrainian authorities estimated in March that at least 27,000 foreign nationals from 135 countries had been recruited by Russia since 2022. The main groups come from Tajikistan, Belarus and Kazakhstan — countries from which there has traditionally been a large flow of migrants to Russia.

A Kremlin spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Why Burnham is making holidays more expensive
World.content:
Having spent the summer trying to ease the cost of living, is a new tourist tax about to hit domestic holiday makers in the pocket?

The government is giving mayors additional powers to introduce a levy on hotel stays, with no cap on how much they can charge.

With the tourism industry already angry, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine the move and why the timing maybe a little uncomfortable for the government.

Elsewhere, Sky News has uncovered more turmoil in Reform-run local councils. With the Metropolitan Police also widening their investigation into allegations of illegal foreign donations, how much trouble is Reform and leader Nigel Farage really in?

Plus, the Assisted Dying Bill returns to parliament tomorrow – can it clear its first major hurdle for a second time? And Anne assesses the international fallout from the UK’s action over Israel.

You can watch Cathy Newman’s full investigation into Durham’s Reform-led Council here.

World.title: Behind Trump’s push to break the International Criminal Court
World.content:
The U.S. is on a public campaign to dismantle the International Criminal Court. Now, it wants help from its NATO allies.

During a closed-door meeting back in July, U.S. envoy to NATO Matthew Whitaker asked allied countries for help in disassembling the international court that addresses genocide and crimes against humanity. On the show, Sarah Wheaton and Kathryn Carlson discuss the European reaction and the motivations behind this American push.

Next, Europe’s housing crisis is deepening. Sarah Wheaton spoke with the Commissioner tasked with tackling the problem, Dan Jørgensen.

And criminal gangs in Europe are using AI to figure out where they can build their illegal tobacco factories to not get caught.

World.title: 25 killed after international cargo ship docked in China catches fire
World.content:
At least 25 people were killed after an international cargo ship docked in eastern China caught fire, state media reported on Thursday.

 

"As of 7:24 pm on September 10, all 25 missing persons had been found, none showing signs of life," state broadcaster CCTV reported.

A photo released by China's official Xinhua news agency identified the ship as the Ocean Melody, which sails under a Liberian flag, according to the public vessel-tracking website VesselFinder.

A total of 42 people had been on the vessel, and 17 of them were safely evacuated, including five who were injured, Xinhua reported.

The ship was docked for repairs at the Beihai Shipbuilding Co. at the port of Qingdao, a major shipping hub on the northeastern Chinese coast.

State media said that the fire broke out at around 11:15 am (03:15 GMT) and that "the open flames were extinguished at around 2:30 pm (0630 GMT)."

China’s President Xi Jinping issued “important instructions” to urgently conduct rescues of missing people.

Premier Li Qiang also urged the search for and rescue of "trapped" people, and for those injured to receive medical treatment, "and strictly prevent secondary disasters".

Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding is a major shipyard that operates as a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation.

Xi warned that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".

World.title: Macron, von der Leyen call for stronger European space sector amid rising security concerns
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to strengthen its space industry on Thursday, the second day of the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.

 

Speaking at the summit, Macron described Europe’s space sector as “fragile” and emphasised the need to bolster its capabilities, calling for “shared governance” of the industry.

“Outer space remains the only major global commons that is not subject to regulations that match the stakes,” he said. “Shared governance is necessary to address these challenges.”

Macron reiterated that more than 51 deals are set to be signed over the course of the summit, with some €20 billion of investments, listing a series of future milestones for Europe.

"In two years' time, I want to see the first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station; in five years' time, the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, land on the Moon's surface."

"And in 10 years' time, the first European manned capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board," he added, referring to Europe's spaceport in French Guiana.

Meanwhile, von der Leyen stressed the importance of Europe stepping up, as she emphasised the crucial role space plays both in terms of both scientific exploration, but also defence — pointing to Russia's war in Ukraine.

"The ability to access and act in space not only underpins our prosperity, it increasingly determines our security and independence. Nowhere is this clearer than in Ukraine."

"Satellite communications keep soldiers connected, while satellite imagery reveal movements hundreds of kilometres away"."

Europe's Space push comes amid aim to cut dependence on US

Europe's push to build up its military space assets has been driven by Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as its decision to distance itself from its longstanding dependence on the US in the space domain.

"Security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space", said von der Leyen, as she went on to underline the significance of IRIS², the European Union's upcoming flagship satellite constellation programme.

"Last month, we decided to accelerate the system, by expanding it to more than 350 satellites."

Von der Leyen also underlined the need for the Commission, the European Space Agency and national governments to "pool" their strengths, while also calling for investment "at scale."

Ahead of the summit, several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."

A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”

Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US. But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.

Macron and Joseph Aschbacher, Director of the European Space Agency (ESA) — who also addressed the summit — were joined for a live call with astronaut Sophie Adenot, who is currently on a nine-month mission aboard the the International Space Station (ISS) named the εpsilon mission.

World.title: Houthis blitz Yemen's Red Sea coastline in push to seize Bab el-Mandeb
World.content:
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday and were advancing towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a Yemeni military source said.

 

Witnesses said they saw Houthi forces entering the city while chanting "death to America, death to Israel," the group's political slogan.

The city which has been held by Yemen’s internationally recognised government has been under sustained attack since early August, when more than 25 missiles struck it in a matter of days and forced port operations to halt.

The Yemeni government is yet to publicly confirm Mokha has fallen.

The same military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters."

The coastal town of Dhubab and Perim Island are now the central military objective, with unconfirmed reports claiming Houthi fighters have landed on the rocky volcanic island that divides Bab el-Mandeb into two shipping channels by Thursday evening.

Plotting another Hormuz

The Houthis, who control about one-third of Yemen's territory — albeit the most densely populated parts — are vying to seize and potentially disrupt the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

Together with Hormuz, cargo traffic through Bab el-Mandeb accounts for one quarter of daily petroleum and crude shipments, and nearly one-third of the world's maritime trade.

The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.

Yemen's government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".

Major-General Sadeq Duwaid, spokesman for the Yemeni government-affiliated National Resistance Forces controlling areas adjacent to the strait, earlier warned that the Houthi siege of Mokha was a key manoeuvre to build operational footing along the Red Sea coast.

"Through their continued attacks on Mokha and its port, the Houthi militia seeks to establish a presence along the shores of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and transform the area into a situation resembling that of the Strait of Hormuz," Major-General Duwaid said in mid-August.

Fighting continues to escalate

Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis launched a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

They also launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held territory.

The Houthis reported on Thursday that about 40 airstrikes were launched by Saudi forces in a fresh salvo.

"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.

On Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of "potential danger" in two areas, Khamis Mushait and Abha.

Inching towards Bab el-Mandeb

The Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.

A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 had largely halted years of active warfare, yet it never resulted in a lasting political settlement.

The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they held territory less than 100 kilometres away.

The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport.

The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the internationally recognised government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".

Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.

Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.

The group previously severely disrupted cargo traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb with their campaign against what they said was Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was a show of support for Palestinians.

World.title: Shadow network of brokers and fixers exploits Syrians at Lebanon border
World.content:
Syrian travellers crossing into Lebanon pay up to 60 times the official entry fee to brokers, fixers and travel agencies behind a profitable parallel market around Lebanese border procedures that have tightened sharply since Bashar al-Assad's fall in December 2024.

 

A driver working the Damascus-Beirut route, speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity for security reasons, described a system in which travel agencies in the Syrian capital, paperwork fixers at the crossing and partners in Beirut sell packaged entry solutions to Syrians who cannot navigate the official process alone.

Lebanon's General Security Directorate charges up to $75 in official fees. The actual cost borne by travellers, according to Euronews' sources, is nowhere near that figure.

A 48-hour stay arranged through the network costs $180, a week costs around $260 and a month runs to $400. A six-month option — currently suspended — was priced at $1,500, while arranging an annual residence costs approximately $4,700.

The difference between the official fee and what travellers actually pay goes to the fixers as "bribes" or "kickbacks" to facilitate paperwork and bypass requirements such as proving cash reserves, presenting a hotel booking, or producing an onward airline ticket.

The process runs on enforced discretion. Travellers must not reveal to Lebanese General Security personnel that a driver or agency arranged their paperwork.

"Revealing this relationship could lead to the driver's arrest and a ban on his entering Lebanese territory," the source said.

Under what he described as the "tourist group" arrangement, travellers must also surrender their passport or identity card to a guarantor or company representative for the duration of the stay, to be returned on departure. Those granted a "free document" arrangement can keep their papers.

Lebanon's punishing penalties

Even categories of travellers who should theoretically benefit from smoother procedures are charged.

Holders of professional union cards, first-category commercial registrations or electronic visas for third countries are asked to pay a $60 "service fee" at the border on top of other costs, with waiting times that remain long and permitted stays that are kept short — 15 days for traders and union members, 24 hours for transit travellers.

The penalties for overstaying are punishing. Exceeding a one-month permit by a single day results in a $60 fine and a one-year ban from Lebanon. Violating a six-month residence limit costs $270 in fines, rising the longer the overstay continues.

Lebanon hosts an estimated 1.5 million Syrian refugees, the highest per capita refugee population in the world relative to the host country's size.

Lebanese authorities have cited pressure on public services, the labour market and the broader refugee dossier as justification for restricting Syrian entry.

The procedures have tightened over several years and have intensified since the fall of al-Assad's regime, which has drawn significant numbers of Syrians back toward the border.

The Syrian side of the crossing has become easier since December 2024. Checkpoints run by the Fourth Division and other Assad-era security units — notorious for extortion and harassment — have gone. The complications are now mostly on the Lebanese side.

Infrastructure issues not helping

Physical damage to infrastructure has added to the journey's cost. Israeli air strikes before al-Assad's fall destroyed the Daboussieh and Arida crossings, which remain closed.

Vehicles from Syria's coastal cities must now travel a significantly longer inland route through Homs, Qusayr, Hermel and Baalbek before entering Lebanon.

The Jisr Qamar-Bekaa crossing is open only to pedestrians after sustaining damage. A car from Damascus to Beirut — 114 kilometres — costs around $100 one way.

The same journey from Latakia, forced along the detour, costs roughly $250, or $500 return, over what becomes up to 800 kilometres of travel.

The source said he and colleagues now frequently cross with only one or two passengers, whereas previously they would have filled a vehicle.

Before 2014, he recalled, a Syrian could present an identity card at the border and receive six months' entry.

He said he hoped movement between the two countries would ease again, restoring business to drivers and opening up travel and tourism that the current system has effectively priced out of reach for many Syrians.

Euronews could not independently verify all figures provided by the source. Lebanese authorities had not responded to a request for comment at the time of publication.

World.title: Caring for others without self-love won’t do as much good
World.content:
People who display compassion towards others, animals and themselves experience better well-being outcomes than those who show only external or only internal compassion, according to researchers at McGill University in Canada.

 

The finding challenges the assumption that caring for others is always psychologically beneficial. According to the study, compassion only "counts" for well-being when it's paired with compassion for oneself.

“Many people, especially caregivers, educators, health professionals, parents and activists, may be very caring toward others while being harsh or neglectful toward themselves,” said Bassam Khoury, lead author of the study at McGill.

He added that the study suggests this imbalance may be linked to poorer mental health, such as higher stress and anxiety, compared to those who feel compassion for themselves and others.

The researchers also found that low self-compassion was associated with lower life satisfaction and social isolation.

In the meantime, those who showed uniformly high levels of compassion towards themselves, other humans, and animals were linked to the most adaptive psychological functioning – a state of optimal mental health, emotional resilience and social well-being.

The researchers looked at over 1,200 participants and classified them into different groups according to their “compassion profiles,” based on questionnaire answers measuring compassion toward the self, other humans, and animals.

“Self-compassion may help people regulate difficult emotions, reduce self-criticism and create a sense of inner safety,” Khoury added.

“It is not selfish or self-indulgent; it is a foundation for sustainable care for others and the ability to extend compassion to all sentient beings,” he added.

World.title: 3,000 drones light up New York skyline in 9/11 tribute
World.content:
Almost 3,000 drones light up the New York City skyline during a test for the 'Tribute in Light' installation, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. The drones fill the night sky with changing formations above the city.

 

A total of 2,977 lights will be used, matching the number of people killed in the attacks on September 11, 2001. The drones form patterns over New York as part of the annual memorial. The test offers a preview of the tribute planned for the 25th anniversary.

The anniversary will be marked on September 11, 2026. The installation will honour those who died in the attacks and keep their memory visible across the New York skyline.

World.title: Giorgos Mazonakis: Interrogation over Greek star's death in a private clinic
World.content:
The investigation into the sudden death of Giorgos Mazonakis, one of the most popular Greek singers of the past three decades, is at the centre of public debate in Greece and Cyprus.

 

The death of the 54-year-old artist remains the leading story in the news in both countries, where Mazonakis enjoyed huge popularity, while media outlets across the Balkans are also following the case.

Attention has now shifted to the circumstances that preceded his death. Giorgos Mazonakis had gone to a private medical practice in central Athens for a scheduled plasmapheresis, a specialised therapeutic procedure to remove blood plasma, before suddenly collapsing.

The authorities must now answer a series of critical questions: what exactly had been planned, whether the procedure had in fact begun, who was in charge of it, what medical assessment had preceded it, and whether the premises had the required licence, the appropriate equipment and specialised staff.

At the same time, the forensic examination is expected to determine the cause of death and help clarify whether there is any link to what happened at the practice.

Three decades on the Greek music scene

Giorgos Mazonakis was born in Nikaia, Piraeus, in 1972 and stood at the forefront of Greek music for more than 30 years.

He began singing professionally at a young age. In 1992, while performing at a night-time venue in Patras, he was spotted by the record company PolyGram and the following year released his first album.

In the years that followed, he became one of the most recognisable figures in contemporary Greek laïko music, a pop-folk Greek music style from the 50s and 60s, delivering a string of commercial hits and maintaining a constant presence on the country's nightlife and live music circuit.

Beyond Greece, Mazonakis had a strong fanbase in Cyprus and among Greek diaspora communities, with performances in Germany, Australia and the United States.

In recent years, he has also been a judge on the popular programme The Voice of Greece.

His appeal extended beyond Greek-speaking audiences, particularly in the Balkans. He had appeared in Sofia as early as 2012 and returned for a concert in 2023, while in December 2024, he performed in Tirana.

News of his death was reported immediately by media outlets in Bulgaria and Albania.

Abrupt deterioration of his condition

One of the main issues the authorities must clarify is what exactly occurred before the cardiac arrest and whether the scheduled treatment had begun.

According to reports in Greek media, the doctor said to have been responsible for Mazonakis's treatment testified that the plasmapheresis had not yet begun and that his condition deteriorated abruptly during the preparations for the procedure.

The same reports, citing her testimony, say that Mazonakis had visited the practice the previous day as well. The doctor is said to have described his condition as already burdened and to have referred to difficulties in his speech.

The authorities are therefore expected to examine which symptoms had been recorded, which tests had been carried out, what medical history had been taken, and on what basis it was considered that the planned procedure could go ahead.

The two doctors were released after giving their statements on Wednesday night, while the preliminary investigation is continuing.

The information published so far by Greek media does not yet paint a fully consistent picture as to whether the plasmapheresis had begun. Exactly what had been carried out, by whom, and under what conditions is among the key questions the authorities must answer.

Greek health minister: 'A very arduous procedure'

A separate inspection is underway into the licensing and operating conditions of the premises.

Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said that the facility was registered as a simple internal medicine practice and not as a clinic.

In his initial comments, he stated that, in such a practice, performing plasmapheresis is not permitted, according to him, and he ordered an immediate inspection by the Athens Medical Association.

On Thursday, he returned to the issue, describing plasmapheresis as a "very heavy" procedure which, he said, is carried out "only in a hospital setting".

The minister has stressed from the outset that the precise causes of death and whether there is any liability will have to emerge from the forensic and wider investigation.

'Specialised medical procedure'

For his part, the president of the Athens Medical Association, Giorgos Patoulis, is focusing on the practice's licence and equipment.

Speaking to the public broadcaster ERT, he said the facility was licensed as an internal medicine practice, while in the Association's file, "we have not recorded such a plasmapheresis machine". He added that in two previous inspections, no plasmapheresis machine had been found and that a new Association committee is currently checking the premises.

He also stressed that plasmapheresis is "a specialised medical procedure" which requires not only appropriate machinery but also specialised staff and specific standards.

On the other hand, the doctors' lawyer has stated that the machines had been duly declared to the Medical Association and that the practice was operating lawfully.

At the same time, Greek reports are also raising questions about the institutional framework governing specialised medical procedures in private practices. The Central Health Council is expected to look into the issue and the conditions under which such therapeutic interventions may be carried out.

What is plasmapheresis?

Therapeutic plasmapheresis (therapeutic plasma exchange) is a procedure in which blood passes through a special device that separates and removes the plasma, while the red and white blood cells and platelets are returned to the body. The plasma that is removed is replaced by a special solution.

According to doctors Konstantinos Giannakas and Thanos Dimopoulos of the Therapeutic Clinic of the University of Athens, who spoke to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency, the method has specific therapeutic indications, including for certain serious haematological, neurological, and immunological diseases.

It requires an assessment of the patient's condition beforehand and continuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation. It is generally considered safe when carried out under the prescribed conditions, but it can cause adverse effects, ranging from a drop in blood pressure and hypocalcaemia to, more rarely, allergic reactions, bleeding or arrhythmias.

World.title: Luxury Airstream camp set to open on the world’s largest salt flat in Bolivia
World.content:
The phrase “bucket list” is bandied about a lot in travel writing, but Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni absolutely deserves its place alongside heavyweights like Machu Picchu or the Pyramids of Giza.

 

Covering more than 10,500 square kilometres, the world’s largest salt flat transforms into a gigantic mirror during the wet season (December to April) – although it’s well-worth visiting year-round to see the criss-cross salt formations.

If you’ve been planning a trip, you might want to hang fire for just a little longer as a new boutique camp is set to open on the flats in late 2027.

Featuring five architect-designed Airstream suites, with a sixth Airstream for dining, Samkani Camp from A&K Sanctuary will be among the most luxurious stays in the area.

While daytime is great for exploration, nighttime might just be even more spectacular with the lack of light pollution offering unbeatable stargazing opportunities.

In fact, the name of the camp, Samkani, means “the one who dreams” in Aymara, the indigenous language of Bolivia's Altiplano.

The camp comes from A&K Sanctuary, the boutique luxury lodge, camp and riverboat collection, and the team used their experience developing low-impact mobile camps in Africa during the design process.

How to get to Salar de Uyuni

The only direct connection to Bolivia from Europe operates from Madrid, with flights offered by both Air Europa and Boliviana de Aviación to Santa Cruz de la Sierra. The flight time is around 11 hours.

Unfortunately, there are no flights from Santa Cruz de la Sierra to Uyuni – you will instead have to fly to the capital La Paz, and then fly on from there.

A better option would be plotting out a multi-country journey, aka “trip-maxxing”. You can fly to Bogotá directly from cities including London, Paris, Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Barcelona, spend some time in the Colombia capital before flying onto La Paz, and then Uyuni.

The only other major airports with direct connections to La Paz are Lima, Peru and Santiago, Chile.

World.title: Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
World.content:
A royal succession committee and the family of late King Oyo Nyimba of Toroo have put forward competing candidates. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his family claims.

Uganda's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor.

Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence.

Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. His ascension celebrations were attended by longtime Ugandan strongman President Yoweri Museveni.

His reign was overseen by a series of relatives acting as regents until he turned 18 in 2010.

He died on August 27 at the age of 34 while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.

Who are the main players in the succession fight?

On Wednesday, the royal clan's succession committee named the late king's cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the next monarch.

Kijanangoma is a television anchor at public broadcaster UBC.

However, Oyo's mother and sister announced on Thursday that they rejected this proposal, indicating that the king had left a will declaring his son his successor.

His mother Queen Kemigisa called the committee a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had named a new king despite knowing the contents of Oyo's will.

She also accused the Ugandan military of placing her family under house arrest.

The identity of Oyo's son and the son's mother remains a mystery. A campaigner for HIV/AIDS prevention and environmental causes, he had not publicly acknowledged a son until Toroo's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced the boy's existence after Oyo's death.

The controversy grew after Andrew Mwenda, a well-known journalist and relative of Oyo's, wrote on social media site X that a son could only succeed a father in Toroo if he was born to a queen, and said that the family had not produced so much as a picture of the boy.

Prime Minister Armstrong called for both sides to remain calm on Thursday, saying the process "should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial."

Oyo's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
World.content:
As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers, while keeping her loyal older fans.

On September 12, Celine Dion kicks off a series of 26 sold-out concerts, part of a Paris residency held through May 2027. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the performances, marking the global star's highly anticipated return to the stage following a prolonged break.

In 2022, she announced that she was battling with a rare and incurable neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome. The health issues led her to cancel her world tour.

In the summer of 2024, she returned to the spotlight atop the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics, her resilience giving hope to fans worldwide.

Now, in the days ahead of her Paris concerts, Dion has been thrilling hundreds of fans gathered in front of her hotel, taking the time to chat with them for a few minutes every day, sometimes even joining them in spontaneous sing-alongs and dances.

Charming her fans with candid moments at the Royal Monceau Hotel in Paris Image: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/picture alliance

The best-selling Canadian artist of all time, Dion has released a total of 27 studio albums, sold more than 200 million records worldwide and earned multiple Grammy Awards.

Even though her most defining hits date back to the 1990s, she is more than a nostalgia act, as her appeal is now skyrocketing with Gen Z and millennial listeners.

How did that happen?

'It's All Coming Back to Me Now': Her power ballads are surging in popularity again Image: Joel Goodman/ZUMA/picture alliance

A modern fashion darling

In her daily exchanges with her fans on her way to rehearsals, she's always wearing fresh couture pieces: an asymmetrical Loewe gown, a bold blue Givenchy leather dress by Sarah Burton or a striking jacket by Tom Ford.

"Celine Dion is turning the streets of Paris into her runway," wrote Vogue magazine in reaction to her stylish outfits.

"She's always really been into fashion, already in the 1990s, even though we long didn't know this," says Quebec cultural reporter Stephane Leclair, author and host of a podcast series on the star's "D'eux" album. "You know, Celine Dion was never considered 'cool.' She's always had that slightly corny, slightly goofy side. But through her genuine interest for fashion, she’s managed to revamp her image quite a bit."

A notable move came in 2016: Dion admired Zendaya's edgy red carpet looks so much that she tracked down her stylist, Law Roach, and asked him to team up with her. She credits Roach with transforming her into a modern fashion darling.

But that's just one aspect that explains her ongoing — and renewed — popularity.

A rags to riches story

Born on March 30, 1968, Celine Dion was the youngest of 14 children of a poor family in French-speaking in Quebec, Canada. As she proudly notes on her official website, the house was so full that, as a baby, she had to sleep in a drawer instead of a crib.

She grew up surrounded by music, and recorded her first song at the age of 12. It impressed music manager René Angélil so much that he mortgaged his house to pay for her first record. She quickly emerged as a child star in Quebec.

Her winning performance at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988 Image: dpa/picture alliance

Inspired by Michael Jackson, she decided that she wanted to become a megastar. She won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 and launched her first English-language album, "Unison," in 1990.

This, however, sparked cultural tension among French-speaking fans in Quebec, who felt she was neglecting her roots to pursue American and international superstardom.

"We were between two referendums on Quebec's independence at the time," points out Leclair. But even after she became a global star, she proudly kept identifying as the "little girl from Charlemagne," the small town near Montreal where she grew up.

"People in Quebec quickly understood that it didn't change anything, that she would always remain one of them, and that it only added another layer to her career," notes the cultural reporter.

Indeed, she also kept working in French all while building her career as a global pop artist. Teaming up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman, they released "D'eux" in 1995. It became the best-selling French-language album of all time.

The theme song for "Beauty and the Beast" (1991) won her both a Grammy and an Academy Award, while her best-selling "My Heart Will Go On" (1997) for the blockbuster film "Titanic" cemented her status alongside music's greatest vocalists.

Adding groundbreaking edge to Las Vegas

While other aging stars would head to the Las Vegas Strip to finish their careers, Dion revolutionized the music industry with "A New Day...," her high-profile residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace: With a total of 714 performances from 2003 to 2007, she demonstrated how such residencies could be modern, cutting-edge — and extremely lucrative.

It served as a blueprint for Las Vegas residencies by younger stars, such as Britney Spears and Adele.

Viral authenticity

"The world's biggest stars are often dead set on protecting a perfect, untouchable image. Celine, on the other hand, is incredibly accessible. She isn't afraid to let her true, authentic personality shine through," points out Leclair.

"And Celine's die-hard fans just love her humorous side," he adds. "They love the fact that she's a bit wacky. It makes her really relatable."

Famous for spontaneously breaking into song during interviews, those moments, as well as various over-the-top scenes from her 1990s music videos, have been picked up in Internet memes and TikTok trends.

Encouraged by her teenage sons, she launched her own official TikTok account in January 2026. She went viral with a "What's in My Bag?" video where she pulls out a mix of everyday essentials and completely unhinged items.

Writing a new chapter

But beyond the humor, she's also ready to share her most vulnerable moments.

In 2016, she lost her husband — her manager, René Angélil — and a brother to cancer within the same week. Her 2019 album "Courage" focused on loss and recovery.

Their 26-year age gap and the fact that Dion was only 12 when she met her manager and future husband made headlines, but they stayed together until his death Image: Ryan Remiorz/empics/picture alliance

Her 2024 documentary "I am: Celine Dion," in which she looks back on her life and career all while addressing how she deals with her stiff-person syndrome diagnosis, has been praised by critics as intensely sincere and visceral.

One scene of the film follows her as she suffers from a painful spasm: "I don't think many stars of that caliber would have agreed to be filmed — and have the footage included in the final cut — in such an unflattering state," notes Leclair. "It was partly out of a desire for transparency, to explain to her fans why she had to step back."

And her fans highly value this authenticity, as well as her resilience.

She is now undergoing physical and therapies to manage her symptoms and be able to perform again for this series of more than 2-hour-long concerts. They will feature 18 musicians and four backing singers; a live choir will also join them on stage for several songs.

Additionally, Paris will mark the start of the concert series with two giant karaoke sessions on September 11. A total of 10,000 people are expected to take part in the participatory event celebrating her four decades of songs.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

World.title: ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
World.content:
The European Central Bank raised borrowing costs and warned that inflation could remain high for an extended period. Energy markets and geopolitical tensions are still major concerns.

The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Rising oil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%.

"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin.

The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.

Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches.

Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Economic outlook remains uncertain

"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB.

For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services.

Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said.

World.title: Are electric vehicles really bad for the environment?
World.content:
Some German politicians are calling for a delay to the EU plan to phase out gas-powered vehicles, saying cars must be judged on the entire carbon footprint. But the full picture still says EVs are more climate friendly.

"The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral.

Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media , he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Such a policy shift, he said, was now backed by "science."

Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM) , which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral."

EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix.

Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling.

It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM .

No new insights in TUM report

Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known.

Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80% .

Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles.

Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe.

Batteries have a high environmental cost

Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water.

The ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine.

While lithium-iron phosphate batteries tend to be cheaper and last longer, nickel manganese cobalt batteries deliver more power and work better in colder climates Image: Rodrigo Freitas/NTB/picture alliance

"We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture.

Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans .

Czechia's lithium mine plans spark resistance To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Renewable energy making the case for EVs

The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas.

But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs.

Home solar power installations have taken off in Germany, giving EV owners a cheaper way to charge their cars Image: Daniel Reinhardt/IMAGO

"Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonised and expected to be almost fully decarbonised by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will also only strengthen the case even more."

Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules.

"Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of ICE vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed."

Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth

Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy.

"The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia .

EV sales have increased in Asia in recent years, with China's BYD leading the pack Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns.

"We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down."

Ethiopia's EV boom: A role model for all? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: India news: Government proposes elected body for Ladakh
World.content:
09/10/2026 September 10, 2026 Indian government proposes legislative body for Ladakh

The Indian government has proposed a new Chapter K under Article 371 of the Constitution that will allow the formation of an elected body for the Union Territory (UT) of Ladakh.

The proposal came in a meeting in Delhi with a delegation of Ladakh's civil society members.

The UT-level body will have legislative power over subjects relating to environment, land, culture, language and other subject matters reserved for the UT under Article 240, civil society members said in a statement, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Hindu.

However, Ladakh's civil society members said they "are not happy" with the meeting's proceedings, as the government repeated what was discussed in the last meeting held on May 22.

"We have not got a draft of the proposal yet," Leh Apex Body (LAB) co-chairman, Chering Dorje Lakruk, who attended the latest meeting in Delhi told DW, adding that the government has promised a draft in the next meeting, which is likely to be held by the second week of October.

While expressing his disappointment over the prolonged delay, Lakruk said, "The government is buying time."

India: Unrest brews in border region Ladakh over autonomy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), the two main political groups in Ladakh, have held several rounds of talks with the government since 2019 — when Ladakh lost its special status under Article 370 and was turned into a Union Territory, which means that unlike earlier, it is now directly governed by the Indian central government in New Delhi.

Ladakh's special status gauranteed it constitutional safeguards to preserve its unique identity, land, jobs, and environment.

Since 2019,the LAB and KDA have been demanding statehood and Sixth Schedule status for Ladakh.

Inclusion in the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution will safeguard tribal lands, local employment, and the fragile Himalayan ecology from outside conglomerates.

The groups had called for a protest march on September 10, following which the government called a meeting in Delhi on September 10.

World.title: Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic offensive since becoming president in April, but foreign friends may still be few and far between.

Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.

There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general's sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar's presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.

As Myanmar's newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He'll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.

"Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing's transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he's really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government's allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.

"Even if they're relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw's strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar's capital.

Aung San Suu Kyi's son on the latest images of his mother To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low

Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.

Since Min Aung Hlaing's military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.

Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.

That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.

Despite that record, "the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections," said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.

"The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public," Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.

Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar

Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.

Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc's most senior-level meetings.

Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.

Myanmar's regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN's special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.

Last month, the country's newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc's peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN's special envoys were no longer needed.

Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN's senior leaders summits "any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand's Thammasat University.

Marston and Marciel, though, say there's a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc's rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.

With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country's regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.

Thailand's premier and foreign minister "have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement," said Marston.

New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Japan willing to restore normal ties?

Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia's authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.

Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was "more than ready" to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

"I don't think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country," he said.

Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.

The civil war in Myanmar has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million since 2021 [FILE: August 10, 2024] Image: AFP/Getty Images

Will the West reengage with Myanmar?

As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.

Pinitbhand says that's especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.

Marston says it's possible Washington would go for "calibrated reengagement" with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.

"But in this case, I don't think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so," he said.

Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration's list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.

On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won't be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.

"I don't see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy," he said. "Things could change, but that is how it looks for now."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: China: Cargo ship fire kills at least 25
World.content:
At least five people are missing after a cargo ship caught fire at the port of Qingdao. The cause remains unclear.

At least 25 people were killed and five remain missing after a fire on a cargo vessel receiving repairs at a shipyard in the northeastern Chinese port city of Qingdao, state media reported on Thursday.

State broadcaster CCTV reported the vessel with 42 people on board caught fire at around 11:15 a.m. local time, and were extinguished around 2:30 p.m. (0630 UTC)."

The ship was identified as the 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier "Ocean Melody," which sails under a Liberian flag, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Cause remains unclear

Chinese President Xi Jinping issued has "important instructions" to conduct a search and rescue mission, while also calling for an investigation into anyone who could be responsible for the incident, Xinhua added.

Xi said that "all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards".

It is currently unclear what could have caused the fire.

The vessel was undergoing repairs at Qingdao's Beihai Shipbuilding Co, part of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), one of the world's largest shipbuilders.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
World.content:
The French president called for setting goals like European cargo missions, lunar landings, and crewed spaceflight while urging the bloc to reduce its reliance on US and Russia.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China.

"Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris.

European-crewed spaceflight

"We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts."

Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station."

He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface."

"And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board."

Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport.

The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance.

ESA's PLATO mission — the search for another Earth To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Passengers or pilots?'

Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space.

After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?"

The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration.

"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said.

Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion).

"Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically."

Europe's new space milestone To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
