World.title: Dimash Calls for Investment, Infrastructure to Unlock Kazakhstan’s Creative Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer, composer and producer Dimash Qudaibergen called for greater investment, infrastructure and legal support for Kazakhstan’s creative industries during the opening ceremony of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 on Sept. 9.

AFD 2026 is a two-day event bringing together more than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries to discuss capital markets, investment, artificial intelligence, innovation, real-economy financing and cross-border capital.

While on stage, Qudaibergen performed “Aqerke,” “Stranger” and “Weekend,” as well as the traditional Kazakh kui “Adai” on dombra.

Following the performance, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov spoke with Qudaibergen about the potential of Kazakhstan’s creative economy, attracting investment to the sector, intellectual property protection and the challenges artists face when entering international markets.

Qudaibergen said the development of the creative industry requires not only investment, but also stronger legal protection for artists and mechanisms to connect creators with investors.

“Artists need legal protection and support from creative industry development funds. These funds can become a bridge between investors and new creative projects,” Qudaibergen said.

Bekturov noted that Kazakhstan’s creative sector brings together thousands of companies and more than 140,000 people, while its contribution to the economy remains relatively small, highlighting the need to develop the sector as a source of future growth.

When asked why investors should consider creative industries, Qudaibergen pointed to Kazakhstan’s culture, history and music as assets with strong international appeal.

“Our culture, our history and the music are truly unique, and that makes them interesting to an international audience,” he said, drawing on his experience of performing around the world.

Protecting creative independence

For Qudaibergen, attracting investment should not come at the expense of an artist’s independence or ownership of intellectual property.

He said the decision to share rights with investors or business partners is ultimately personal, but artists should understand the financial and contractual side of their profession before making such decisions.

“I choose the second option, because for me it is essential to keep both creative independence and ownership of my intellectual property,” he said.

Qudaibergen stressed that financial literacy is part of an artist’s professional responsibility, allowing creators to better understand contracts, finances and the business side of the industry.

“Education everywhere is very important,” he said, adding that understanding contracts, finances and the business side of the industry allows artists to make informed decisions and retain control over their work.

He also cited his own career as an example of how an artist can gradually move from performer to producer and entrepreneur.

Qudaibergen said he now works directly with business partners and operates his own label, established by his father, which promotes not only his work but also young artists.

His transition into production included an international vocal project on China’s Hunan TV, where he first gained international recognition through “I’m a Singer” show. Returning to the network as a producer, he said, gave him an opportunity to introduce other Kazakh talents to a global audience.

From Kazakh roots to global audiences

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s cultural identity can become a competitive advantage internationally when traditional heritage is combined with contemporary approaches.

“Our uniqueness comes from combining respect for our roots with a desire to innovate,” he said. “We can make traditional things feel fresh and turn something authentic into a modern trend.”

During his tours, Qudaibergen has introduced audiences to musicians from his team and traditional Kazakh instruments, including dombra and kobyz. He said some international fans also became interested in Kazakhstan’s history, language and traditional music.

He also encouraged young Kazakh artists to remain connected to their identity while pursuing international careers.

“To become an international artist, you have to follow your own path, first of all. And then you need to believe in yourself,” he said.

He warned young artists against changing direction simply because of short-term financial opportunities.

“Professional career management means thinking long term,” he said. “You shouldn’t accept every offer just because it looks profitable today. You always have to remember the goal you are moving towards.”

Building a system for young talent

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s creative sector needs a more systematic approach to developing talent, particularly in management, professional training, broadcasting and distribution.

He identified a shortage of qualified professionals as one of the industry’s key challenges, arguing that talented artists need more than opportunities to perform.

“We have not yet become a full-fledged industry with a clear system. So, we need to do our best to train professionals,” he said.

He also pointed to the limited presence of creative projects across television, radio and large-scale distribution platforms.

“The main task is to build professional infrastructure and create a clear, systematic path to international markets,” Qudaibergen said.

Qudaibergen said this was particularly important because young artists should not have to rely on chance encounters or simply hope that someone will discover them.

“This is exactly what I was missing when I started,” he said, recalling his own experience as a young artist from Aktobe who had little understanding of how to build an international career.

“Right now, it has become one more mission,” he said. “Young talents should grow inside a real creative development system, instead of simply hoping that one day they will get lucky and someone will invite them somewhere.”

Qudaibergen’s own career, from a young performer in Aktobe to an internationally recognized artist and producer, illustrates the potential of such opportunities. Reflecting on his journey, he emphasized that talent alone is not enough to build a lasting career.

“Hard work is also very important. It’s the most important thing,” he said. “When the universe turns to your side, you need to be ready.”

Qudaibergen is now preparing his new Dimensions world tour, continuing his international career while expanding his work as a producer and supporting young Kazakh artists.

World.title: AFD 2026: Creative Industry Pushes Investors to Rethink What Counts as Financial Asset
World.content:
ASTANA – What if a song, a game, a digital creator or a piece of intellectual property could be treated not only as a cultural product, but as an investable asset? For Kazakhstan’s emerging creative economy, that shift in thinking could be as important as the creative output itself.

The question was at the center of discussions on the second day of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026, held on Sept. 10 and dedicated to creative industries as an asset class, moderated by David Tuganov, president of the Creative Industries Alliance of Qazaqstan (CIAQ), the panel brought together Aizatulla Hussein, founder of Õzen; Olzhas Akparov, CBDO of Cyber Temple; Julia Kushnir, head of business development for Eastern Europe and Central Asia at TikTok; and Askar Bilisbekov, CEO of Alem Capital Management Limited.

Tokenization of the song?

One of the clearest examples of that shift came from the music industry, where Õzen is working on what Hussein described as a new way to turn music intellectual property into a financial asset through blockchain-based tokenization.

“For the last seven years that we have been working in the music industry, our core business has been the distribution of music content in the digital space. But music is not simply entertainment. It is a full-fledged financial asset that can generate income over many years, and that income continues to grow,” Hussein said.

The concept is to tokenize music rights through smart contracts and allow investors to acquire a fractional economic interest in a song, with returns linked to the income generated by the underlying music.

“What we are doing now is tokenizing the music asset, the music intellectual property, through smart contracts. Now we give anyone the opportunity to come and buy a piece of this song, and when the income comes to the artist, proportionally to how many tokens they have acquired, they will receive those payments,” Hussein said.

The model, he said, could effectively create an internal marketplace for music, where investors can assess the performance and potential of individual compositions using data generated across digital platforms. Õzen’s model is still building the necessary legal and regulatory framework, with Hussein identifying jurisdiction as the key challenge rather than the technology itself.

“In principle, the technology is not a problem at all. These technologies have already been developed. The only serious thing that we need to implement correctly is the jurisdiction, how we can turn a contract into tokens,” he said, noting that the company hopes to launch pilot projects by the end of the year.

The move is significant because it changes the conversation around creative industries from one centered primarily on grants, promotion and audience growth to one centered on ownership, cash flows and investment returns.

Shift in investors’ mindset

Bilisbekov also emphasized this shift in investor thinking, noting that the main obstacle facing creative entrepreneurs in Kazakhstan is often not a lack of talent, but an insufficient understanding of how to present that talent as a business proposition.

Drawing a comparison with Hollywood’s film industry, he said investors have long understood that creative investments can be approached through venture capital strategies, where a number of projects are financed with the understanding that some will fail while a smaller number generate significant returns.

“In Hollywood, the principle was quite simple: invest in a large number of films, knowing and understanding that most of the films will fail,” Bilisbekov said.

He said similar venture-style approaches already finance creative projects globally, while Kazakhstan’s creative sector remains constrained by a fragmented market and a limited understanding of the investor relationship.

“In the creative industry in Kazakhstan and in our region, the attitude toward investors is always somewhat residual. Why? Because there is no understanding that an investor is, first of all, your partner,” he said.

For Bilisbekov, that means creative entrepreneurs also need to change how they themselves approach investment.

“We need to change our mindset,” he said, highlighting that creative founders must be able to understand the financial side of their businesses, communicate their models clearly and demonstrate that they can operate beyond the strength of an idea alone.

“One investor has never bought into a company simply because you are talented, simply because you have an idea,” he said.

From creativity to business value

The point is particularly relevant as the creative economy increasingly intersects with technology. TikTok, for example, is no longer simply a platform for entertainment, according to Kushnir, but part of Kazakhstan’s broader digital creative economy, giving creators, entrepreneurs and businesses direct access to audiences.

“The platform is part of Kazakhstan’s digital creative economy,” Kushnir said, emphasizing what she described as the democratization of creativity.

“Absolutely any person has all the tools and all the opportunities to interact with an audience,” she said, noting that creators do not necessarily need millions of followers or an established public profile to find an audience.

For businesses, that audience can translate into commercial value, with TikTok’s research with the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs showing that 80% of surveyed small and medium-sized businesses said the platform helps them attract new customers, 79% said it helps them retain customers, and around 70% said it helps them differentiate themselves from competitors. The next step, however, is converting reach and creativity into durable businesses and investable assets. That is where the convergence of creativity, technology and capital becomes particularly important.

Where AI meets creativity

Akparov described how artificial intelligence is already changing parts of game development, including early-stage concept work and the creation of visual references, while Bilisbekov said that Kazakhstan’s strongest competitive advantage may ultimately lie in its human capital.

“Our brains are absolutely competitive. There are simply a little bit more efforts needed in this direction. There will be more of these startups,” Bilisbekov said.

Hussein likewise pointed to a growing convergence between Kazakhstan’s technology and creative communities, arguing that the two sectors need to become less separate.

“IT people should come to creatives, and creatives should come to IT,” he said, describing them as two communities that have traditionally developed in parallel rather than together.

That convergence could become increasingly important as AI lowers some of the technical barriers to building digital products and puts greater value on ideas, storytelling, design and other forms of creative input.

For Kazakhstan, however, panelists suggested that the missing piece is still capital. Hussein noted that the country needs to create conditions for creative talent to develop into sustainable businesses, while Bilisbekov pointed to two priorities: dedicated programs for the creative industries and a deeper capital market.

“We don’t have, as far as I know, even a single acceleration program that has been launched for the creative industry. That is something that needs to be launched,” Bilisbekov said.

He also stressed the importance of developing Kazakhstan’s capital market more broadly, saying creative businesses need financing mechanisms that go beyond traditional business models.

“It is very important to develop the capital market. What we unfortunately lack today is exactly that,” he said.

That is perhaps the broader investment question emerging from Kazakhstan’s creative economy: not whether the country has talent, but whether it can build the financial, technological and regulatory infrastructure needed to turn that talent into assets that can be valued, financed and scaled.

The tokenization initiative being developed by Õzen offers one early example of what that could look like, moving music from a product consumed by an audience toward an asset in which an investor could potentially hold an economic interest.

For a country seeking to deepen its capital markets while developing a new generation of creative businesses, the shift may ultimately require both sides of the equation to rethink their roles: creatives need to become more financially literate, and investors need to become more comfortable assessing assets whose value may be built around intellectual property, audience, technology and cultural relevance rather than factories, equipment or conventional balance sheets.

World.title: ADCB Kazakhstan Plans to Triple Project Financing in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank plans to triple project financing in Kazakhstan over the next 18 months, from the current 2.5 trillion tenge (US$5.5 billion), as the bank expands its role in supporting the country’s real economy and infrastructure development.

The plans were discussed during a Sept. 9 meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Farooq Abdulrahman Al Marzooqi, Chairman of Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank Kazakhstan (ADCB Kazakhstan).

The meeting focused on expanding ADCB Group’s participation in projects in Kazakhstan, with particular attention to the development of the real sector and the modernization of digital infrastructure, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Bektenov highlighted Kazakhstan’s ongoing economic and institutional reforms to strengthen the country’s investment appeal. He also pointed to the growing role of the United Arab Emirates as an investment partner for Kazakhstan. UAE investments in the country have exceeded $7 billion over the past 20 years, with around $3 billion invested during the last two and a half years.

According to Bektenov, deeper involvement by ADCB Group could help Kazakhstan attract additional capital from the UAE and other Middle Eastern markets, while diversifying external sources of project financing.

Al Marzooqi highlighted the bank’s experience in Kazakhstan, including financing for energy and railway infrastructure, as well as projects in petrochemicals, transport and logistics.

Over the past 15 years, ADCB Kazakhstan has supported more than 100 business initiatives. Small and medium-sized enterprises account for around 90% of these projects.

ADCB explores energy financing opportunities

ADCB’s potential involvement in Kazakhstan’s energy projects was also discussed at a Sept. 10 meeting between Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov and an ADCB delegation led by Al Marzooqi.

The ministry outlined key investment priorities for the next three to five years, including the modernization of 77,500 kilometers of power grids, the addition of 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity by 2035, and the development of gas processing facilities at major fields such as Kashagan and Karachaganak.

The talks also covered major value-added projects, including a 1.25-million-ton-per-year polyethylene complex, planned butadiene and alkylate production, and the expansion of oil refining capacity.

Kazakhstan proposed project financing, joint credit facilities and public-private partnerships as potential mechanisms for ADCB’s participation. Islamic financing was also highlighted, given the presence of ADCB Islamic in Kazakhstan.

The meeting follows growing UAE-Kazakhstan cooperation in the energy sector, including Masdar’s 1 gigawatt (GW) wind power project in the Zhambyl Region. ADCB said it was ready to further assess the projects presented by the Kazakh side.

The bank’s planned expansion comes as Kazakhstan seeks to mobilize greater private investment for infrastructure and economic diversification. The increased financing capacity is expected to support new projects across key sectors of the economy.

World.title: Rare-Earth Oxide Separation Facility Planned for Stepnogorsk
World.content:
ASTANA – Australian critical minerals company Lindian Resources and French rare-earth specialist Carester have agreed to advance plans for an 8,000-ton-per-year solvent extraction and rare-earth oxide separation facility in Stepnogorsk, Kazakhstan.

Under the agreement, Carester and Australian engineering company Tetra Tech Coffey will progress a definitive feasibility study (DFS), targeted for completion in the fourth quarter of 2026, reported Mining Technology on Sept. 3.

The facility is planned to produce separated rare-earth oxides, including neodymium and praseodymium, alongside a mixed heavy rare-earth compound containing dysprosium, terbium and yttrium.

The project will build on Lindian’s SARECO mixed rare-earth concentrate (MREC) processing facility in Stepnogorsk. Carester will provide process technology and engineering services and review the existing facility for potential optimization and upgrades.

The company’s integrated strategy links its Kangankunde rare-earths project in Malawi, where it plans to produce monazite concentrate, with downstream processing facilities in Kazakhstan.

The proposed solvent extraction facility is designed to receive SARECO product liquor solution and compatible third-party MREC. Lindian is also evaluating additional rare-earth feed sources in Kazakhstan.

The agreement includes a binding 10-year offtake arrangement, with two potential five-year extensions. Carester will purchase 70% of SEGH production and hold a right of first refusal over 70% of mixed heavy rare-earth carbonate produced at SARECO.

Carester will supply the heavy rare-earth products to its Caremag refinery in Lacq, France. Carester, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) and Iwatani Corporation are developing the refinery.

The Stepnogorsk facility is expected to benefit from existing power, gas, water, rail and reagent infrastructure, potentially providing cost advantages for the proposed expansion.

Lindian Executive Chairman Robert Martin said the agreement supports the company’s strategy of moving further downstream.

“The agreement with Carester represents another significant step in Lindian’s strategy to move further downstream to expand our markets and to capture more of the value from the rare earths that we produce,” Martin said.

The DFS is expected to be completed by the end of this year and will determine the next stage of development for the proposed facility.

World.title: CPC Oil Loading Operations Resume After Drone Incident
World.content:
ASTANA – Oil loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal have resumed in normal mode after a Sept. 8 drone incident near the facility, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy said.

Following the incident, loading operations at Single Point Moorings (SPM) 2 and 3 were temporarily suspended.

The ministry said inspections of CPC’s cargo systems and tankers found no issues affecting the continuation of loading operations. No environmental impact was recorded.

“Following the necessary checks of the condition of CPC’s cargo systems and tankers, no issues affecting the further conduct of loading operations were identified. No environmental impact was recorded,” the ministry said.

Loading operations have since resumed and are currently operating normally.

The ministry also stressed that it imposed no restrictions on accepting oil from Kazakh shippers.

CPC remains a key export route for Kazakhstan’s crude, despite the country’s efforts to expand alternative transportation channels. As The Astana Times reported earlier, despite several disruptions from attacks on infrastructure, oil transportation into the CPC-K system increased 39% in January-August, while flows through several alternative routes also grew.

Experts have noted that disruptions to major export infrastructure create a strategic challenge for Kazakhstan. If the largest route is disrupted or becomes less available, the country cannot simply redirect all affected production elsewhere without hitting capacity, infrastructure and logistical constraints.

The latest developments therefore underscore the importance of maintaining reliable established export infrastructure while continuing to develop alternative routes.

World.title: AFD 2026: Kazakhstan Seeks Role in Finance’s Next Digital Frontier
World.content:
ASTANA – We want to take it out of the unregulated area and make it work, because it works whether we want it or not,” National Bank Chairman Timur Suleimenov said during the plenary session Rewiring the Architecture of Finance at Astana Finance Days 2026 on Sept. 9, capturing the regulatory dilemma at the center of a financial transformation that is rapidly moving from experiment to infrastructure.

As blockchain, stablecoins, tokenization, programmable money and AI reshape how assets are created, moved and managed, Kazakhstan is betting that an early embrace of new financial technologiesm, combined with rules and institutional trust, can become a competitive advantage.

The discussion brought together Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov, Freedom Holding Corp. CEO Timur Turlov, Anchorage Digital Global Head of Stablecoin Solutions Sergio Mello and technology entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan, who approached that transformation from different angles, but agreed that the financial system is changing not only in how services are delivered, but also in the infrastructure underpinning them.

Suleimenov identified geopolitical fragmentation and technology as two of the forces reshaping global finance, arguing that changes in trade and investment flows are already translating into changes in financial flows.

“Trade flows, the finance flows are changing fundamentally. We’re seeing division across the Atlantic. We’re seeing division on the North American continent. We’re seeing trade wars and semi-trade wars across the world. And, of course, finance has always been a part of the debate. They always went hand-in-hand,” he said.

At the same time, the emergence of blockchain and tokenized assets is challenging financial regulators to develop rules for technologies that did not exist within the traditional architecture.

“We’re still in the rule-setting phase. There is no set of rules for decentralized finance, for digital finance, crypto finance,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, however, he described that uncertainty as an opportunity to establish a regulatory framework while the global market is still taking shape.

“We have adopted a very comprehensive set of rules, not only frameworks, but rules, very hands-on with how you trade cryptocurrency, how you trade stablecoins, what you do with the real world tokenized assets and things like that,” Suleimenov said

The task, he added, is not to stop technologies that are already finding users, but to ensure they operate within a system that protects trust and financial stability.

“We want to take it out of the unregulated area and make it work, because it works whether we want it or not. It will be working, but I think it is to the greater good of all of us that it works in rightly regulated area,” he said.

AIFC as a testing ground

AIFC Governor Bekturov said Kazakhstan’s advantage lies not simply in the technologies themselves, but in the people and institutions willing to experiment with them.

“I think that the first competitive advantage of Kazakhstan is its people,” he said, pointing to regulators, entrepreneurs and younger generations that are more open to new financial models.

He also highlighted the political decision to establish the AIFC as a separate jurisdiction, noting that it has created space for Kazakhstan to test new financial products before deciding how they should be treated across the wider economy.

“You give the optionality to yourself, but also to the investors coming into the country, so they can kind of choose with which system they would like to work,” Bekturov said.

The AIFC, he added, has provided a practical environment in which regulators can observe new products, assess their risks and determine what works.

“I think in that terms, AIFC, was also helpful to the national regulators to kind of test out certain products and to see how that works, what are the risks, where we want to adapt and which part we want to regulate more or less,” he said.

That approach, Bekturov said, has helped Kazakhstan move comparatively quickly in areas including digital assets, the digital tenge, stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets.

“We are one of the leaders in the region in terms of adapting digital assets, digital tenge, stable coins in tenge and what goes beyond like tokenization of real assets,” he said.

For Turlov, the transformation is already visible from the customer and business perspective, although he cautioned that technological innovation does not necessarily change the underlying nature of a financial asset.

“Many products change their form. Very rarely they change the substance of them,” he said.

Tokenization, in his view, is often another way of representing assets that financial markets have long known how to securitize. The more meaningful change is the ability to deliver those products faster, more efficiently and across borders. Turlov said Kazakh financial companies are already competing with global firms, which makes the ability to innovate domestically increasingly important.

“We have rules, we have trust, we have money on this market. Because sometimes if it’s very easy to innovate, but it’s not much trust, not much rules, not much money, it’s also very hard to do business. But I think now here in Kazakhstan, we have this perfect balance of many different factors,” he said.

According to him, that’s why Kazakhstan can function as a testing ground for global financial technology companies.

“Kazakhstan is feeling like a great laboratory for global fintechs because if you can succeed here, so maybe you can scale out to other markets,” he added.

From digital money to digital property

Technology entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan offered the most expansive vision of where the transformation could lead, noting that the rise of digital finance should be understood through what he called “technopolitics.”

“You can think of the cloud as almost like a new continent that has arisen above us,” he said, suggesting that the digital economy is creating a new domain through which people, businesses and assets can interact regardless of geography.

“That’s a huge opportunity for Kazakhstan because Kazakhstan is landlocked, but it’s not cloud-locked. It can access any country in the world, any person in the world through the cloud,” he said.

In his view, the next stage could involve much more than moving existing financial assets onto blockchain. Real estate, vehicles, infrastructure and other forms of capital could increasingly be represented through digital credentials and cryptographic keys.

“The fundamental innovation of Bitcoin was Internet-first registry of assets. Now, it’s a smart contract. Now, it’s code. So it actually lives in the cloud primarily,” Srinivasan said.

His proposition was that Kazakhstan could eventually position itself as a trusted physical and regulatory gateway connecting these digital assets with the real economy.

“Kazakhstan can be the registry where those things can be traded from the cloud back to the land and back to the world,” he said.

Mello took a more immediate view, saying that some of the technologies discussed are already becoming standard financial infrastructure.

“Stablecoins are a very clear example. It’s an instrument that is no longer an experiment,” he said.

According to him, the next stage is less about proving that digital finance works and more about building the regulatory and physical infrastructure to support it at scale.

“After 10 years of experimentation, the next 10 years of crypto becoming a technology standard that leads us to financial systems,” Mello said.

He compared the process to building airports, highways and railroads, saying that governments have to think ahead about the infrastructure required to support future economic activity.

“With all the rest of the world moving really fast, the pace at which innovation extends not only in financial infrastructure but also elsewhere is such that any moment of inaction today, from a regulatory policy perspective, is equivalent to a decade of inaction in the last century,” Mello said.

Digital tenge moves beyond payments

Kazakhstan’s own experience with digital currency illustrates how quickly priorities can evolve. Suleimenov said the National Bank has shifted away from viewing the digital tenge primarily as a retail payment instrument, given the range of digital payment solutions commercial banks already offer. Instead, one of the most promising uses is programmable public spending, allowing funds to be tracked and used according to the purpose for which they were allocated.

“I think the best usage for the central bank’s digital currency that we see is actually program and track the public spending,” Suleimenov said.

He said the approach can be applied to projects ranging from a kindergarten in a rural area to major industrial developments, with smart contracts helping ensure that public funds are spent as originally intended. The initiative began as a pilot in 2023 and has since been incorporated into legislation, with the government and the National Bank working to expand the areas where such mechanisms can be applied.

“It’s not just about public finances. It’s about overall government’s efficiency of running the economy, of running the social sphere, running the infrastructure to make it work with less amount of resources included,” Suleimenov said.

As financial platforms become more sophisticated, Turlov said another challenge is emerging: customers may struggle to navigate the very technology designed to make their lives easier.

“Adoption of technology sometimes is a much greater challenge than inventing some technology itself,” he said, noting that modern financial applications can combine banking, insurance, brokerage, travel and other services in a single platform.

He believes AI assistants could become an important interface between customers and increasingly complex financial infrastructure, allowing people to describe what they want in ordinary language rather than understanding the mechanics of each service.

“They just need to tell it in normal words, and that’s how I believe we can really improve the quality of life. Because sometimes products became so sophisticated that they need a very professional customer to consume them. And maybe AI Assistant will help to solve that,” Turlov said.

For Kazakhstan’s regulators, the challenge will be maintaining that openness without moving so far ahead of the market that innovation becomes detached from actual demand.

“When you’re a little front-run, you have a chance of failure or being too premature with some innovation. You are a little bit ahead because it’s still a competition, right? But yet you are not far behind because then the market is capturing this moment,” Bekturov said, describing regulation as a continuous balancing act.

That balance between innovation and trust, experimentation and regulation, the physical economy and the digital one may ultimately determine whether Kazakhstan becomes simply an early adopter of the next generation of financial technology or one of the places where that new architecture is actually built.

World.title: Rybakina Makes History as Kazakhstan’s First World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA – Elena Rybakina has made history for Kazakhstan, becoming the first athlete from the country to rise to the top of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) singles rankings, a breakthrough that puts Kazakh tennis at the summit of the sport.

Rybakina secured the top position in the WTA live rankings after defeating China’s Qinwen Zheng in the quarterfinals on Sept. 9. She overtook Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka, who had previously held the top spot. The official rankings will be updated on Monday, Sept. 14.

Rybakina is the first player representing Kazakhstan, in either women’s or men’s singles, to reach the leading position in the global rankings.

Rybakina later reflected on the milestone in an Instagram post, highlighting its significance for her country.

“Anything is possible when you believe! Proud to represent Kazakhstan and make history as the country’s first world number 1,” she wrote.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Rybakina on the achievement, praising her talent, dedication and determination.

“Reaching the top of the WTA rankings is a sporting pinnacle achieved by you through phenomenal talent, tremendous hard work and an unwavering belief in yourself,” Tokayev said in his congratulatory message.

He noted that the achievement had brought prominence to Kazakh sport and placed Rybakina’s name in the history of world tennis.

“Your journey serves as an inspiring example for thousands of young athletes in our country and millions of tennis fans around the world,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev also highlighted Rybakina’s conduct both on and off the court, noting her high standards of behavior and communication with people from different backgrounds.

He wished the tennis player continued success and urged her to maintain her champion’s mindset as she pursues new achievements.

Rybakina’s rise to the top marks a landmark moment for Kazakhstan’s tennis, giving the country its first-ever world No. 1 in singles and adding a new chapter to its sporting history.

On Sept. 11, Rybakina will face U.S. Coco Gauff in the semifinals.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan Move to Revive Caspian Passenger Ferry Service
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are working to resume passenger ferry services across the Caspian Sea, reopening a route that connected the two countries until 2020 and could provide an additional boost to tourism and regional connectivity.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Azerbaijan Alim Bayel said the Kazakh side had proposed restoring passenger services on the Kuryk–Baku–Kuryk ferry route, which was suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Bayel, around 1,500 passengers used the ferry service annually before its suspension. He expressed confidence that demand could be higher when the route resumes, as travel and tourism links between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have expanded in recent years. The resumption of the ferry line, he said, will give impetus to the development of passenger traffic between the two countries, strengthen tourism exchange and expand the opportunities of the Middle Corridor.

The Azerbaijani side has supported Kazakhstan’s proposal, and the transport authorities of both countries have begun working on the necessary steps to restore passenger services as soon as possible.

A specific launch date has not yet been announced.

Ferry link to complement growing air connectivity

The proposed ferry service would add a maritime connection to an already expanding network of links between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. Currently, 37 flights connect Baku with Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Aktau and Atyrau, providing the main passenger connection between the two countries.

The revival of the Kuryk–Baku route would offer a different mode of travel across the Caspian, potentially creating additional opportunities for tourists and travelers interested in combining land and maritime journeys.

The route also has a broader regional significance because Kuryk is one of Kazakhstan’s key ports on the Caspian Sea and forms part of the country’s transport infrastructure supporting the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor.

The Middle Corridor connects China and Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Europe through the Caspian Sea. While its primary role is the movement of cargo, stronger passenger connectivity can contribute to wider economic and tourism ties along the same geographic corridor.

A route returning to a changing Caspian

The planned revival comes as Kazakhstan and other Caspian countries are paying increasing attention to changes in the sea’s water level. A newly emerged island was recently reported in the Caspian Sea amid a continued decline in water levels. The development has renewed attention to the environmental and economic consequences of the Caspian’s shallowing, including potential implications for maritime transport and coastal infrastructure.

The passenger ferry proposal therefore comes at a time when the Caspian is gaining importance as a regional transport link, while its changing physical conditions are creating new challenges for maritime activity.

World.title: Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists
World.content:
Civil rights activist and blogger Tornike Razmadze says Georgia’s Interior Ministry has summoned him to court to impose a fine or administrative detention because he insulted Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov in response to their insults against Georgian King Erekle II.

Georgia’s recently established Hate Speech Unit at the Interior Ministry has accused Razmadze of violating Article 166, Part 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The provision covers swearing in a public place and carries a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari ($185–1,110) or administrative detention for up to 20 days.

According to the activist, the case concerns a video he posted several weeks ago in which Russian propagandists discussed Erekle II, calling him a “king who crawled on his knees”. Margarita Simonyan, in particular, claimed that King Erekle had begged the Russians for help “on his knees” and that modern Georgians would likewise get down on their knees and ask Russia to take them under its protection.

Tornike Razmadze explains that this was why he used obscene language against Simonyan and Solovyov — more precisely, against their mothers.

According to the blogger, Simonyan and Solovyov effectively insulted the ruling Georgian Dream party as well. What angers him most is that, instead of taking offence at the Russian propagandists, the government wants to punish the person who insulted them. Razmadze sees this message from the authorities as the most important aspect of the whole case.

The activist also appealed to Georgia’s Public Defender (Ombudsman):

“I am not asking you for protection or support. I have one simple request: record your position on the case opened against me. I simply want to hear your position.”

However, the Interior Ministry’s Hate Speech Unit said the case had nothing to do with kings or propagandists. It said Tornike Razmadze was accused of insulting Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

“Insulting comments on social media by citizen Tornike Razmadze and Anna Bdeyan directed at Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze were identified. Administrative proceedings have been launched against them under Articles 166 and 173,” the Interior Ministry said.

The blogger’s lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili, in turn, says the Interior Ministry deliberately added Article 173, which concerns insulting a public official, to the charges. He says the original reports did not contain such wording. The lawyer is convinced that the case was opened specifically because of the insults directed at Simonyan and Solovyov.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) considers the case against Razmadze another example of restrictions on freedom of expression. The association says prosecuting people over statements made on social media violates their fundamental constitutional rights and freedom of expression.

What is the Hate Speech Unit

The new Hate Speech Unit at Georgia’s Interior Ministry began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the ministry, its main task is to identify public statements that demean human dignity or are offensive and may constitute administrative offences.

Over the past three months, the unit has fined dozens of people. Vakhtang Sanaya, a journalist and presenter on Formula TV, became the first person to receive a two-week administrative detention sentence. Activist Giorgi Akhobadze also received a one-month detention sentence for a Facebook post.
